The dataset covers 30 days in June 2013, with an overall mean daily conversion rate of 69.3% and a range from 58.0% to 82.0%. Day-to-day variation is non-trivial — a gap of roughly 24 percentage points between the worst and best days — which motivates the forecasting exercise.

docs.title: (4) Time Series Visualisation
docs.text:
Before building models, we visualise the daily conversion rate time series to understand its structure. This mirrors the exploratory step in the lecture before any model is fitted.

# Time series plot of daily conversion rate over the full sample
plot_ts <- daily |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = daily_cvr)) +
  geom_line(colour = palette_okabe_ito()[1], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = palette_okabe_ito()[1], size = 2) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(daily$daily_cvr),
    linetype   = "dashed",
    colour     = "grey50",
    linewidth  = 0.7
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x     = min(daily$date) + 1,
    y     = mean(daily$daily_cvr) + 0.015,
    label = paste0("Overall mean: ", percent(mean(daily$daily_cvr), accuracy = 0.1)),
    hjust = 0,
    size  = 3.5,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "5 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "Daily Conversion Rate on Expedia — June 2013",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the overall mean. Vertical patterns suggest a day-of-week effect.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Daily Conversion Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

plot_ts

The conversion rate fluctuates noticeably from day to day with no obvious upward or downward trend over the month. The dashed mean line at 69.3% provides a natural benchmark. Visual inspection suggests a mild day-of-week rhythm — weekend days (Saturday, Sunday) often sit above the mean — which motivates including is_weekend as a predictor in the OLS model.

# Bar chart: average conversion rate by day of week to verify the weekend pattern
plot_dow <- daily |>
  group_by(day_of_week) |>
  summarise(mean_cvr = mean(daily_cvr), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    day_of_week = factor(
      day_of_week,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day_of_week, y = mean_cvr, fill = day_of_week)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(daily$daily_cvr),
    linetype   = "dashed",
    colour     = "grey50"
  ) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.85)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Average Daily Conversion Rate by Day of Week",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the overall mean.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Mean Conversion Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )

plot_dow

Saturday and Sunday consistently record the highest average conversion rates, roughly 4–6 percentage points above the weekday average. This pattern supports the inclusion of is_weekend as a predictor in the OLS model.

docs.title: (5) Train / Test Split
docs.text:
We use a time-based split, consistent with how forecasting models would be used in practice: we fit on earlier data and evaluate on data the model has never seen. Using a random split would allow the model to learn from future observations, which produces optimistically biased error estimates.

The first 21 days (June 1–21) form the training set; the final 9 days (June 22–30) form the test set. This gives a roughly 70/30 split — a common convention that leaves enough test days to compute stable error metrics while retaining sufficient training history for the rolling-window models.

# Define the split date
split_date <- as.Date("2013-06-22")

# Training set: days strictly before the split date
train <- daily |> filter(date < split_date)

# Test set: days from the split date onward
test  <- daily |> filter(date >= split_date)

cat("Training set:", nrow(train), "days (", min(train$date), "to", max(train$date), ")\n")
cat("Test set:    ", nrow(test),  "days (", min(test$date),  "to", max(test$date),  ")\n")

Training set: 21 days ( 2013-06-01 to 2013-06-21 )
Test set:     9 days  ( 2013-06-22 to 2013-06-30 )

Why is a time-based split more realistic than a random split for this forecasting problem?

A random split would allow training observations from, say, June 25 to inform predictions for June 20. In practice, a forecaster on June 20 cannot observe what happens on June 25. By splitting on a calendar boundary, we ensure that every training observation precedes every test observation, exactly mirroring the information constraint a real forecaster faces.

docs.title: (6) Building the Four Prediction Models
docs.text: We now construct four models. For each model, we compute predictions on the test set only. All predictors use information that would be available before the target day, which is the core requirement of a valid forecasting exercise.

docs.title: Model 1: Lag-1 (Yesterday's Rate)
docs.text:
The lag-1 model predicts tomorrow's conversion rate using today's observed rate. It is the simplest possible time-series model and often performs surprisingly well when outcomes are autocorrelated.

# Compute lag-1 predictions on the full daily series (shifted by one day)
# The prediction for day t is the observed rate on day t-1
daily_with_preds <- daily |>
  mutate(
    pred_lag1 = lag(daily_cvr, n = 1)
  )

docs.title: Model 2: Trailing 3-Day Average
docs.text:
The trailing 3-day average smooths short-term noise by averaging the three most recent observations. slide_dbl() from the slider package computes this with an explicit look-back window; .before = 3 and .complete = TRUE ensure we only use the three days immediately before day t (not including day t itself).

# Trailing 3-day average: mean of the 3 days immediately before day t
# slide_dbl() with .before = 3 and .after = -1 creates a window of [t-3, t-1]
daily_with_preds <- daily_with_preds |>
  mutate(
    pred_trail3 = slide_dbl(
      daily_cvr,
      mean,
      .before   = 3,
      .after    = -1,
      .complete = TRUE
    )
  )

docs.title: Model 3: Historical (Cumulative) Mean
docs.text:
The historical mean uses the average of all days observed up to (but not including) day t. Unlike the trailing average, it never forgets older observations. As the window grows, this estimate stabilises and becomes equivalent to using the overall training mean.

# Historical mean: cumulative mean of all days before day t
# We use slide_dbl() with .before = Inf to include the entire history
# .after = -1 ensures day t itself is excluded from the calculation
daily_with_preds <- daily_with_preds |>
  mutate(
    pred_hist = slide_dbl(
      daily_cvr,
      mean,
      .before   = Inf,
      .after    = -1,
      .complete = FALSE
    )
  )

docs.title: Model 4: OLS Regression
docs.text:
The OLS model uses three predictors: the lag-1 conversion rate (the most recent signal), is_weekend (1 for Saturday/Sunday, 0 otherwise), and avg_booking_window (the mean search lead time for that day). All three are observable before the outcome is realized.

Critically, the OLS model is fitted on the training set only, and its coefficients are then applied to the test set. This is the correct procedure: fitting on the full dataset would allow test-set information to leak into the model, producing over-optimistic error estimates.

# Prepare lag-1 values in the training and test sets
# (lag-1 must be constructed from the full series to avoid NA at the split boundary)
train_ols <- daily_with_preds |>
  filter(date < split_date) |>
  drop_na(pred_lag1)           # lag-1 is NA for the very first day; drop that row

test_ols <- daily_with_preds |>
  filter(date >= split_date) |>
  drop_na(pred_lag1)

# Fit OLS on the training set
# Outcome  : daily_cvr (daily conversion rate)
# Predictors: pred_lag1 (yesterday's rate), is_weekend, avg_booking_window
ols_model <- lm(
  daily_cvr ~ pred_lag1 + is_weekend + avg_booking_window,
  data = train_ols
)

summary(ols_model)

Call:
lm(formula = daily_cvr ~ pred_lag1 + is_weekend + avg_booking_window,
   data = train_ols)

(Intercept)         0.48231    0.09871   4.886  0.00014 ***

Multiple R-squared:  0.3821,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2662

The OLS model explains approximately 38% of the variance in the training set (R² = 0.38). The is_weekend coefficient is positive and statistically significant, consistent with the exploratory finding that weekend days convert at a higher rate. The lag-1 coefficient is positive but only marginally significant, and the booking window coefficient is small and not significant, suggesting limited incremental predictive value beyond the other two predictors in this short sample.

# Generate OLS predictions on the test set using the training-fit model
test_ols <- test_ols |>
  mutate(pred_ols = predict(ols_model, newdata = test_ols))

docs.title: (7) Assembling the Test-Set Predictions
docs.text:
We join all four sets of predictions onto the test rows, then pivot to long format for a unified evaluation workflow.

# Merge the OLS predictions back into the full predictions table
# Then filter to the test set only, keeping all four prediction columns
test_preds <- daily_with_preds |>
  filter(date >= split_date) |>
  left_join(
    test_ols |> select(date, pred_ols),
    by = "date"
  ) |>
  drop_na(pred_lag1)   # first test row may have NA lag-1 if split falls exactly on day 2

# Pivot to long format so all models can be evaluated in one pipeline
test_long <- test_preds |>
  select(date, daily_cvr, pred_lag1, pred_trail3, pred_hist, pred_ols) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = starts_with("pred_"),
    names_to  = "model",
    values_to = "prediction"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(
      model,
      pred_lag1   = "Lag-1",
      pred_trail3 = "Trailing 3-Day Avg",
      pred_hist   = "Historical Mean",
      pred_ols    = "OLS"
    ),
    model = factor(model, levels = c("Lag-1", "Trailing 3-Day Avg", "Historical Mean", "OLS"))
  )

docs.title: (8) Computing Forecast Error Metrics
docs.text:
We compute three standard error metrics for each model on the test set:

  • MAE (Mean Absolute Error): the average absolute difference between predicted and actual conversion rate. Directly interpretable in percentage-point units.
  • RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): like MAE but penalises large errors more heavily. More sensitive to occasional big misses.
  • MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error): expresses the average error as a percentage of the actual value, making it comparable across different outcome scales.
# Compute MAE, RMSE, and MAPE for each model on the test set
model_metrics <- test_long |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    MAE  = mean(abs(prediction - daily_cvr), na.rm = TRUE),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((prediction - daily_cvr)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    MAPE = mean(abs((prediction - daily_cvr) / daily_cvr), na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(MAE)

model_metrics

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model                 MAE   RMSE  MAPE
  <fct>               <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 OLS                0.0312 0.0378  4.49
2 Lag-1              0.0381 0.0462  5.48
3 Trailing 3-Day Avg 0.0402 0.0489  5.79
4 Historical Mean    0.0447 0.0531  6.43

# Visualise: grouped bar chart of MAE, RMSE, MAPE by model
metrics_long <- model_metrics |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(MAE, RMSE, MAPE),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("MAE", "RMSE", "MAPE")))

plot_metrics <- metrics_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = value, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(value, 3)),
    vjust  = -0.4,
    size   = 3,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    title    = "Forecast Accuracy Metrics by Model (Test Set)",
    subtitle = "Lower values indicate better forecast accuracy.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

plot_metrics

The OLS model achieves the lowest error on all three metrics. Its MAE of 3.12 percentage points means that, on average, the predicted conversion rate is within about 3 percentage points of the actual rate — a margin that is operationally meaningful. The Historical Mean performs worst, reflecting the fact that a static average does not adapt to short-term fluctuations. The Lag-1 and Trailing 3-Day models sit in the middle.

docs.title: (9) Benchmarking Against a Random Baseline
docs.text:
The lecture emphasises benchmarking model performance against a random baseline. A model is only useful if it beats a naive guess. Here, we define the random baseline as drawing predictions from a uniform distribution over the observed range of daily conversion rates in the training set. We repeat this 1,000 times and compute the average MAE across simulations to obtain a stable estimate of random performance.

set.seed(42)

# Define the range of the outcome in the training set
cvr_min <- min(train$daily_cvr)
cvr_max <- max(train$daily_cvr)

n_test <- nrow(test_preds |> drop_na(pred_lag1))

# Simulate 1,000 random forecast sets and compute MAE for each
random_maes <- replicate(
  1000,
  {
    rand_preds <- runif(n_test, min = cvr_min, max = cvr_max)
    mean(abs(rand_preds - (test_preds |> drop_na(pred_lag1) |> pull(daily_cvr))))
  }
)

random_baseline_mae <- mean(random_maes)

cat("Random baseline MAE (mean over 1,000 simulations):", round(random_baseline_mae, 4), "\n")
cat("OLS model MAE:                                    ", round(filter(model_metrics, model == "OLS")$MAE, 4), "\n")
cat("Improvement over random baseline:                 ",
    percent((random_baseline_mae - filter(model_metrics, model == "OLS")$MAE) / random_baseline_mae, accuracy = 0.1), "\n")

Random baseline MAE (mean over 1,000 simulations): 0.0731
OLS model MAE:                                     0.0312
Improvement over random baseline:                  57.3%

All four models substantially outperform the random baseline (MAE ≈ 0.073). The OLS model reduces error by approximately 57% relative to random guessing, confirming that the historical structure of the data is genuinely informative for prediction.

docs.title: (10) Visualising Predictions vs Actuals on the Test Set
docs.text:
Finally, we plot predicted versus actual conversion rates over the test period to visualise where each model tracks the outcome well and where it diverges. This plot mirrors the forecasting visualisation style from the lecture.

# Line plot: predicted vs actual daily conversion rate on the test set
plot_preds <- test_long |>
  drop_na(prediction) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date)) +
  # Actual values as a thick black line
  geom_line(
    data   = test_preds |> drop_na(pred_lag1),
    aes(y  = daily_cvr),
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data   = test_preds |> drop_na(pred_lag1),
    aes(y  = daily_cvr),
    colour = "black",
    size   = 2.5
  ) +
  # Model predictions as coloured lines
  geom_line(
    aes(y = prediction, colour = model),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype  = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = prediction, colour = model),
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_colour_okabe_ito(name = "Model") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "2 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "Predicted vs Actual Daily Conversion Rate — Test Period (June 22–30)",
    subtitle = "Black line = actual rate. Dashed coloured lines = model predictions.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Daily Conversion Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "bottom"
  )

plot_preds

The OLS model tracks the actual conversion rate most closely, particularly on days with large swings. The Historical Mean barely moves across the test period, reflecting its inability to adapt to recent shifts. The Lag-1 and Trailing 3-Day models show some responsiveness to daily fluctuations but tend to lag behind the actual rate by one or more days.

docs.title: 1. Research Question
docs.text:
• Our research question is: can we predict the next day's hotel booking conversion rate on Expedia using historical patterns and observable search characteristics available before the outcome is realised?
  • This question matters operationally because conversion rate is a direct driver of platform revenue, and a reliable daily forecast would allow Expedia to dynamically adjust ranking algorithms, set realistic targets for promotional interventions, and anticipate revenue shortfalls before they occur.

docs.title: 2. Data & Approach
docs.text:
• We used the Expedia hotel search dataset, aggregated from 158,269 listing-level observations to a daily time series of 30 observations covering June 2013.
  • The outcome variable is daily_cvr — the share of clicked listings on each day that resulted in a booking — which ranges from 58.0% to 82.0% with a mean of 69.3%.
  • We applied a $500 price cap and restricted to clicked listings (consistent with Demo 1) before aggregating; two daily predictors were also computed: avg_booking_window (mean search lead time for that day) and is_weekend (Saturday or Sunday indicator).
  • The data were split chronologically: the first 21 days (June 1–21) formed the training set and the final 9 days (June 22–30) formed the test set, mirroring how a real forecasting model would be deployed — trained on past data, evaluated on future data it never observed.
  • We built and evaluated four models: a Lag-1 model (yesterday's rate), a Trailing 3-Day Average, a Historical (Cumulative) Mean, and an OLS regression with three predictors (pred_lag1, is_weekend, avg_booking_window).
  • Model accuracy was assessed on the test set using MAE, RMSE, and MAPE, and all four models were benchmarked against a random baseline that draws predictions from a uniform distribution over the training-set outcome range.

docs.title: 3. Preliminary Findings
docs.text:
• The OLS model achieves the best forecast accuracy on all three metrics. Its test-set MAE of 3.12 percentage points means the predicted conversion rate is within roughly 3 points of the actual rate on a typical day — a margin that is operationally useful for day-ahead planning.
  • All four models substantially outperform the random baseline (MAE ≈ 7.31 percentage points), with the OLS model reducing error by approximately 57% relative to random guessing; this confirms that the historical structure of the data contains genuine predictive signal.
  • The Historical Mean performs worst among the four models (MAE = 4.47 pp), because it does not adapt to recent fluctuations — as the cumulative mean stabilises, it effectively converges to a fixed constant that ignores short-term dynamics.
  • Weekend days convert at a systematically higher rate (approximately 4–6 percentage points above the weekday average), and the OLS coefficient on is_weekend is statistically significant (p = 0.037), confirming that day-of-week structure is a genuine predictive feature rather than noise.
  • The lag-1 predictor provides useful but limited signal on its own: its OLS coefficient is positive and directionally correct but only marginally significant (p = 0.080) in a 20-observation training set, likely because the short window limits statistical power rather than because the signal is absent.

docs.title: 4. Assumptions & Limitations
docs.text:
• We assume that a 30-day sample is sufficient to estimate meaningful daily patterns, but this is a strong assumption: 30 observations is a very small time series, and both the model coefficients and the error metrics should be interpreted with caution given this sample size.
  • The avg_booking_window predictor is computed from clicked listings on the target day; in a real deployment, this would require using search-log data observed earlier in the day, introducing a timing assumption that we have not verified against the actual data collection process.
  • The test set contains only 9 days, which means the MAE and MAPE estimates themselves are subject to considerable sampling variability; a single anomalous day can shift the metrics by several percentage points.
  • Our analysis treats each day as independent, but conversion rates on consecutive days are likely correlated (as suggested by the positive lag-1 coefficient); more sophisticated time-series models (e.g., ARIMA) might better capture this autocorrelation structure.

docs.title: 5. Open Questions for Feedback
docs.text:
• The OLS model's R² of 0.38 on the training set suggests moderate in-sample fit; should we explore whether adding day-of-week dummies (Monday through Sunday) rather than just the binary is_weekend indicator would improve test-set accuracy, given the exploratory finding that within-weekday variation is also present?
  • We used the final 9 days as a single test set; would it be more rigorous to use a rolling origin (expanding window) evaluation that produces one forecast error per day across a longer horizon, reducing the influence of any particular 9-day stretch?
  • The historical mean model converges to a fixed constant as the training window grows; should we replace it with a weighted average that gives more weight to recent observations (e.g., exponentially weighted mean), which would be more comparable to the trailing average while still using the full history?

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text:
• We would extend the dataset to cover multiple months or years, which would allow us to estimate a model on a larger training set, produce more stable error estimates on a longer test set, and test whether seasonal patterns (e.g., summer vs winter booking behaviour) are present.
  • We would add day-of-week dummies as individual indicator variables (replacing the binary is_weekend) and explore whether position — the hotel's rank in search results — provides incremental predictive signal at the daily level, given the finding from Demo 1 that position is associated with click and conversion rates.
  • We would implement a rolling-origin evaluation scheme (re-fitting the OLS model at each forecast origin with an expanding training window) to obtain a more robust and generalisable assessment of model performance across the full available sample.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: This analysis asked whether Expedia's daily booking conversion rate — the share of hotel listings that users click on and then book — can be reliably predicted one day ahead using historical patterns and observable search data. We built and tested four models on 30 days of June 2013 data, using the first 21 days for training and the final 9 days for out-of-sample testing. The best-performing model, an OLS regression incorporating yesterday's conversion rate, a weekend indicator, and the average user booking lead time, predicted the daily conversion rate within approximately 3 percentage points on average — a 57% improvement over random guessing. These findings demonstrate that day-ahead conversion forecasting is feasible with even simple models, and that a small set of observable features can meaningfully reduce uncertainty for platform planning teams.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Day-ahead forecasting is viable at the daily level. The OLS model's mean absolute error of 3.1 percentage points on the held-out test period represents a substantial and actionable reduction in uncertainty compared to having no model at all (random baseline MAE: 7.3 pp).
  • Weekend days convert at a structurally higher rate. Saturday and Sunday conversion rates average 4–6 percentage points above weekday rates; this pattern is stable enough across the training set to improve test-set predictions when incorporated as a model feature.
  • Simple models beat static baselines, but more data is needed for confident deployment. All four forecasting models outperform a random baseline, but the test set covers only 9 days, meaning the error estimates themselves carry uncertainty; a longer evaluation period is needed before committing to a production forecast.

docs.title: Business Implications
docs.text:
• Conversion forecasts can support dynamic listing prioritisation. If Expedia can predict that tomorrow's conversion rate will be significantly below average — for example, on a Monday following a high-converting weekend — the ranking algorithm could proactively surface higher-quality listings or trigger promotional interventions to partially offset the expected dip.
  • Weekend demand patterns are an underexploited signal. The consistent weekend uplift in conversion rate is predictable and systematic; Expedia could use this pattern to adjust staffing, promotional spend, and partner communications on a weekly cadence rather than reacting to outcomes after the fact.
  • Forecast error magnitude sets the floor for action thresholds. An MAE of roughly 3 percentage points means that predictions within a ±3 pp band of the actual rate should be treated as "on target"; business decisions — such as triggering a price promotion or adjusting ranking weights — should only be activated when the forecast signals a deviation larger than this threshold.

docs.title: Recommended Actions
docs.text:
• Deploy the OLS model as a day-ahead conversion rate dashboard, updated each morning using the previous day's observed rate, the upcoming day's calendar features (weekend vs weekday), and early-morning search log data on booking lead times; monitor test-set MAE on a rolling 30-day basis to detect model drift.
  • Expand the training dataset to cover at least 6–12 months before committing to production deployment; a longer history will allow the model to capture seasonal variation in booking intent (e.g., summer travel peaks, holiday periods) and will produce more stable coefficient estimates and error metrics.
  • Commission a segmented forecast analysis that builds separate daily conversion rate models for distinct hotel segments (e.g., budget vs luxury, based on the clustering from Demo 1), since aggregate platform-level forecasts may mask segment-level dynamics that are more actionable for partner-facing account management teams.

# Naive comparison: promoted vs. non-promoted listings among all clicked rows
naive_compare <- expedia |>
  filter(!is.na(converted)) |>
  group_by(promotion_flag) |>
  summarise(
    n_clicked       = n(),
    conversion_rate = mean(converted, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_star        = mean(prop_starrating, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price       = mean(price_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_position    = mean(position, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(promotion_flag = if_else(promotion_flag == 1, "Promoted", "Not Promoted"))

The naive comparison shows that promoted listings have a 7.9-percentage-point higher conversion rate. But notice that promoted listings also appear in higher positions (11.3 vs. 19.8 on average) and have lower prices ($130 vs. $163). These are confounders: factors correlated with both the treatment (promotion flag) and the outcome (conversion). Because Expedia is more likely to show the promotion badge to hotels that are already performing well — lower-priced, better-positioned — we cannot attribute the higher conversion rate to the promotion alone. This is the same problem as the August–September before/after comparison in the DonorsChoose example: the groups differ in ways that have nothing to do with the intervention we want to study.

  filter(

    position       <= 5,
    prop_starrating == 3

  summarise(

Within this restricted subgroup, the conversion gap narrows to 4.6 percentage points (0.764 − 0.718). Prices and positions are now much more balanced between groups, suggesting that controlling for these confounders removes a large share of the naive bias. The remaining difference is a more credible — though still assumption-dependent — estimate of the promotion effect. The limitation: we cannot be certain that all confounders are controlled for. Perhaps promoted hotels within this subgroup also have better photos or more recent reviews. This is why model-based inference is only as good as our model of the world.

# Step 1: Take the clicked-only dataset as the "eligible population"

  select(

    srch_booking_window, converted

# Step 2: Randomly assign treatment (promotion displayed) vs. control
experiment_pool <- experiment_pool |>

docs.title: Expedia Case Demo 3: Does Promotion Cause Higher Conversion on Expedia?¶
Part A. Cleaning and Analysing Data¶
1. Introduction¶
docs.text:
Research Question: Does displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing cause a higher booking conversion rate among users who click on that listing on Expedia?

Method: This is a causal analysis. We begin by showing why a naive before/after or simple comparison of promoted vs. non-promoted listings is insufficient, then use the potential outcomes framework to formalise what we are estimating. We simulate a field experiment embedded in the Expedia platform — in which hotels are randomly assigned to display a promotion flag — and estimate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) as a difference in means. We also conduct a balance test, explore mid-funnel behaviour, and report the effect in absolute, relative, and standard-deviation units.

docs.title: (3) Why a Naive Comparison Fails¶
docs.text: Before building any causal model, we must show why simply comparing promoted vs. non-promoted listings in the raw data does not give us the causal effect.

docs.title: (4) Model-Based Inference: Controlling for Confounders¶
docs.text:
One way to approximate the causal effect is to hold confounders constant and compare promoted vs. non-promoted listings within homogeneous subgroups. This is model-based inference: we use our knowledge of the data-generating process to make the comparison fairer.

We know from the naive comparison that position and star rating are the main confounders. Among hotels shown in the top 5 positions with 3-star ratings, the hotels likely differ less in quality and placement, so the promotion flag itself becomes the main remaining source of variation.

docs.title: (5) Design-Based Inference: Simulating a Field Experiment¶
docs.text:
The gold standard for causal inference is a randomized experiment: assign the promotion flag randomly, so that promoted and non-promoted hotels are comparable in every other respect by design, not by assumption.

Because the Expedia dataset is observational, we simulate a field experiment embedded in the platform. We draw a random sample of clicked listings, randomly assign half to display a promotion flag (treatment) and half to keep it hidden (control), and then compare conversion rates. This mirrors the DonorsChoose randomization logic.

docs.title: (6) Balance Test¶
docs.text: Before estimating the treatment effect, we verify that random assignment produced comparable groups. A balance test checks whether the treatment and control groups look similar on pre-treatment characteristics. If randomisation worked, any differences should be small and consistent with chance variation.

docs.title: (7) Estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE)¶
docs.text: With groups confirmed as balanced, we can now estimate the causal effect of the promotion flag using the difference in means estimator: ATE = Ȳ(1) − Ȳ(0).

docs.title: (8) Is This a Big Effect? Interpreting Effect Size¶
docs.text: The lecture emphasises that knowing an effect is causal is only part of the story; we also need to assess whether it is practically meaningful.

docs.title: (9) Mid-Funnel Analysis: Where in the Journey Does the Promotion Help?¶
docs.text: The tutorial's Exercise 6 asks what happens inside the funnel — not just whether users completed, but where they dropped off or accelerated. We mirror this by asking: does the promotion flag change conversion differently for users at different stages of purchase intent (as proxied by booking window)?

docs.title: (10) Checking Experimental Assumptions¶
docs.text: The lecture identifies two main categories of assumptions that experiments rely on. We document the status of each for our simulated experiment.

docs.title: 1. Research Question¶
docs.text:
• Our research question is: does displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing on Expedia cause a higher booking conversion rate among users who click on that listing — and if so, how large is the effect and for which users is it strongest?
  • This question matters because the promotion flag is a platform-side intervention that Expedia controls directly; a credible causal estimate of its effect would inform decisions about which hotels to badge, when to display the flag, and how to target high-intent search sessions.

docs.title: 2. Data & Approach¶
docs.text:
• We used the Expedia hotel search dataset (158,269 listing-level observations), restricting to the 5,485 clicked listings for outcome analysis.
  • The outcome variable is converted (1 = clicked and booked, 0 = clicked but not booked); listings never clicked were excluded.
  • We first demonstrated why a naive comparison of promoted vs. non-promoted listings in the observational data is misleading: promoted listings appear in higher positions and at lower prices — both independent drivers of conversion — creating confounders that inflate the observed effect.
  • We then conducted a model-based inference check by restricting the sample to top-5-position, 3-star hotels, which partially controls for the main confounders and narrows the naive estimate from 7.9 pp to 4.6 pp.
  • We simulated a field experiment (design-based inference) by randomly assigning the promotion flag to 50% of clicked listings and confirmed group balance on six pre-treatment covariates.
  • We estimated the ATE as a difference in means (Ȳ(1) − Ȳ(0)) and reported the effect in absolute percentage points, relative terms, and standard deviation units, following the lecture's three-metric framework.
  • We conducted a mid-funnel analysis segmenting the ATE by booking urgency to identify where the promotion effect is strongest.

docs.title: 3. Preliminary Findings¶
docs.text:
• The naive comparison overstates the promotion effect by roughly 7 percentage points. The raw difference in conversion between promoted and non-promoted listings is 7.9 pp, but once we control for position and star rating (model-based inference) the estimate drops to 4.6 pp, and the randomised experiment estimates the true ATE at only 0.5 pp — illustrating how confounding can dramatically inflate observational comparisons.
  • The promotion flag generates a small but causally credible lift in conversion. The randomised ATE is +0.50 percentage points (67.9% vs. 67.4%), a relative increase of 0.74% and an effect size of 0.011 SD — consistent with the 0.01–0.05 SD range typical of large-scale digital A/B tests described in the lecture.
  • The effect is larger for last-minute searchers. The mid-funnel analysis shows a 0.90 pp lift for users searching within 7 days of check-in (relative: 1.05%), versus 0.50–0.60 pp for short-lead and long-lead users, suggesting that the promotion badge provides the strongest nudge to users who are already close to committing.
  • Balance testing confirms the randomisation worked. All six pre-treatment covariates (star rating, price, position, length of stay, party size, booking window) are nearly identical across groups, validating that the difference-in-means estimator is a credible causal estimate.
  • All major experimental assumptions are plausible given the platform context. The promotion flag is a server-side display change, making compliance issues and between-user spillovers unlikely, though the SUTVA assumption would need monitoring if promoted listings were shared on social media.

docs.title: 4. Assumptions & Limitations¶
docs.text:
• The experiment is simulated from observational data rather than conducted on the live platform; in a real field experiment, the random assignment mechanism would be embedded in Expedia's display logic, and compliance would be guaranteed by the platform rather than assumed.
  • We assumed SUTVA holds — that a user's conversion does not depend on whether other users in the same search session see a promotion. In practice, if users compare promoted and non-promoted listings side by side in the same search results page, the badge may have a relative rather than absolute effect.
  • The ATE is estimated across all clicked listings; it does not distinguish between different hotel quality tiers or search contexts beyond the urgency segmentation, and there may be meaningful effect heterogeneity that a single pooled estimate masks.
  • The simulated experiment uses 50% treatment probability, which is efficient for estimation but may not match the real-world constraint that only a subset of hotels are eligible for promotional badging due to pricing agreements with hotel partners.

docs.title: 5. Open Questions for Feedback¶
docs.text:
• Our mid-funnel analysis used booking window as the only segmentation variable — should we also examine whether the promotion effect differs by star rating tier, given that a badge on a 5-star listing may carry different credibility signals than the same badge on a 2-star listing?
  • The ATE of 0.5 pp is small in SD units but may be commercially significant at scale; what is the team's threshold for "actionable" effect size, and would a lift of this magnitude justify the cost of maintaining the promotional badging infrastructure?
  • We have not assessed whether the promotion flag creates any negative externalities — for instance, whether non-promoted listings in the same search session see a lower conversion rate when competing against a promoted listing, which would indicate that the badge redistributes rather than creates bookings.

docs.title: 6. Next Steps¶
docs.text:
• We would conduct a formal statistical significance test (t-test or equivalent) on the ATE to assess whether the observed 0.5-pp lift is distinguishable from random variation, given the sample size and the standard deviation of the conversion outcome.
  • We would run a heterogeneous treatment effects analysis by star rating, price tier, and device type to identify which hotel segments benefit most from the promotion flag, enabling Expedia to target the badge more precisely rather than applying it uniformly.
  • We would design a real field experiment embedded in the Expedia platform — with the promotion flag randomly assigned at the search-session level rather than the listing level — to test whether the SUTVA assumption holds when users see promoted and non-promoted listings side by side in the same results page.

docs.title: Executive Summary¶
docs.text: This analysis assessed whether displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing on Expedia causes a measurable increase in booking conversion — the share of users who click a listing and go on to book it. A naive comparison of promoted and non-promoted listings in historical data suggested a 7.9-percentage-point advantage for promoted hotels, but this overstates the true effect: promoted hotels also tend to appear in higher positions and at lower prices, both of which independently drive conversion. A simulated randomized experiment, in which the promotion badge was assigned by chance rather than by Expedia's existing algorithm, estimates the true causal effect at +0.50 percentage points — a small but credibly estimated lift that is consistent with the scale of effects typically observed in large digital A/B tests. The promotion badge produces the largest lift for last-minute searchers (+0.90 pp), who are already primed to book and appear to respond most strongly to value signals at the listing level.

docs.title: Key Insights¶
docs.text:
• The raw data misleads: confounders inflate the apparent promotion effect by more than 15-fold. The observational comparison attributes 7.9 pp of the conversion difference to the promotion badge, but the randomised experiment shows the true causal effect is only 0.50 pp — a 15× overestimate driven by position and price confounding.
  • The promotion badge works, but its effect is modest and highly context-dependent. The 0.50 pp overall lift is commercially meaningful at platform scale but is concentrated among last-minute searchers (0.90 pp lift), suggesting the badge is most effective as a closing signal for high-intent users rather than a general visibility driver.
  • Causal credibility requires experimental design, not just good data. The comparison of model-based inference (4.6 pp after subgroup restriction) versus design-based inference (0.50 pp from randomisation) illustrates that assumptions about which factors to control for can still leave substantial bias — only random assignment gives us a clean causal estimate.

docs.title: Business Implications¶
docs.text:
• Expedia's current promotion-badging algorithm may be rewarding hotels that would convert well anyway. If badges are preferentially shown to well-positioned, lower-priced hotels, the observed lift in the historical data reflects selection, not causation — meaning the badging system may not be generating as much incremental revenue as the raw data suggests.
  • Targeting the promotion badge toward last-minute, high-intent search sessions could amplify its commercial value. A 0.90-pp lift for last-minute searchers versus 0.50 pp overall implies that precision targeting — rather than broad application — would improve the return on the promotional badging investment.
  • Design-based causal analysis should become a standard component of Expedia's product evaluation process. The large gap between the naive and experimental estimates demonstrates that observational data alone cannot reliably quantify the effect of platform interventions; A/B testing infrastructure is a prerequisite for sound decision-making.

docs.title: Recommended Actions¶
docs.text:
• Run a live randomised A/B test on the promotion badge using Expedia's platform. Randomly assign the badge at the search-session level for a defined period and measure the causal lift in completed bookings, using this analysis as the pre-registered hypothesis and benchmark.
  • Pilot a targeting strategy that reserves the promotion badge for last-minute search sessions. Based on the mid-funnel ATE estimates, restrict badge display to users with booking windows under 7 days and compare booking revenue per search session against the current untargeted approach.
  • Commission a competitive-effects audit before scaling. Before broadening the promotion badge programme, measure whether promoted listings in the same results page displace bookings from adjacent non-promoted listings — if the badge redistributes rather than creates bookings, its aggregate revenue value is lower than the single-listing ATE implies.

docs.title: Expedia Case Demo 3: Does Promotion Cause Higher Conversion on Expedia?
Part A. Cleaning and Analysing Data
1. Introduction
docs.text:
Research Question: Does displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing cause a higher booking conversion rate among users who click on that listing on Expedia?

Method: This is a causal analysis. We begin by showing why a naive before/after or simple comparison of promoted vs. non-promoted listings is insufficient, then use the potential outcomes framework to formalise what we are estimating. We simulate a field experiment embedded in the Expedia platform — in which hotels are randomly assigned to display a promotion flag — and estimate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) as a difference in means. We also conduct a balance test, explore mid-funnel behaviour, and report the effect in absolute, relative, and standard-deviation units.

docs.title: (1) Load Libraries
docs.text:
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling and visualization
library(scales)      # formatting axis labels (e.g., percent)
library(patchwork)   # combining multiple plots
library(ggokabeito)  # colour-blind-friendly palette (course default)
library(lubridate)   # date parsing
library(janitor)     # clean_names(), get_dupes()

docs.title: (2) Load the Dataset
docs.text:
expedia <- read_csv("data/expedia.csv")

# Create the conversion indicator on the full dataset before any filtering.
# converted = 1: user clicked AND booked (successful conversion)
# converted = 0: user clicked but did NOT book (failed conversion)
# converted = NA: user never clicked (not applicable)
expedia <- expedia |>
  mutate(
    converted = case_when(
      click_bool == 1 & booking_bool == 1 ~ 1,
      click_bool == 1 & booking_bool == 0 ~ 0,
      .default = NA
    )
  )

docs.title: (3) Why a Naive Comparison Fails
docs.text:
Before building any causal model, we must show why simply comparing promoted vs. non-promoted listings in the raw data does not give us the causal effect.

# Naive comparison: promoted vs. non-promoted listings among all clicked rows
naive_compare <- expedia |>
  filter(!is.na(converted)) |>
  group_by(promotion_flag) |>
  summarise(
    n_clicked       = n(),
    conversion_rate = mean(converted, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_star        = mean(prop_starrating, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price       = mean(price_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_position    = mean(position, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(promotion_flag = if_else(promotion_flag == 1, "Promoted", "Not Promoted"))

naive_compare

| promotion_flag | n_clicked | conversion_rate | avg_star | avg_price | avg_position |
|----------------|-----------|-----------------|----------|-----------|--------------|
| Not Promoted   |      5011 |           0.662 |     2.74 |    163.2  |        19.8  |
| Promoted       |       474 |           0.741 |     2.98 |    130.4  |        11.3  |

The naive comparison shows that promoted listings have a 7.9-percentage-point higher conversion rate. But notice that promoted listings also appear in higher positions (11.3 vs. 19.8 on average) and have lower prices ($130 vs. $163). These are confounders: factors correlated with both the treatment (promotion flag) and the outcome (conversion). Because Expedia is more likely to show the promotion badge to hotels that are already performing well — lower-priced, better-positioned — we cannot attribute the higher conversion rate to the promotion alone. This is the same problem as the August–September before/after comparison in the DonorsChoose example: the groups differ in ways that have nothing to do with the intervention we want to study.

# Visualise the confounder imbalance
plot_confound <- naive_compare |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(avg_star, avg_price, avg_position),
    names_to  = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(variable = recode(
    variable,
    avg_star     = "Avg. Star Rating",
    avg_price    = "Avg. Price (USD)",
    avg_position = "Avg. Listing Position"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = promotion_flag, y = value, fill = promotion_flag)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    title    = "Confounder Imbalance: Promoted vs. Non-Promoted Listings (Observational Data)",
    subtitle = "Promoted listings have lower prices and higher positions — both drive conversion independently",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Average Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40")
  )

plot_confound

The chart confirms the confounder story: promoted listings are systematically different from non-promoted ones in multiple ways. Any naive difference in conversion is therefore confounded — it mixes the effect of the promotion badge with the effect of position and price.

docs.title: (4) Model-Based Inference: Controlling for Confounders
docs.text:
One way to approximate the causal effect is to hold confounders constant and compare promoted vs. non-promoted listings within homogeneous subgroups. This is model-based inference: we use our knowledge of the data-generating process to make the comparison fairer.

We know from the naive comparison that position and star rating are the main confounders. Among hotels shown in the top 5 positions with 3-star ratings, the hotels likely differ less in quality and placement, so the promotion flag itself becomes the main remaining source of variation.

# Model-based inference: restrict to top-5 positions, 3-star hotels
# Within this subgroup, promotion assignment is less likely to reflect other quality differences
model_based <- expedia |>
  filter(
    !is.na(converted),
    position       <= 5,
    prop_starrating == 3
  ) |>
  group_by(promotion_flag) |>
  summarise(
    n_clicked       = n(),
    conversion_rate = mean(converted, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price       = mean(price_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_position    = mean(position, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(promotion_flag = if_else(promotion_flag == 1, "Promoted", "Not Promoted"))

model_based

| promotion_flag | n_clicked | conversion_rate | avg_price | avg_position |
|----------------|-----------|-----------------|-----------|--------------|
| Not Promoted   |       312 |           0.718 |    141.3  |         2.9  |
| Promoted       |        89 |           0.764 |    138.1  |         2.7  |

Within this restricted subgroup, the conversion gap narrows to 4.6 percentage points (0.764 − 0.718). Prices and positions are now much more balanced between groups, suggesting that controlling for these confounders removes a large share of the naive bias. The remaining difference is a more credible — though still assumption-dependent — estimate of the promotion effect. The limitation: we cannot be certain that all confounders are controlled for. Perhaps promoted hotels within this subgroup also have better photos or more recent reviews. This is why model-based inference is only as good as our model of the world.

docs.title: (5) Design-Based Inference: Simulating a Field Experiment
docs.text:
The gold standard for causal inference is a randomized experiment: assign the promotion flag randomly, so that promoted and non-promoted hotels are comparable in every other respect by design, not by assumption.

Because the Expedia dataset is observational, we simulate a field experiment embedded in the platform. We draw a random sample of clicked listings, randomly assign half to display a promotion flag (treatment) and half to keep it hidden (control), and then compare conversion rates. This mirrors the DonorsChoose randomization logic.

set.seed(42)

# Step 1: Take the clicked-only dataset as the "eligible population"
# (users who reached the listing detail page — the point at which a
#  promotion badge would be displayed)
experiment_pool <- expedia |>
  filter(!is.na(converted)) |>
  select(
    srch_id, prop_id, prop_starrating, prop_review_score,
    price_usd, position, srch_length_of_stay, srch_adults_count,
    srch_booking_window, converted
  )

# Step 2: Randomly assign treatment (promotion displayed) vs. control
experiment_pool <- experiment_pool |>
  mutate(
    treatment = if_else(runif(n()) < 0.5, 1L, 0L),
    variation = if_else(treatment == 1, "Treatment (Promoted)", "Control (Not Promoted)")
  )

nrow(experiment_pool)

[1] 5485

# Step 3: Quick peek at the experiment data
experiment_pool |>
  count(variation)

| variation              |    n |
|------------------------|------|
| Control (Not Promoted) | 2755 |
| Treatment (Promoted)   | 2730 |

docs.title: (6) Balance Test
docs.text:
Before estimating the treatment effect, we verify that random assignment produced comparable groups. A balance test checks whether the treatment and control groups look similar on pre-treatment characteristics. If randomisation worked, any differences should be small and consistent with chance variation.

# Balance table: compare means of pre-treatment covariates across groups
balance_table <- experiment_pool |>
  group_by(variation) |>
  summarise(
    n                   = n(),
    avg_star_rating     = mean(prop_starrating,      na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price_usd       = mean(price_usd,            na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_position        = mean(position,             na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_length_of_stay  = mean(srch_length_of_stay,  na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_adults          = mean(srch_adults_count,     na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_booking_window  = mean(srch_booking_window,   na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

balance_table

| variation              |    n | avg_star_rating | avg_price_usd | avg_position | avg_length_of_stay | avg_adults | avg_booking_window |
|------------------------|------|-----------------|---------------|--------------|---------------------|------------|--------------------|
| Control (Not Promoted) | 2755 |            2.77 |        155.5  |         20.2 |                2.06 |       2.03 |              22.5  |
| Treatment (Promoted)   | 2730 |            2.76 |        154.9  |         20.1 |                2.05 |       2.02 |              22.4  |

# Visualise balance across key covariates
plot_balance <- balance_table |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = starts_with("avg_"),
    names_to  = "covariate",
    values_to = "mean_value"
  ) |>
  mutate(covariate = recode(
    covariate,
    avg_star_rating    = "Star Rating",
    avg_price_usd      = "Price (USD)",
    avg_position       = "Listing Position",
    avg_length_of_stay = "Length of Stay",
    avg_adults         = "Adults in Party",
    avg_booking_window = "Booking Window (days)"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variation, y = mean_value, fill = variation)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ covariate, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    title    = "Balance Test: Pre-Treatment Covariate Means by Experimental Group",
    subtitle = "Groups should look similar on all covariates — differences here are due to chance",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Group Mean"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_balance

The balance table confirms that the treatment and control groups are nearly identical on all six pre-treatment covariates. This is what we expect from random assignment: any remaining differences are pure noise, not systematic. We can therefore attribute any difference in conversion rates to the promotion flag itself, not to pre-existing differences between groups.

docs.title: (7) Estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
docs.text:
With groups confirmed as balanced, we can now estimate the causal effect of the promotion flag using the difference in means estimator: ATE = Ȳ(1) − Ȳ(0).

# Compute conversion rate and SD by treatment group
ate_summary <- experiment_pool |>
  group_by(variation) |>
  summarise(
    n               = n(),
    conversion_rate = mean(converted, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_conversion   = sd(converted,   na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ate_summary

| variation              |    n | conversion_rate | sd_conversion |
|------------------------|------|-----------------|---------------|
| Control (Not Promoted) | 2755 |           0.674 |         0.469 |
| Treatment (Promoted)   | 2730 |           0.679 |         0.467 |

# Extract values for effect-size calculations
cvr_control   <- ate_summary |> filter(variation == "Control (Not Promoted)") |> pull(conversion_rate)
cvr_treatment <- ate_summary |> filter(variation == "Treatment (Promoted)")   |> pull(conversion_rate)
sd_control    <- ate_summary |> filter(variation == "Control (Not Promoted)") |> pull(sd_conversion)

# ATE in absolute percentage points
ate_pp <- cvr_treatment - cvr_control

# ATE as a relative (percentage) change
ate_relative <- ate_pp / cvr_control

# ATE in standard deviation units (effect size)
ate_sd_units <- ate_pp / sd_control

tibble(
  metric       = c("ATE (percentage points)", "Relative change (%)", "Effect size (SD units)"),
  value        = c(ate_pp * 100, ate_relative * 100, ate_sd_units)
) |>
  mutate(value = round(value, 3))

| metric                   |  value |
|--------------------------|--------|
| ATE (percentage points)  |  0.500 |
| Relative change (%)      |  0.742 |
| Effect size (SD units)   |  0.011 |

# Visualise the ATE
plot_ate <- ate_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variation, y = conversion_rate, fill = variation)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(conversion_rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.4, size = 4
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = cvr_control + 0.02, yend = cvr_control + 0.02),
    linewidth = 0.6, colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 1.5, y = cvr_control + 0.035,
    label = paste0("ATE = +", round(ate_pp * 100, 2), " pp"),
    size = 3.5, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.8)) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    title    = "Estimated Causal Effect of Promotion Flag on Booking Conversion",
    subtitle = "Difference in means from randomized experiment (ATE = Ȳ(1) − Ȳ(0))",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Conversion Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_ate

The randomized experiment estimates the ATE at +0.50 percentage points (67.9% vs. 67.4%). The relative increase is 0.74%, and the effect size in standard deviation units is 0.011 SD — consistent with the range of 0.01–0.05 SD that the lecture describes as typical for large-scale digital experiments.

docs.title: (8) Is This a Big Effect? Interpreting Effect Size
docs.text:
The lecture emphasises that knowing an effect is causal is only part of the story; we also need to assess whether it is practically meaningful.

# Summary of effect size interpretation
effect_interp <- tibble(
  dimension         = c(
    "Absolute (pp)",
    "Relative (%)",
    "SD units",
    "Scale interpretation"
  ),
  value             = c(
    paste0(round(ate_pp * 100, 2), " percentage points"),
    paste0(round(ate_relative * 100, 2), "%"),
    paste0(round(ate_sd_units, 3), " SD"),
    "Typical for large-scale digital A/B tests (0.01–0.05 SD)"
  ),
  interpretation    = c(
    "For every 200 users who click a listing, 1 additional booking is generated by the promotion",
    "Less than 1% relative lift — the underlying conversion rate barely moves",
    "Very small fraction of natural variation in donor behaviour",
    "Small but potentially valuable at platform scale with millions of daily searches"
  )
)

effect_interp |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Dimension", "Value", "Interpretation"),
    align     = c("l", "l", "l")
  )

At first glance, 0.5 percentage points sounds modest. But consider Expedia's scale: with millions of hotel searches each day, even a 0.5-pp lift in conversion translates into thousands of additional bookings. The lecture's DonorsChoose example showed a similar pattern: a 0.7-pp lift in sharing that appeared small in absolute terms but was commercially meaningful at platform scale.

docs.title: (9) Mid-Funnel Analysis: Where in the Journey Does the Promotion Help?
docs.text:
The tutorial's Exercise 6 asks what happens inside the funnel — not just whether users completed, but where they dropped off or accelerated. We mirror this by asking: does the promotion flag change conversion differently for users at different stages of purchase intent (as proxied by booking window)?

# Segment the ATE by booking urgency: does promotion help more for last-minute or long-lead users?
midfunnel_ate <- experiment_pool |>
  mutate(
    urgency_group = case_when(
      srch_booking_window <= 7  ~ "Last-Minute (0-7 days)",
      srch_booking_window <= 28 ~ "Short-Lead (8-28 days)",
      .default                  ~ "Long-Lead (29+ days)"
    ),
    urgency_group = factor(
      urgency_group,
      levels = c("Last-Minute (0-7 days)", "Short-Lead (8-28 days)", "Long-Lead (29+ days)")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(urgency_group, variation) |>
  summarise(
    n               = n(),
    conversion_rate = mean(converted, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Compute ATE within each urgency segment
midfunnel_ate_wide <- midfunnel_ate |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = variation,
    values_from = c(n, conversion_rate)
  ) |>
  rename(
    n_control        = `n_Control (Not Promoted)`,
    n_treatment      = `n_Treatment (Promoted)`,
    cvr_control      = `conversion_rate_Control (Not Promoted)`,
    cvr_treatment    = `conversion_rate_Treatment (Promoted)`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    ate_pp           = cvr_treatment - cvr_control,
    ate_relative_pct = ate_pp / cvr_control * 100
  )

midfunnel_ate_wide |>
  mutate(
    cvr_control      = percent(cvr_control,      accuracy = 0.1),
    cvr_treatment    = percent(cvr_treatment,     accuracy = 0.1),
    ate_pp           = paste0(round(ate_pp * 100, 2), " pp"),
    ate_relative_pct = paste0(round(ate_relative_pct, 2), "%")

    ),

The mid-funnel breakdown reveals a nuanced pattern: the promotion flag generates a slightly larger lift for last-minute searchers (0.90 pp, 1.05% relative) than for short-lead or long-lead users. This makes intuitive sense — users searching close to check-in are already primed to book and a promotion badge may provide the final nudge they need. For long-lead browsers, the promotion produces a smaller lift because they are still in an exploratory phase and less responsive to scarcity or value signals at the listing level.

docs.title: 1. Research Question
docs.text:
• Our research question is: does displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing on Expedia cause a higher booking conversion rate among users who click on that listing — and if so, how large is the effect and for which users is it strongest?
  • This question matters because the promotion flag is a platform-side intervention that Expedia controls directly; a credible causal estimate of its effect would inform decisions about which hotels to badge, when to display the flag, and how to target high-intent search sessions.

docs.title: 2. Data & Approach
docs.text:
• We used the Expedia hotel search dataset (158,269 listing-level observations), restricting to the 5,485 clicked listings for outcome analysis.
  • The outcome variable is converted (1 = clicked and booked, 0 = clicked but not booked); listings never clicked were excluded.
  • We first demonstrated why a naive comparison of promoted vs. non-promoted listings in the observational data is misleading: promoted listings appear in higher positions and at lower prices — both independent drivers of conversion — creating confounders that inflate the observed effect.
  • We then conducted a model-based inference check by restricting the sample to top-5-position, 3-star hotels, which partially controls for the main confounders and narrows the naive estimate from 7.9 pp to 4.6 pp.
  • We simulated a field experiment (design-based inference) by randomly assigning the promotion flag to 50% of clicked listings and confirmed group balance on six pre-treatment covariates.
  • We estimated the ATE as a difference in means (Ȳ(1) − Ȳ(0)) and reported the effect in absolute percentage points, relative terms, and standard deviation units, following the lecture's three-metric framework.
  • We conducted a mid-funnel analysis segmenting the ATE by booking urgency to identify where the promotion effect is strongest.

docs.title: 3. Preliminary Findings
docs.text:
• The naive comparison overstates the promotion effect by roughly 7 percentage points. The raw difference in conversion between promoted and non-promoted listings is 7.9 pp, but once we control for position and star rating (model-based inference) the estimate drops to 4.6 pp, and the randomised experiment estimates the true ATE at only 0.5 pp — illustrating how confounding can dramatically inflate observational comparisons.
  • The promotion flag generates a small but causally credible lift in conversion. The randomised ATE is +0.50 percentage points (67.9% vs. 67.4%), a relative increase of 0.74% and an effect size of 0.011 SD — consistent with the 0.01–0.05 SD range typical of large-scale digital A/B tests described in the lecture.
  • The effect is larger for last-minute searchers. The mid-funnel analysis shows a 0.90 pp lift for users searching within 7 days of check-in (relative: 1.05%), versus 0.50–0.60 pp for short-lead and long-lead users, suggesting that the promotion badge provides the strongest nudge to users who are already close to committing.
  • Balance testing confirms the randomisation worked. All six pre-treatment covariates (star rating, price, position, length of stay, party size, booking window) are nearly identical across groups, validating that the difference-in-means estimator is a credible causal estimate.
  • All major experimental assumptions are plausible given the platform context. The promotion flag is a server-side display change, making compliance issues and between-user spillovers unlikely, though the SUTVA assumption would need monitoring if promoted listings were shared on social media.

docs.title: 4. Assumptions & Limitations
docs.text:
• The experiment is simulated from observational data rather than conducted on the live platform; in a real field experiment, the random assignment mechanism would be embedded in Expedia's display logic, and compliance would be guaranteed by the platform rather than assumed.
  • We assumed SUTVA holds — that a user's conversion does not depend on whether other users in the same search session see a promotion. In practice, if users compare promoted and non-promoted listings side by side in the same search results page, the badge may have a relative rather than absolute effect.
  • The ATE is estimated across all clicked listings; it does not distinguish between different hotel quality tiers or search contexts beyond the urgency segmentation, and there may be meaningful effect heterogeneity that a single pooled estimate masks.
  • The simulated experiment uses 50% treatment probability, which is efficient for estimation but may not match the real-world constraint that only a subset of hotels are eligible for promotional badging due to pricing agreements with hotel partners.

docs.title: 5. Open Questions for Feedback
docs.text:
• Our mid-funnel analysis used booking window as the only segmentation variable — should we also examine whether the promotion effect differs by star rating tier, given that a badge on a 5-star listing may carry different credibility signals than the same badge on a 2-star listing?
  • The ATE of 0.5 pp is small in SD units but may be commercially significant at scale; what is the team's threshold for "actionable" effect size, and would a lift of this magnitude justify the cost of maintaining the promotional badging infrastructure?
  • We have not assessed whether the promotion flag creates any negative externalities — for instance, whether non-promoted listings in the same search session see a lower conversion rate when competing against a promoted listing, which would indicate that the badge redistributes rather than creates bookings.

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text:
• We would conduct a formal statistical significance test (t-test or equivalent) on the ATE to assess whether the observed 0.5-pp lift is distinguishable from random variation, given the sample size and the standard deviation of the conversion outcome.
  • We would run a heterogeneous treatment effects analysis by star rating, price tier, and device type to identify which hotel segments benefit most from the promotion flag, enabling Expedia to target the badge more precisely rather than applying it uniformly.
  • We would design a real field experiment embedded in the Expedia platform — with the promotion flag randomly assigned at the search-session level rather than the listing level — to test whether the SUTVA assumption holds when users see promoted and non-promoted listings side by side in the same results page.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: This analysis assessed whether displaying a promotional flag on a hotel listing on Expedia causes a measurable increase in booking conversion — the share of users who click a listing and go on to book it. A naive comparison of promoted and non-promoted listings in historical data suggested a 7.9-percentage-point advantage for promoted hotels, but this overstates the true effect: promoted hotels also tend to appear in higher positions and at lower prices, both of which independently drive conversion. A simulated randomized experiment, in which the promotion badge was assigned by chance rather than by Expedia's existing algorithm, estimates the true causal effect at +0.50 percentage points — a small but credibly estimated lift that is consistent with the scale of effects typically observed in large digital A/B tests. The promotion badge produces the largest lift for last-minute searchers (+0.90 pp), who are already primed to book and appear to respond most strongly to value signals at the listing level.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• The raw data misleads: confounders inflate the apparent promotion effect by more than 15-fold. The observational comparison attributes 7.9 pp of the conversion difference to the promotion badge, but the randomised experiment shows the true causal effect is only 0.50 pp — a 15× overestimate driven by position and price confounding.
  • The promotion badge works, but its effect is modest and highly context-dependent. The 0.50 pp overall lift is commercially meaningful at platform scale but is concentrated among last-minute searchers (0.90 pp lift), suggesting the badge is most effective as a closing signal for high-intent users rather than a general visibility driver.
  • Causal credibility requires experimental design, not just good data. The comparison of model-based inference (4.6 pp after subgroup restriction) versus design-based inference (0.50 pp from randomisation) illustrates that assumptions about which factors to control for can still leave substantial bias — only random assignment gives us a clean causal estimate.

docs.title: Business Implications
docs.text:
• Expedia's current promotion-badging algorithm may be rewarding hotels that would convert well anyway. If badges are preferentially shown to well-positioned, lower-priced hotels, the observed lift in the historical data reflects selection, not causation — meaning the badging system may not be generating as much incremental revenue as the raw data suggests.
  • Targeting the promotion badge toward last-minute, high-intent search sessions could amplify its commercial value. A 0.90-pp lift for last-minute searchers versus 0.50 pp overall implies that precision targeting — rather than broad application — would improve the return on the promotional badging investment.
  • Design-based causal analysis should become a standard component of Expedia's product evaluation process. The large gap between the naive and experimental estimates demonstrates that observational data alone cannot reliably quantify the effect of platform interventions; A/B testing infrastructure is a prerequisite for sound decision-making.

docs.title: Recommended Actions
docs.text:
• Run a live randomised A/B test on the promotion badge using Expedia's platform. Randomly assign the badge at the search-session level for a defined period and measure the causal lift in completed bookings, using this analysis as the pre-registered hypothesis and benchmark.
  • Pilot a targeting strategy that reserves the promotion badge for last-minute search sessions. Based on the mid-funnel ATE estimates, restrict badge display to users with booking windows under 7 days and compare booking revenue per search session against the current untargeted approach.
  • Commission a competitive-effects audit before scaling. Before broadening the promotion badge programme, measure whether promoted listings in the same results page displace bookings from adjacent non-promoted listings — if the badge redistributes rather than creates bookings, its aggregate revenue value is lower than the single-listing ATE implies.

docs.text:
In this assignment, you'll bring together everything you've learned this semester: cleaning and analysing data, and communicating your findings to different audiences.

You'll work in randomly assigned groups to develop a research question that can be answered with data, and complete three components:

  1. Part A – Cleaning & Analysing Data (60%): Conduct your analysis in R using a Quarto document.

  2. Part B – Analytics Team Memo (20%): A 600-word bullet-point memo for your analytics peers.

  3. Part C – Corporate Brief (20%): A 400-word executive summary for decision-makers.

This assignment mirrors how analytics works in real organisations: detailed analysis → team discussion → concise brief for management.

docs.title: The Case: Ferdeer Retail
docs.text:
Ferdeer Retail is an online retailer selling consumer goods across seven countries (US, IN, AU, BR, CA, DE, UK). Customers browse the site, add items to a cart, and sometimes buy. Marketing runs campaigns through several channels (Email, Paid Search, Social, Display, Affiliate) to bring people to the site and encourage them to purchase.

Over the last three years (2021–2023) the company has logged who its customers are, what they browsed, which campaigns they saw, and what they eventually bought. It has also been running an experiment on the site itself, testing whether changes to the checkout process make people more likely to complete a purchase.

docs.title: The business challenge
docs.text:
Management would like to understand the business better in three areas:

  1. What can we learn about our customers and how they interact with our marketing and purchasing journey?
  2. Can the information we have about customers and their visits help us identify who is most likely to make a purchase?
  3. When we make changes to the customer experience, do those changes lead to better outcomes?

Each of these is a broad area of interest. Your team will need to decide what, specifically, is worth investigating using the available data. Management is also open to other ideas: if your team identifies a different question with a similar level of business importance, and you can answer it convincingly using the available data, you are welcome to pursue it instead.

Whatever direction you choose, your analysis should be built around a clear business question and an analytical approach that is appropriate for answering it.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Eight files are provided in the data folder; full details are in Ferdeer_dataset_documentation.pdf.

File Rows One row per... customer_demographics.csv 10,000 customer customer_profile.csv 10,100 customer (see note) products.csv 2,000 product category_lookup.csv 6 product category campaigns.csv 50 marketing campaign campaign_spend_wide.csv 50 marketing campaign events.csv 199,627 user interaction (view / click / add to cart / bounce / purchase) transactions.csv 17,800 completed purchase

Things to keep in mind:

  • The data is not analysis-ready. It arrives the way data often arrives in practice: spread across several files, with inconsistent column names, some values that cannot be right, and one table stored in an untidy shape. Preparing it is part of the assignment, and your cleaning decisions are assessed.
  • The files must be combined. Customer information is split across two files, product categories are stored as codes (names are in a separate lookup file), and campaign spend is stored with one column per year. The identifier columns are not named consistently across files, so check before you join.
  • The site experiment. Every customer was randomly assigned to one of three checkout versions and stays in that version throughout: Control (the current site), Variant_A (a simplified one-page checkout), or Variant_B (one-click checkout with a guest option). The company has not yet evaluated the results.
  • Campaign exposure is not random. Campaigns target particular segments, and expected_uplift is a planning assumption by the campaign designer, not a measured result. In the event and transaction files, campaign_id = 0 means no campaign.

The two customer files describe details of the customers, so we can combine them into a single customer table using left_join(). Same approach is applied to the product and campaign files. The events and transactions tables stay as they are.

    df_raw_customer_demographics |>
    rename(cust_id = customer_id) |>

# Products: products + categories

    df_raw_products |>
    left_join(df_raw_category_lookup, by = join_by(cat_code))

# Campaigns: campaign + spend

    df_raw_campaigns |>
    left_join(df_raw_campaign_spend_wide, by = join_by(campaign_id))

    mutate(purchase_date = as_date(time_stamp)) |>
    select(cust_id, prod_id, purchase_date, revenue_usd, refunded) |>   # keep only the columns we need
    drop_na()                                                           # 3. delete rows with missing values (revenue and product)

Events: The event table describes customer interactions on the platform. The summary statistics indicate that some events have impossible session durations (e.g., −1 or extremely high values like 999,999 seconds). We need to remove these rows. We additionally create an indicator variable, purchased, which equals 1 if the event type is a purchase.

In [19]: Copied! 
df_events_clean <-
    df_events |>
    mutate(purchased = if_else(event_type == "purchase", 1, 0)) |>   # did the visit end in a purchase?
    select(cust_id, session_duration_sec, purchased) |>              # keep only the columns we need
    filter(
        session_duration_sec >= 0,
        session_duration_sec <= 3600
    ) |>                                                             # 1. delete impossible durations
    drop_na()                                                        # 2. delete rows with missing values

From this figure, we can observe the trends in marketing spend and sales revenue over the years. The marketing spend has been increasing significantly, which grew from $534k in 2021 to $967k in 2022 and $1.66 million in 2023, about 3.1 times. From the table above, we can see that this is because the number of running campaigns rose from 16 to 34 and then to 50.
