(a) RFM Data Preparation

We first prepare the data for the RFM method from class. RFM scores are defined for buyers only, so we keep the buyers from the customer full table. Each of the three measures is converted into quintile scores from 1 to 5 with ntile(), and the recency score is reversed so that 5 always means "better" (more recent, more frequent, higher spend). Before using the scores, we check what the frequency quintiles actually contain.

In [41]: Copied! 
df_rfm_data <-
    df_customer_full_clean |>
    filter(buyer == "Buyer") |>   # RFM scores are defined for buyers only
    select(cust_id, recency, frequency, monetary) |>
    mutate(
        r_tile = ntile(recency, 5),
        f_tile = ntile(frequency, 5),
        m_tile = ntile(monetary, 5)
    ) |>
    mutate(
        # Reverse R so that R = 5 means the most recent buyers, in line with F and M
        r_tile = max(r_tile) - r_tile + 1
    )

The table and the chart above show clearly that different types of customers are not equally important. Four groups stand out:

  • Potential Loyalists are the largest segment, with 38% of buyers, and contribute more than half of revenue. On average they bought about six months ago, placed about three orders and spent $345 each.
  • Champions are only 5% of buyers (344) but generate the second-largest share of revenue. They bought within the last month on average, placed almost five orders and spent $702 each, the highest of all segments.
  • Lost customers are 15% of buyers but generate only 6% of revenue. They last bought more than two years ago, placed about one order and spent about $100 each.
  • At Risk and Can't Lose Them customers (486 buyers combined) are small groups that spent about $460 each, but have not bought for almost two years.

First, we remove the extreme values from the dataset: the spending more than $1,500 and the average session duration longer than 300 seconds. Such values make most customers be concentrated and squeezed into one corner, and they pull the cluster centres towards them. We therefore leave these customers out of the clustering.

    mutate(avg_conversion = percent(avg_conversion, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
    knitr::kable()
# Give each cluster a descriptive name, based on the profile table above # (cluster numbers are fixed by set.seed(123)) df_behaviour_clustered <- df_behaviour_clustered |> mutate( segment = case_when( .cluster == 1 ~ "Long Sessions", .cluster == 2 ~ "High Spenders", .cluster == 3 ~ "Low Spenders" ) ) # Compare the outcome: the average conversion rate of each cluster df_behaviour_clustered |> group_by(segment) |> summarise( n_customers = n(), avg_conversion = mean(conversion) ) |> ungroup() |> arrange(desc(avg_conversion)) |> mutate(avg_conversion = percent(avg_conversion, accuracy = 0.1)) |> knitr::kable() 

|segment       | n_customers|avg_conversion |
|:-------------|-----------:|:--------------|
|High Spenders |        1882|17.1%          |
|Long Sessions |        1373|7.9%           |
|Low Spenders  |        6702|6.7%           |

The High Spenders convert at 17.1%, about two and a half times the rate of the Low Spenders (6.7%), while the Long Sessions customers convert at 7.9%. The link between spending and conversion is largely by construction: the purchase events in the event table almost coincide with the orders in the transaction table (the two counts have a correlation of 0.97 across customers), so the customers who spend the most are mostly those who buy most often. The more informative result is the role of session duration: the customers who stay longest on the site spend only $143 on average, far less than the High Spenders, who have ordinary session lengths. Staying longer on the site does not go together with spending more.

These are descriptive results: they show how browsing time, spending and conversion go together, but not what causes what.

docs.title: Ferdeer Case Demo: Who Are Ferdeer Retail's Most Valuable Customers?¶
Part A. Cleaning and Analysing Data¶
1. Introduction¶
docs.text:
Research Question: Who are Ferdeer Retail's most valuable customers, and how do they differ from the other customers in how much they spend, how long they stay on the site and how often their visits end in a purchase?

Method: This is a descriptive analysis. We summarise three years of customer, sales, campaign and browsing data to describe what happened. We first set the scene with a short overview of sales revenue by year, product category and country. We then identify the valuable customers with a rule-based segmentation (RFM) and with a data-driven segmentation (K-means clustering) on customers' spending and session duration, and we compare the clusters on their conversion rate. We do not claim that any pattern is caused by marketing or by customer behaviour — campaigns and customer behaviour were not randomly assigned — and we do not build a model to predict future purchases.

docs.title: (2) Data Loading¶
docs.text:
(a) Load Raw Datasets

Then, we load each of the eight files into R as a tibble. Here we use clean_names() to convert the column names into lower-case snake_case.

docs.title: (3) Data Cleaning¶
docs.text:
(a) Prepare the Clean Datasets

The summary statistics above show what is wrong with the data. We now clean the five tables one by one. For all five tables, some common cleaning steps are applied, e.g., dropping exact duplicate rows, retaining only the necessary columns, and deleting rows with missing values.

docs.title: (4) Data Processing¶
docs.text:
In this step, we build the customer-level variables used in the analysis, in two groups: how customers purchase, from the transaction table, and how customers browse, from the event table. In the end, we join both groups to the clean customer table, so that all later customer analyses use one table.

(a) Customer Purchasing Behavior

In this part, we prepare the necessary customer-level purchasing variables for RFM analysis. We start with the purchasing records. The basis is the completed purchases: the non-refunded transactions, with the product category attached from the clean product table. Excluding refunds means that we count only sales that the customer kept.

docs.title: (1) Sales Overview¶
docs.text: We first set the scene with a short overview of where the sales revenue comes from: over the three years, by product category and by country. All three views use the completed purchases.

docs.title: (2) Rule-Based Segmentation: RFM¶
docs.text: We now turn to rule-based segmentation (RFM) of customers analyzing their Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value.

docs.title: (3) Data-Driven Segmentation: K-Means¶
docs.text: We now bring in the event table and use K-means to group customers by how much they spend and how long they stay on the site. For every customer we use two features: the total spend and the average session duration. Using only two features has a practical advantage: the clusters can be drawn directly on these two axes, instead of being projected onto abstract principal components. The outcome we want to understand is the conversion rate, the share of visits that ended in a purchase. We do not use it to build the clusters; we compare it across the clusters afterwards.

docs.title: 1. Research Question¶
docs.text:
• Our research question is: who are Ferdeer Retail's most valuable customers, and how do they differ from the other customers in spending, time on site and conversion?
  • The question matters because Ferdeer tripled its marketing spend between 2021 and 2023 while sales revenue stayed flat, so management needs to know which customers deserve the investment.

docs.title: 2. Data & Approach¶
docs.text:
• We cleaned the eight source files into five tables, excluded refunds, and joined them into one table of 10,000 customers with their RFM measures (recency, frequency, monetary value) from 16,236 completed purchases, and their visits, average session duration and conversion rate from 198,094 site visits.
  • The analysis is descriptive: we scored buyers on RFM quintiles with ntile() and mapped the scores to standard segments, and we ran K-means with k = 3 on two standardised features, total spend and average session duration, after removing extreme customers.
  • The conversion rate, the share of a customer's visits that ended in a purchase, is the outcome we compare across clusters, not a feature, and summaries of revenue by year, product category and country give the background.

docs.title: 3. Preliminary Findings¶
docs.text:
• RFM shows that value is concentrated: Potential Loyalists (38% of buyers) generate 51% of revenue, and Champions (5%) generate 13% at $702 per buyer.
  • Some valuable customers are slipping away: 486 At Risk or Can't Lose Them buyers spent about $460 each but have not bought for almost two years.
  • K-means finds three clusters: the 1,882 High Spenders (19%) spend $563 and convert at 17.1%, against $97 and 6.7% for the 6,702 Low Spenders.
  • The 1,373 Long Sessions customers stay 189 seconds per visit, against about 120 for the others, but spend only $143, so time on site does not signal value.
  • Where customers live does not distinguish them: US and Indian customers are 55% of customers and generate 56% of revenue, and customers in every country spend $184 to $196 each, whereas what they buy matters more, as customers' Electronics purchases generate 42% of revenue.
  • As background, marketing spend grew 3.1 times to $1.66 million while revenue stayed flat, so revenue per dollar of spend fell from $1.23 to $0.38.

docs.title: 4. Assumptions & Limitations¶
docs.text:
• Spending and conversion are linked by construction, because purchase events and orders almost coincide (correlation 0.97), so the High Spenders' high conversion is expected rather than a separate finding.
  • The RFM cut-offs from ntile() are arbitrary, so segment boundaries are a judgement call, and k = 3 rests on the silhouette width alone, since the elbow curve shows no clear bend.
  • We leave customers with spending above $1,500 or sessions above 300 seconds out of the clustering, so the cluster averages understate the largest spenders, and the analysis is descriptive, so the spend and revenue trends do not measure the effect of marketing.

docs.title: 5. Open Questions for Feedback¶
docs.text:
• Should management define high-value customers with the transparent but arbitrary RFM segments, or with the data-driven K-means clusters?
  • Did revenue stay flat because extra spend earns diminishing returns, or because the data does not capture the sales that campaigns generate?
  • Should refunds reduce a customer's value, rather than being excluded from it?

docs.title: 6. Next Steps¶
docs.text:
• We would track the High Spenders cluster over time to see whether customers move in and out of it.
  • We would analyse the checkout experiment to test whether the new checkout designs raise conversion.
  • We would compare spend and revenue by channel and campaign to find where the extra spend earned no return.

docs.title: Executive Summary¶
docs.text: We examined who Ferdeer Retail's most valuable customers are, using three years of customer, sales, browsing and campaign data. Ranking customers on how recently, how often and how much they buy (RFM) shows that a small group carries the business: the Champions, only 5% of buyers, generate 13% of revenue. An algorithm that groups customers by spending and time on site finds high spenders who buy in 17% of their visits, against 7% for typical customers, while customers who stay longest on the site do not spend more. Because marketing spend tripled while revenue did not grow, knowing who these customers are should guide next year's budget.

docs.title: Key Insights¶
docs.text:
• RFM shows that value is concentrated: Champions (5% of buyers) generate 13% of revenue and Potential Loyalists (38%) generate 51%, so fewer than half of our buyers bring in almost two thirds of revenue.
  • An algorithm that groups customers by spending and time on site finds 1,882 customers who spend $563 each and buy in 17% of their visits, against $97 and 7% for the 6,702 typical customers; those who stay longest on the site spend only $143.
  • Where customers live hardly affects what they spend ($184 to $196 each), but what they buy does: Electronics purchases bring in 42% of revenue.

docs.title: Business Implications¶
docs.text:
• A small group of high-spending customers carries the revenue, so keeping them matters more than winning many typical customers.
  • Time on site and country do not signal value, so what customers have bought is the better guide for judging them.
  • Marketing spend grew from $534k in 2021 to $1.66 million in 2023 while revenue slipped from $655k to $630k, so each dollar now returns $0.38 instead of $1.23 and the added spend is the first place to look for savings.

docs.title: Recommended Actions¶
docs.text:
• Launch a retention programme for the Champions and for the 486 At Risk and Can't Lose Them customers, who spent about $460 each but have not bought for almost two years.
  • Choose the audience of each campaign by what customers have bought, such as Electronics, rather than by country or time on site.
  • Pause further increases in marketing spend until a review by channel and campaign shows which ones earn a return.

docs.title: Ferdeer Case Demo 1: Who Are Ferdeer Retail's Most Valuable Customers?
Part A. Cleaning and Analysing Data
1. Introduction
docs.text:
Research Question: Which groups of customers generate most of Ferdeer Retail's revenue, and how do these groups differ in who they are and in how their visits to the site turn into purchases?

Method: This is a descriptive analysis. We summarise three years of customer, purchase and browsing data to describe what happened: we segment buyers with a rule-based method (RFM) and a data-driven method (K-means clustering), profile the resulting segments with grouped summary statistics, and compare how often site visits from different traffic sources and devices end in a purchase. We do not claim that any characteristic causes customers to spend more — loyalty tiers and campaign exposure were not randomly assigned — and we do not build a model to predict future purchases.

docs.title: (1) Load Libraries
docs.text:
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling and visualisation
library(janitor)     # clean_names(): tidy column names
library(scales)      # formatting axis labels (e.g., percent, dollar)
library(patchwork)   # combining multiple plots
library(ggokabeito)  # colour-blind-friendly palette (course default)
library(recipes)     # scaling variables before clustering
library(cluster)     # K-means
library(factoextra)  # choosing k and visualising clusters
library(broom)       # augment(): attach cluster labels back to the data

options(repr.plot.width = 10, repr.plot.height = 6, repr.plot.res = 150)  # figure size in the notebook

docs.title: (2) Load the Datasets
docs.text:
The case comes as eight files. The column names are inconsistent across files (e.g. CustomerID, cust_id, Signup Date, Revenue (USD)), so we pass every file through clean_names() as it is loaded, which turns all column names into lower-case snake_case.

# clean_names() converts every column name to snake_case so that names are consistent,
# e.g. "Signup Date" -> signup_date, "Revenue (USD)" -> revenue_usd, "discount %" -> discount_percent
demographics <- read_csv("data/customer_demographics.csv") |> clean_names()
profile      <- read_csv("data/customer_profile.csv")      |> clean_names()
products     <- read_csv("data/products.csv")              |> clean_names()
categories   <- read_csv("data/category_lookup.csv")       |> clean_names()
campaigns    <- read_csv("data/campaigns.csv")             |> clean_names()
spend_wide   <- read_csv("data/campaign_spend_wide.csv")   |> clean_names()
events       <- read_csv("data/events.csv")                |> clean_names()
transactions <- read_csv("data/transactions.csv")          |> clean_names()

A quick look at the two largest tables shows their structure: each row of transactions is one purchase, and each row of events is one interaction with the site, recorded with its traffic source, device and linked campaign.

# Quick preview of the raw transaction table
transactions |> slice_head(n = 5)

docs.title: (3) Data Cleaning
docs.text:
The data documentation warns that the files are not analysis-ready. We clean them table by table, and for each table we follow the same three steps: inspect the problem, decide what to do, and apply the decision. Our general rule is to set a value that cannot be right to missing rather than delete the whole customer, and to delete a row only when the row itself cannot be used.

Step 1: Customer tables

customer_profile.csv has 10,100 rows for 10,000 customers. We first check whether some customers appear more than once.

# customer_profile.csv has 10,100 rows, but there are only 10,000 customers.
# Count each identifier and keep those that appear more than once
profile |>
  count(cust_id) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()

100

# Are the repeated rows exact copies? distinct() keeps one copy of each identical row
profile |>
  distinct() |>
  nrow()

10000

100 customers appear twice, and after distinct() exactly 10,000 rows remain — so the repeated rows are exact copies and can be dropped safely.

Next, we inspect the demographic variables.

# Country codes: inspect every value that appears
demographics |>
  count(cntry)

| cntry <chr> | n <int> |
|---|---|
| AU |  610 |
| BR |  929 |
| CA |  880 |
| DE |  723 |
| IN | 1856 |
| UK |  961 |
| US | 3241 |
| au |   58 |
| br |   81 |
| ca |   78 |
| de |   66 |
| in |  168 |
| uk |   81 |
| us |  268 |

# Age and gender: look for impossible or missing values
demographics |>
  summarise(
    n_customers    = n(),
    age_min        = min(age),
    age_max        = max(age),
    n_age_invalid  = sum(age < 18 | age > 100),   # documentation: adult customers only
    n_gender_na    = sum(is.na(gender))
  )

| n_customers <int> | age_min <dbl> | age_max <dbl> | n_age_invalid <int> | n_gender_na <int> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10000 | -5 | 999 | 30 | 200 |

Three problems appear. Each of the seven countries is recorded in both upper and lower case (e.g. US and us), which would split one country into two groups. 30 customers have an impossible age (as low as −5 or as high as 999), although the documentation says all customers are adults. 200 customers have no gender recorded.

We standardise the country codes with case_when(), set impossible ages to missing, and label missing gender as "Not stated" instead of dropping these customers. We also rename customer_id to cust_id, the name used in every other file, before joining the two customer tables.

demographics_clean <-
  demographics |>
  # Use the same identifier name as all other files, so that joins are straightforward
  rename(cust_id = customer_id) |>
  mutate(
    # Standardise country codes to upper case
    cntry = case_when(
      cntry %in% c("au", "AU") ~ "AU",
      cntry %in% c("br", "BR") ~ "BR",
      cntry %in% c("ca", "CA") ~ "CA",
      cntry %in% c("de", "DE") ~ "DE",
      cntry %in% c("in", "IN") ~ "IN",
      cntry %in% c("uk", "UK") ~ "UK",
      cntry %in% c("us", "US") ~ "US"
    ),
    # Ages below 18 or above 100 cannot be right: set them to missing rather than dropping the customer
    age = if_else(age >= 18 & age <= 100, age, NA),
    # Keep customers with missing gender, but label them explicitly
    gender = coalesce(gender, "Not stated")
  )

# Remove the 100 exact duplicate rows in the profile table
profile_clean <-
  profile |>
  distinct()

# Combine the two customer files into one customer-level table
customers <-
  demographics_clean |>
  left_join(profile_clean, by = join_by(cust_id))

# Check the join: one row per customer, and every customer found a profile
customers |>
  summarise(
    n_rows           = n(),
    n_customers      = n_distinct(cust_id),
    n_no_profile     = sum(is.na(loyalty_tier)),
    n_age_missing    = sum(is.na(age)),
    n_country_values = n_distinct(cntry)
  )

| n_rows <int> | n_customers <int> | n_no_profile <int> | n_age_missing <int> | n_country_values <int> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10000 | 10000 | 0 | 30 | 7 |

The combined customers table has exactly one row for each of the 10,000 customers, every customer found a matching profile, and only seven country codes remain.

Step 2: Products

# A price should be a positive amount
products |>
  summarise(
    n_products          = n(),
    n_price_missing     = sum(is.na(base_price)),
    n_price_nonpositive = sum(base_price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

| n_products <int> | n_price_missing <int> | n_price_nonpositive <int> |
|---|---|---|
| 2000 | 15 | 15 |

15 products have no price and 15 have a non-positive price, which is impossible. We do not rely on base price in this analysis, but we still set non-positive prices to missing so that no later step uses them by accident. We also join the category lookup table to replace codes such as C02 with readable names.

products_clean <-
  products |>
  # Non-positive prices are impossible: set them to missing
  mutate(base_price = if_else(base_price > 0, base_price, NA)) |>
  # Replace the category code with its readable name from the lookup table
  left_join(categories, by = join_by(cat_code))

products_clean |>
  count(category_name)

| category_name <chr> | n <int> |
|---|---|
| Beauty      | 201 |
| Electronics | 455 |
| Fashion     | 418 |
| Grocery     | 312 |
| Home        | 396 |
| Sports      | 218 |

Step 3: Transactions

transactions |>
  summarise(
    n_rows            = n(),
    n_txn_ids         = n_distinct(txn_id),       # fewer IDs than rows means repeated transactions
    n_exact_dups      = n() - nrow(distinct(transactions)),
    n_qty_invalid     = sum(qty < 1),             # a purchase involves at least one unit
    n_revenue_missing = sum(is.na(revenue_usd)),
    n_product_missing = sum(is.na(prod_id)),
    n_both_missing    = sum(is.na(revenue_usd) & is.na(prod_id))
  )

| n_rows <int> | n_txn_ids <int> | n_exact_dups <int> | n_qty_invalid <int> | n_revenue_missing <int> | n_product_missing <int> | n_both_missing <int> |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 17800 | 17650 | 150 | 50 | 1087 | 1087 | 1087 |

# How do refunds show up? Compare the refund flag with the sign of revenue
transactions |>
  count(
    refunded,
    revenue_sign = case_when(
      revenue_usd < 0  ~ "negative",
      revenue_usd >= 0 ~ "positive",
      .default         = "missing"
    )
  )

| refunded <chr> | revenue_sign <chr> | n <int> |
|---|---|---|
| No  | missing  |  1062 |
| No  | positive | 16426 |
| Yes | missing  |    25 |
| Yes | negative |   287 |

The checks reveal four issues:

  • Duplicates: there are 17,800 rows but only 17,650 transaction IDs, and all 150 extra rows are exact copies of another row.
  • Impossible quantities: 50 transactions have a quantity of 0 or less, although a purchase involves at least one unit.
  • Missing values: 1,087 transactions have neither revenue nor product. We cannot tell what was bought or for how much, so they cannot contribute to spending measures.
  • Refunds: 312 transactions are flagged as refunded. Their revenue is negative (or missing), while no non-refunded transaction has negative revenue, so the refund flag is reliable.

We drop the duplicate, impossible and unvalued rows. Because refunded purchases do not represent value the customer kept, we exclude them from all customer value measures and keep only completed purchases in a separate table, purchases.

transactions_clean <-
  transactions |>
  distinct() |>                          # 1. drop exact duplicate rows
  filter(
    qty >= 1,                            # 2. drop impossible quantities (0 or negative)
    !is.na(revenue_usd)                  # 3. drop rows we cannot value (product also unknown)
  ) |>
  mutate(purchase_date = as_date(time_stamp)) |>
  # Attach product category and premium flag
  left_join(
    products_clean |> select(prod_id, category_name, is_premium),
    by = join_by(prod_id)
  )

# Completed (non-refunded) purchases are the basis of all customer value metrics
purchases <-
  transactions_clean |>
  filter(refunded == "No")

tibble(
  raw_rows       = nrow(transactions),
  clean_rows     = nrow(transactions_clean),
  refunded_rows  = sum(transactions_clean$refunded == "Yes"),
  purchase_rows  = nrow(purchases)
)

| raw_rows <int> | clean_rows <int> | refunded_rows <int> | purchase_rows <int> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17800 | 16518 | 282 | 16236 |

After cleaning, 16,518 transactions remain, of which 16,236 are completed (non-refunded) purchases.

Step 4: Events

# Traffic source labels: inspect every value that appears
events |>
  count(traffic_source)

| traffic_source <chr> | n <int> |

| DIRECT      |   605 |
| Direct      | 19282 |
| EMAIL       |   874 |
| Email       | 29093 |
| ORGANIC     |  2445 |
| Organic     | 77388 |
| PAID SEARCH |  1271 |
| Paid Search | 38627 |
| SOCIAL      |   906 |
| Social      | 29136 |

events |>
  summarise(
    n_rows               = n(),
    n_device_missing     = sum(is.na(device)),
    n_duration_negative  = sum(session_duration_sec < 0),
    n_duration_over_hour = sum(session_duration_sec > 3600),   # "a session lasts minutes, not days"
    duration_max         = max(session_duration_sec)
  )

| n_rows <int> | n_device_missing <int> | n_duration_negative <int> | n_duration_over_hour <int> | duration_max <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 199627 | 4027 | 750 | 783 | 999999 |

# How many events does one visit contain? A visit is a customer + session pair
events |>
  count(cust_id, session_id, name = "n_events") |>
  count(n_events, name = "n_visits")

| n_events <int> | n_visits <int> |
|---|---|
| 1 | 199613 |
| 2 |      7 |

The traffic source has the same case problem as country (Email and EMAIL). 4,027 events have no device recorded. Session duration contains 750 values of −1 and 783 values above one hour, up to 999,999 seconds (about 11.6 days), which contradicts the documentation's note that a session lasts minutes, not days.

The last check is important for how we analyse the events: almost every visit (a customer and session pair) contains exactly one event. We therefore treat each event row as one visit, and its event type (view, click, add to cart, bounce or purchase) as the outcome of that visit.

We merge the traffic source labels, label missing devices as "unknown", set impossible durations to missing, and create two variables: campaign_linked (remember that campaign_id = 0 means no campaign) and purchased, which equals 1 if the visit ended in a purchase.

events_clean <-
  events |>
  mutate(
    # Merge upper-case duplicates of the same traffic source
    traffic_source = case_when(
      traffic_source %in% c("Direct", "DIRECT")           ~ "Direct",
      traffic_source %in% c("Email", "EMAIL")             ~ "Email",
      traffic_source %in% c("Organic", "ORGANIC")         ~ "Organic",
      traffic_source %in% c("Paid Search", "PAID SEARCH") ~ "Paid Search",
      traffic_source %in% c("Social", "SOCIAL")           ~ "Social"
    ),
    # Keep events with no recorded device, but label them explicitly
    device = coalesce(device, "unknown"),
    # Negative durations and durations above one hour cannot be right: set to missing
    session_duration_sec = if_else(
      session_duration_sec >= 0 & session_duration_sec <= 3600,
      session_duration_sec,
      NA
    ),
    # campaign_id = 0 means "no campaign", it is not a real campaign
    campaign_linked = if_else(campaign_id != 0, "Campaign", "No campaign"),
    # Outcome of the visit: did it end in a purchase?
    purchased = if_else(event_type == "purchase", 1, 0)
  )

events_clean |>
  count(traffic_source, campaign_linked)

| traffic_source <chr> | campaign_linked <chr> | n <int> |
|---|---|---|
| Direct      | No campaign | 19887 |
| Email       | Campaign    | 29967 |
| Organic     | No campaign | 79833 |
| Paid Search | Campaign    | 39898 |
| Social      | Campaign    | 30042 |

The output also reveals a useful fact: every Email, Paid Search and Social visit is linked to a campaign, while no Organic or Direct visit is.

Step 5: Campaign spend

Campaign spend is stored in a wide layout, with one column per year.

# One column per year: an untidy (wide) layout
spend_wide |> slice_head(n = 5)

| campaign_id <dbl> | spend_2021 <dbl> | spend_2022 <dbl> | spend_2023 <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 |  5476 | 28884 | 52396 |
| 2 | 49538 | 30047 | 59294 |
| 3 |    NA |    NA | 43200 |
| 4 |    NA | 31095 | 36248 |
| 5 |    NA | 48683 | 31072 |

We reshape it into a tidy long table (one row per campaign and year) with pivot_longer(), drop the years in which a campaign was not running, and attach each campaign's channel.

spend_long <-
  spend_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols           = starts_with("spend_"),
    names_to       = c(".value", "year"),   # "spend_2021" -> column "spend", year "2021"
    names_sep      = "_",
    values_drop_na = TRUE                   # NA = campaign was not running that year
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) |>
  left_join(campaigns |> select(campaign_id, channel), by = join_by(campaign_id))

spend_long |> slice_head(n = 5)

| campaign_id <dbl> | year <dbl> | spend <dbl> | channel <chr> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2021 |  5476 | Paid Search |
| 1 | 2022 | 28884 | Paid Search |
| 1 | 2023 | 52396 | Paid Search |
| 2 | 2021 | 49538 | Email       |
| 2 | 2022 | 30047 | Email       |

docs.title: (4) Data Processing
docs.text:
We now build the customer-level variables used in the analysis. Following the RFM approach from class, we describe each buyer by three measures computed from completed purchases:

  • Recency: whole months between the customer's last purchase and the analysis date, 1 January 2024 (the day after the data end);
  • Frequency: the number of completed purchases;
  • Monetary: the total amount spent, in USD.
# Analysis date: the day after the last transaction in the data
analysis_date <- as_date("2024-01-01")

customer_rfm <-
  purchases |>
  group_by(cust_id) |>
  summarise(
    last_purch_date = max(purchase_date),
    frequency       = n(),               # number of completed purchases
    monetary        = sum(revenue_usd)   # total spend in USD
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    # interval() measures the time between two dates; %/% months(1) converts it to whole months
    recency = interval(last_purch_date, analysis_date) %/% months(1)
  ) |>
  select(cust_id, recency, frequency, monetary)

customer_rfm |> slice_head(n = 5)

| cust_id <dbl> | recency <dbl> | frequency <int> | monetary <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|
|  1 | 11 | 1 |  88.80 |
| 26 | 20 | 1 |  54.35 |
| 27 |  8 | 1 |  81.30 |
| 32 | 23 | 1 | 100.17 |
| 49 | 34 | 1 |  39.19 |

We also describe each buyer's basket — average order value, the share of premium products and the share of electronics purchases — and attach all of these measures to the full customer table. Customers who registered but never completed a purchase keep missing values for these measures and are labelled "No purchase".

# Basket characteristics of each buyer, used later to describe the segments
customer_basket <-
  purchases |>
  group_by(cust_id) |>
  summarise(
    avg_order_value   = mean(revenue_usd),
    share_premium     = mean(is_premium),
    share_electronics = mean(category_name == "Electronics")
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Customer master table: everyone who registered, with purchase metrics where available
customers_full <-
  customers |>
  left_join(customer_rfm, by = join_by(cust_id)) |>
  left_join(customer_basket, by = join_by(cust_id)) |>
  mutate(buyer = if_else(is.na(frequency), "No purchase", "Buyer"))

customers_full |>
  count(buyer)

| buyer <chr> | n <int> |
|---|---|
| Buyer       | 7627 |
| No purchase | 2373 |

Of the 10,000 registered customers, 7,627 completed at least one purchase between 2021 and 2023.

docs.title: (1) Customer Base and Sales Overview
docs.text:
We start with a summary of the customer base as a benchmark for the segment comparisons that follow.

customers_full |>
  summarise(
    n_customers          = n(),
    n_buyers             = sum(buyer == "Buyer"),
    share_buyers         = n_buyers / n_customers,
    total_revenue        = sum(monetary, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_orders_per_buyer = mean(frequency, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_spend_per_buyer  = mean(monetary, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

| n_customers <int> | n_buyers <int> | share_buyers <dbl> | total_revenue <dbl> | avg_orders_per_buyer <dbl> | avg_spend_per_buyer <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10000 | 7627 | 0.7627 | 1929144 | 2.128753 | 252.9362 |

76% of registered customers have bought at least once. Over three years they generated $1.93 million in completed purchases, with the average buyer placing 2.1 orders and spending $253.

Averages hide how unevenly this revenue is spread, so we split buyers into five equal-sized groups by total spend with ntile().

# How concentrated is revenue? Split buyers into five equal-sized groups by total spend
customer_rfm |>
  mutate(spend_quintile = ntile(monetary, 5)) |>
  group_by(spend_quintile) |>
  summarise(
    n_customers = n(),
    min_spend   = min(monetary),
    revenue     = sum(monetary)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(revenue_share = revenue / sum(revenue)) |>
  arrange(desc(spend_quintile))

| spend_quintile <int> | n_customers <int> | min_spend <dbl> | revenue <dbl> | revenue_share <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1525 | 398.02 | 963345.19 | 0.49936398 |
| 4 | 1525 | 234.11 | 470302.53 | 0.24378815 |
| 3 | 1525 | 138.08 | 280120.55 | 0.14520456 |
| 2 | 1526 |  68.85 | 154495.87 | 0.08008518 |
| 1 | 1526 |   4.87 |  60880.19 | 0.03155813 |

Revenue is highly concentrated: the top 20% of buyers (those who spent at least $398) generate 50% of all revenue, while the bottom 20% generate only 3%. This concentration is the main reason to segment customers rather than treat them all alike.

# Revenue by product category (completed purchases only)
plot_category <-
  purchases |>
  group_by(category_name) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(revenue_usd)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(category_name = reorder(category_name, revenue)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = revenue, y = category_name)) +
  geom_col(fill = palette_okabe_ito()[5], width = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(
    title = "Revenue by Product Category, 2021–2023",
    x     = "Revenue (USD)",
    y     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )

plot_category

Electronics is by far the largest category, contributing about $0.8 million, or 42% of revenue, followed by Home and Fashion. Beauty and Grocery are small revenue categories, consistent with their low prices.

docs.title: (2) Rule-Based Segmentation: RFM
docs.text:
We first segment buyers with the RFM method from class. Each of the three measures is converted into quintile scores from 1 to 5 with ntile(), and the recency score is reversed so that 5 always means "better" (more recent, more frequent, higher spend). Before using the scores, we check what the frequency quintiles actually contain.

rfm_data <-
  customer_rfm |>
  mutate(
    r_tile = ntile(recency, 5),
    f_tile = ntile(frequency, 5),
    m_tile = ntile(monetary, 5)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Reverse R so that R = 5 means the most recent buyers, in line with F and M
    r_tile = max(r_tile) - r_tile + 1
  )

# Check what each frequency tile actually contains
rfm_data |>
  group_by(f_tile) |>
  summarise(
    n_customers   = n(),
    min_frequency = min(frequency),
    max_frequency = max(frequency)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

| f_tile <int> | n_customers <int> | min_frequency <int> | max_frequency <int> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1526 | 1 |  1 |
| 2 | 1526 | 1 |  1 |
| 3 | 1525 | 1 |  2 |
| 4 | 1525 | 2 |  3 |
| 5 | 1525 | 3 | 11 |

This check reveals a weakness of quintile scoring on this data. Most buyers made only one or two purchases, so frequency quintiles 1 and 2 contain only one-time buyers, and quintile 3 mixes one- and two-time buyers. ntile() must still create five equal-sized groups, so it splits identical customers into different scores. This is a concrete example of the arbitrary cut-offs of rule-based segmentation discussed in class.

We now map score combinations to the ten standard segment names used in class.

# Map R, F, M score combinations to the standard segment names used in class
rfm_segmented <-
  rfm_data |>
  mutate(
    rfm_segment = case_when(
      r_tile == 5 & f_tile == 5 & m_tile == 5                   ~ "Champions",
      r_tile %in% 3:5 & f_tile %in% 3:5 & m_tile %in% 2:5       ~ "Potential Loyalist",
      r_tile %in% 2:4 & f_tile %in% 2:4 & m_tile %in% 2:4       ~ "Loyal Customers",
      r_tile %in% 3:4 & f_tile %in% 1:3 & m_tile %in% 3:5       ~ "Promising",
      r_tile %in% 4:5 & f_tile %in% 1:3 & m_tile %in% 1:5       ~ "New Customers",
      r_tile %in% 1:2 & f_tile %in% 3:4 & m_tile %in% 4:5       ~ "Can't Lose Them",
      r_tile %in% 1:2 & f_tile %in% 2:5 & m_tile %in% 4:5       ~ "At Risk",
      r_tile %in% 1:3 & f_tile %in% 3:5 & m_tile %in% 3:5       ~ "Need Attention",
      r_tile %in% 2:3 & f_tile %in% 1:3 & m_tile %in% 1:4       ~ "About To Sleep",
      r_tile == 1                                               ~ "Lost",
      .default = "Unclassified"
    )
  )

rfm_summary <-
  rfm_segmented |>
  group_by(rfm_segment) |>
  summarise(
    n_customers   = n(),
    avg_recency   = mean(recency),
    avg_frequency = mean(frequency),
    avg_monetary  = mean(monetary),
    revenue       = sum(monetary)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    customer_share = n_customers / sum(n_customers),
    revenue_share  = revenue / sum(revenue)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(revenue_share))

rfm_summary |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)

|rfm_segment        | n_customers| avg_recency| avg_frequency| avg_monetary|   revenue| customer_share| revenue_share|
|:------------------|-----------:|-----------:|-------------:|------------:|---------:|--------------:|-------------:|
|Potential Loyalist |        2871|        6.07|          2.91|       345.29| 991331.27|           0.38|          0.51|
|Champions          |         344|        1.12|          4.77|       702.41| 241629.29|           0.05|          0.13|
|Loyal Customers    |         956|       15.41|          1.62|       183.26| 175193.44|           0.13|          0.09|
|Lost               |        1179|       28.79|          1.08|        99.58| 117403.26|           0.15|          0.06|
|At Risk            |         252|       21.19|          2.90|       456.61| 115066.06|           0.03|          0.06|
|Can't Lose Them    |         234|       22.72|          2.25|       474.39| 111007.52|           0.03|          0.06|
|About To Sleep     |         827|       15.24|          1.04|        66.68|  55147.85|           0.11|          0.03|
|New Customers      |         628|        3.14|          1.10|        86.02|  54022.15|           0.08|          0.03|
|Promising          |         125|        9.36|          1.00|       269.08|  33635.24|           0.02|          0.02|
|Need Attention     |         143|       24.20|          2.35|       183.96|  26306.19|           0.02|          0.01|
|Unclassified       |          68|       12.19|          2.15|       123.56|   8402.06|           0.01|          0.00|

# Compare each segment's share of customers with its share of revenue
plot_rfm <-
  rfm_summary |>
  select(rfm_segment, customer_share, revenue_share) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(customer_share, revenue_share),
    names_to  = "measure",
    values_to = "share"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure     = if_else(measure == "customer_share", "Share of buyers", "Share of revenue"),
    rfm_segment = factor(rfm_segment, levels = rev(rfm_summary$rfm_segment))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = rfm_segment, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito(name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "RFM Segments: Share of Buyers vs Share of Revenue",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position    = "top",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )

plot_rfm

The RFM segments are easy to interpret. Champions (344 buyers, 5% of buyers) bought within the last month on average, placed almost five orders and spent $702 each, together generating 13% of revenue. Potential Loyalists form the largest segment (38% of buyers) and generate half of all revenue. At the other end, Lost customers (15% of buyers) last bought more than two years ago and generate 6% of revenue. Two small segments deserve attention: At Risk and Can't Lose Them customers (486 buyers combined) spent around $460 each but have not bought for almost two years.

However, the segments are very unequal in size, and the largest one, Potential Loyalist, groups customers whose scores range widely. The next section tests whether a data-driven method finds a clearer structure.

docs.title: (3) Data-Driven Segmentation: K-Means
docs.text:
K-means clustering lets the algorithm group buyers with similar recency, frequency and monetary values, instead of relying on cut-offs we choose. Because K-means is based on distances, we first standardise the three variables with a recipe(); otherwise monetary value, measured in hundreds of dollars, would dominate recency (months) and frequency (counts).

# Standardise R, F and M so that monetary (hundreds of dollars) does not dominate
# recency (months) and frequency (counts) in the distance calculation
rfm_rec <-
  recipe(~ recency + frequency + monetary, data = rfm_segmented) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

rfm_scaled <-
  rfm_rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

# Verify: every scaled variable should have mean 0 and standard deviation 1
rfm_scaled |>
  summarise(across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |>
  round(3)

| recency_mean <dbl> | recency_sd <dbl> | frequency_mean <dbl> | frequency_sd <dbl> | monetary_mean <dbl> | monetary_sd <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 |

All three scaled variables now have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

K-means does not choose the number of clusters for us. We use the elbow method on all buyers and, as in class, the silhouette method on a random sample of 1,000 buyers to keep the computation fast.

# Elbow method: total within-cluster sum of squares for k = 1 to 10
plot_elbow <-
  fviz_nbclust(rfm_scaled, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 10, nstart = 10) +
  labs(
    title = "Elbow Method",
    x     = "Number of Clusters (k)",
    y     = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# Silhouette method on a random sample of 1,000 buyers (as in class, to keep computation fast)
set.seed(42)
rfm_scaled_sample <-
  rfm_scaled |>
  sample_n(1000)

plot_silhouette <-
  fviz_nbclust(rfm_scaled_sample, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 10) +
  labs(
    title = "Silhouette Method",
    x     = "Number of Clusters (k)",
    y     = "Average Silhouette Width"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

plot_elbow | plot_silhouette

The elbow plot falls steeply up to k = 3 and flattens after k = 4, where each extra cluster brings much smaller reductions in within-cluster variation. The silhouette method gives its highest score at k = 2, with k = 3 and k = 4 close behind. As in class, the methods do not agree exactly, so we balance the statistics with business usefulness: we choose k = 4, which the elbow plot supports and which separates high-value buyers into two groups of very different size and value — a distinction that two or three clusters would hide.

set.seed(123)

# nstart = 25: try 25 random starting points and keep the best solution
kmeans_4 <- kmeans(rfm_scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

plot_kmeans <-
  fviz_cluster(
    kmeans_4,
    data            = rfm_scaled,
    geom            = "point",
    shape           = 16,
    pointsize       = 1,
    ellipse         = FALSE,
    show.clust.cent = FALSE,
    ggtheme         = theme_minimal()
  ) +
  scale_color_okabe_ito() +
  labs(title = "K-Means Clustering of Buyers on Recency, Frequency and Monetary (k = 4)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

plot_kmeans

The cluster plot projects the three standardised variables onto two dimensions, so the axes have no direct business meaning. It does show that the four groups occupy distinct regions, with one small cluster stretched far out along the first dimension. To understand what each cluster represents, we summarise the clusters in their original units.

# Attach the cluster label to each buyer, then describe each cluster in original units
rfm_clustered <- augment(kmeans_4, rfm_segmented)

rfm_clustered |>
  group_by(.cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n_customers   = n(),
    avg_recency   = mean(recency),
    avg_frequency = mean(frequency),
    avg_monetary  = mean(monetary),
    avg_r_tile    = mean(r_tile),
    avg_f_tile    = mean(f_tile),
    avg_m_tile    = mean(m_tile),
    revenue       = sum(monetary)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(revenue_share = revenue / sum(revenue)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

|.cluster | n_customers| avg_recency| avg_frequency| avg_monetary| avg_r_tile| avg_f_tile| avg_m_tile|  revenue| revenue_share|
|:--------|-----------:|-----------:|-------------:|------------:|----------:|----------:|----------:|--------:|-------------:|
|1        |         645|        5.58|          4.95|       780.33|       4.06|       4.92|       4.99| 503313.0|          0.26|
|2        |        2052|        7.78|          3.04|       374.19|       3.65|       4.27|       4.18| 767828.2|          0.40|
|3        |        2260|       25.34|          1.30|       140.18|       1.34|       2.06|       2.27| 316815.3|          0.16|
|4        |        2670|        7.61|          1.45|       127.79|       3.65|       2.35|       2.23| 341187.9|          0.18|

The four clusters have clear and distinct profiles:

  • Cluster 1 (645 buyers) bought recently (5.6 months ago on average), placed about five orders and spent $780 each. It is only 8% of buyers but generates 26% of revenue.
  • Cluster 2 (2,052 buyers) also bought recently, placed three orders and spent $374 each. It is the largest source of revenue (40%).
  • Cluster 3 (2,260 buyers) last bought more than two years ago (25 months), mostly only once, and spent $140.
  • Cluster 4 (2,670 buyers) bought as recently as clusters 1 and 2 (7.6 months), but placed only 1.5 orders and spent $128.

The average quintile scores confirm the pattern: cluster 1 has near-maximum F and M scores, while clusters 3 and 4 have similar low F and M scores and differ almost only in recency. We give the clusters names that describe these profiles and compare them with the RFM segments.

# Give each cluster a business-friendly name based on the profile table above
# (cluster numbers are fixed by set.seed(123))
rfm_clustered <-
  rfm_clustered |>
  mutate(
    segment = case_when(
      .cluster == 1     ~ "VIP Spenders",
      .cluster == 2     ~ "Regular Buyers",
      .cluster == 4   ~ "Recent Light Buyers",
      .cluster == 3  ~ "Lapsed Buyers"
    )
  )

# How do the data-driven clusters line up with the rule-based RFM segments?
rfm_clustered |>
  count(segment, rfm_segment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = segment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

| rfm_segment <chr> | Lapsed Buyers <int> | Recent Light Buyers <int> | Regular Buyers <int> | VIP Spenders <int> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| About To Sleep     |  333 | 494 |    0 |   0 |
| At Risk            |   86 |   0 |  124 |  42 |
| Can't Lose Them    |  121 |   0 |  104 |   9 |
| Lost               | 1179 |   0 |    0 |   0 |
| Loyal Customers    |  408 | 434 |  114 |   0 |
| Need Attention     |  114 |   0 |   29 |   0 |
| Unclassified       |   19 |  39 |   10 |   0 |
| New Customers      |    0 | 619 |    9 |   0 |
| Potential Loyalist |    0 | 969 | 1551 | 351 |
| Promising          |    0 | 115 |   10 |   0 |
| Champions          |    0 |   0 |  101 | 243 |

The comparison shows how the two methods relate. All Lost customers fall into Lapsed Buyers, and most Champions fall into VIP Spenders, so the methods agree on the extremes. However, the large RFM Potential Loyalist segment is split across three clusters: 351 of its members behave like VIP Spenders, 1,551 like Regular Buyers and 969 like Recent Light Buyers. K-means therefore separates customers that the RFM rules had grouped together, which is exactly where a data-driven method adds insight. We use the four K-means segments for the rest of the analysis.

docs.title: (4) Who Is in Each Segment?
docs.text:
We now bring the segment labels back to the full customer table and add the 2,373 registered customers who never completed a purchase as a fifth group, "No Purchase Yet". For each segment we summarise purchase behaviour, basket characteristics, loyalty status and demographics.

segment_levels <- c("VIP Spenders", "Regular Buyers", "Recent Light Buyers",
                    "Lapsed Buyers", "No Purchase Yet")

# Bring the segment label back to the full customer table;
# registered customers who never completed a purchase form a fifth group
customers_segmented <-
  customers_full |>
  left_join(rfm_clustered |> select(cust_id, segment), by = join_by(cust_id)) |>
  mutate(
    segment = coalesce(segment, "No Purchase Yet"),
    segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_levels)
  )

segment_profile <-
  customers_segmented |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    n_customers        = n(),
    avg_recency        = mean(recency),
    avg_frequency      = mean(frequency),
    avg_monetary       = mean(monetary),
    revenue            = sum(monetary, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_order_value    = mean(avg_order_value),
    share_premium      = mean(share_premium),
    share_electronics  = mean(share_electronics),
    share_gold_plat    = mean(loyalty_tier %in% c("Gold", "Platinum")),
    avg_age            = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    share_female       = mean(gender == "Female"),
    share_us           = mean(cntry == "US"),
    share_paid_acq     = mean(acquisition_channel == "Paid Search")
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(revenue_share = revenue / sum(revenue))

segment_profile |>
  select(-revenue) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

|segment             | n_customers| avg_recency| avg_frequency| avg_monetary| avg_order_value| share_premium| share_electronics| share_gold_plat| avg_age| share_female| share_us| share_paid_acq| revenue_share|
|:-------------------|-----------:|-----------:|-------------:|------------:|---------------:|-------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|-------:|------------:|--------:|--------------:|-------------:|
|VIP Spenders        |         645|        5.58|          4.95|       780.33|          171.58|          0.60|              0.30|            0.56|   35.44|         0.47|     0.35|           0.28|          0.26|
|Regular Buyers      |        2052|        7.78|          3.04|       374.19|          137.67|          0.55|              0.26|            0.26|   34.92|         0.45|     0.35|           0.30|          0.40|
|Recent Light Buyers |        2670|        7.61|          1.45|       127.79|           92.24|          0.45|              0.19|            0.10|   35.25|         0.46|     0.36|           0.29|          0.18|
|Lapsed Buyers       |        2260|       25.34|          1.30|       140.18|          111.22|          0.51|              0.23|            0.10|   35.28|         0.47|     0.34|           0.30|          0.16|
|No Purchase Yet     |        2373|          NA|            NA|           NA|              NA|            NA|                NA|            0.03|   34.84|         0.46|     0.35|           0.29|          0.00|

# Loyalty tier mix within each segment
plot_tier <-
  customers_segmented |>
  count(segment, loyalty_tier) |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(loyalty_tier = factor(loyalty_tier, levels = c("Platinum", "Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = segment, y = share, fill = loyalty_tier)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito(name = "Loyalty Tier") +
  labs(
    title = "Loyalty Tier Mix by Customer Segment",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Share of customers in segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position    = "right",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )

plot_tier

Three patterns stand out:

  • Basket: more valuable segments buy more expensive baskets. VIP Spenders spend $172 per order, against $92 for Recent Light Buyers; 60% of their purchases are premium products (against 45%) and 30% are electronics (against 19%).
  • Loyalty tier: loyalty status lines up closely with value. 56% of VIP Spenders hold Gold or Platinum status, compared with 26% of Regular Buyers, 10% of Lapsed and Recent Light Buyers, and only 3% of customers who have not bought yet.
  • Demographics: in contrast, who the customers are barely differs across segments. Average age is about 35, 45–47% are female, about 35% live in the US and 28–30% were acquired through Paid Search in every segment, including customers who have not bought yet.

In other words, high-value customers can be recognised by how they buy and by their loyalty status, but not by their demographic profile or acquisition channel.

docs.title: (5) How Do Site Visits Turn into Purchases?
docs.text:
Finally, we look at the customer journey. For each visit we know its traffic source and device, so we can compare the share of visits that end in a purchase — the purchase rate.

# Each row of events_clean is one visit; purchase_rate = share of visits that end in a purchase
visits_by_source <-
  events_clean |>
  group_by(traffic_source, campaign_linked) |>
  summarise(
    n_visits         = n(),
    purchase_rate    = mean(purchased),
    bounce_rate      = mean(event_type == "bounce"),
    avg_duration_min = mean(session_duration_sec, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
    .groups          = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(share_of_visits = n_visits / sum(n_visits)) |>
  arrange(desc(purchase_rate))

visits_by_source |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)

|traffic_source |campaign_linked | n_visits| purchase_rate| bounce_rate| avg_duration_min| share_of_visits|
|:--------------|:---------------|--------:|-------------:|-----------:|----------------:|---------------:|
|Email          |Campaign        |    29967|         0.123|       0.089|            2.168|            0.15|
|Paid Search    |Campaign        |    39898|         0.120|       0.093|            2.169|            0.20|
|Social         |Campaign        |    30042|         0.111|       0.093|            2.163|            0.15|
|Direct         |No campaign     |    19887|         0.059|       0.102|            2.166|            0.10|
|Organic        |No campaign     |    79833|         0.058|       0.097|            2.152|            0.40|

Visits from the three campaign-linked sources — Email (12.3%), Paid Search (12.0%) and Social (11.1%) — end in a purchase about twice as often as Organic (5.8%) and Direct (5.9%) visits. Yet Organic is the largest source, accounting for 40% of all visits. Notably, bounce rates and visit durations are almost identical across sources, so campaign visitors are not more engaged in general; they are simply more likely to buy.

We next add the device dimension.

# Purchase rate by traffic source and device
# (the small "unknown" device group is left out of the chart)
plot_visits <-
  events_clean |>
  filter(device != "unknown") |>
  group_by(traffic_source, device) |>
  summarise(purchase_rate = mean(purchased), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    traffic_source = factor(traffic_source,
                            levels = c("Email", "Paid Search", "Social", "Organic", "Direct")),
    device         = factor(device, levels = c("desktop", "tablet", "mobile"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = traffic_source, y = purchase_rate, fill = device)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(events_clean$purchased),
    linetype   = "dashed",
    colour     = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_okabe_ito(name = "Device") +
  labs(
    title    = "Share of Visits Ending in a Purchase, by Traffic Source and Device",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = average across all visits",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Purchase rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey40"),
    legend.position    = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )

plot_visits

# Where do visits come from, by device?
events_clean |>
  group_by(device) |>
  summarise(
    n_visits      = n(),
    purchase_rate = mean(purchased)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(share_of_visits = n_visits / sum(n_visits))

| device <chr> | n_visits <int> | purchase_rate <dbl> | share_of_visits <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|
| desktop |  68379 | 0.11101362 | 0.34253383 |
| mobile  | 117555 | 0.07531794 | 0.58887325 |
| tablet  |   9666 | 0.09197186 | 0.04842030 |
| unknown |   4027 | 0.07847033 | 0.02017262 |

Within every traffic source, desktop visits end in a purchase more often than mobile visits, with tablets in between. Overall, 11.1% of desktop visits end in a purchase compared with 7.5% of mobile visits — yet mobile accounts for 59% of all visits. The pattern is consistent across sources, which suggests that the gap is not explained by mobile users arriving through weaker channels.

To put the campaign-linked traffic in context, we summarise marketing spend by channel from the reshaped spend table.

# Marketing spend by campaign channel and year (from the reshaped spend table)
spend_long |>
  group_by(channel, year) |>
  summarise(spend = sum(spend), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Spread years back into columns: wide is fine for a display table
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = spend, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(
    total_spend    = `2021` + `2022` + `2023`,
    share_of_spend = total_spend / sum(total_spend)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_spend))

| channel <chr> | 2021 <dbl> | 2022 <dbl> | 2023 <dbl> | total_spend <dbl> | share_of_spend <dbl> |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Email       | 130451 | 236122 | 424659 | 791232 | 0.2500965 |
| Paid Search | 175164 | 203715 | 367392 | 746271 | 0.2358850 |
| Affiliate   | 153461 | 181877 | 321377 | 656715 | 0.2075777 |
| Display     |   8143 | 258451 | 275439 | 542033 | 0.1713284 |
| Social      |  66582 |  86513 | 274361 | 427456 | 0.1351124 |

Total campaign spend almost tripled from 2021 to 2023, and Email and Paid Search received the largest budgets — the two sources with the highest purchase rates. However, Display and Affiliate campaigns received $1.2 million (38% of spend), yet no visit in the event data is recorded as coming from these channels. Either these campaigns bring visitors through other recorded sources, or their visits are not tracked; this is an open question for the marketing team rather than something we can resolve with this data.

Because campaigns target particular customer segments, the higher purchase rate of campaign-linked visits describes who these visits come from as much as what the campaigns do. It should not be read as the effect of the campaigns.

docs.title: 1. Research Question
docs.text:
• Our research question is: which groups of customers generate most of Ferdeer Retail's revenue, and how do these groups differ in who they are and in how their site visits turn into purchases?
  • This question matters because marketing resources are limited, and knowing which customers carry the business and which visits convert shows where retention and acquisition efforts are most likely to pay off.

docs.title: 2. Data & Approach
docs.text:
• We combined all eight Ferdeer Retail files for 2021–2023, covering 10,000 registered customers, 16,236 completed purchases and 199,627 site visits.
  • Cleaning removed exact duplicate rows (100 profile rows and 150 transactions), standardised inconsistent country and traffic-source labels, set impossible ages, prices and session durations to missing, and excluded 1,132 transactions with no revenue or an impossible quantity.
  • We described each buyer by the recency, frequency and monetary value of completed purchases at 1 January 2024, and treated each event row as one visit, because 99.99% of visits contain a single event.
  • We segmented buyers with the rule-based RFM scheme and with K-means clustering (k = 4) on standardised RFM values, then profiled the segments with grouped summaries.

docs.title: 3. Preliminary Findings
docs.text:
• Revenue is highly concentrated: the top 20% of buyers by spend generate 50% of revenue, while the bottom 20% generate only 3%.
  • K-means identifies two high-value segments, VIP Spenders and Regular Buyers, which together make up 35% of buyers but generate 66% of revenue (Exhibit 1).
  • VIP Spenders place about five orders, spend $780 each and buy more premium and electronics products, while Recent Light Buyers and Lapsed Buyers place only one or two orders and spend under $150.
  • Loyalty tier lines up with value, but age, gender, country and acquisition channel are almost identical across all segments, so demographics do not identify valuable customers.
  • 2,373 registered customers (24%) have never completed a purchase, and most of them are Bronze members.
  • Visits from campaign-linked sources (Email, Paid Search and Social) end in a purchase about twice as often as Organic and Direct visits, and desktop visits convert better than mobile visits within every source (Exhibit 2).

Exhibit 1. Customer segments

|Segment             | Customers| Share of Revenue| Recency (months)| Orders| Spend (USD)| Gold/Platinum| Avg. Age|
|:-------------------|---------:|----------------:|----------------:|------:|-----------:|-------------:|--------:|
|VIP Spenders        |       645|            26.1%|              5.6|    5.0|        $780|           56%|     35.4|
|Regular Buyers      |      2052|            39.8%|              7.8|    3.0|        $374|           26%|     34.9|
|Recent Light Buyers |      2670|            17.7%|              7.6|    1.5|        $128|           10%|     35.3|
|Lapsed Buyers       |      2260|            16.4%|             25.3|    1.3|        $140|           10%|     35.3|
|No Purchase Yet     |      2373|             0.0%|               NA|     NA|          NA|            3%|     34.8|

Exhibit 2. Purchase rate by traffic source and device

docs.title: 4. Assumptions & Limitations
docs.text:
• We assume the 1,132 excluded transactions (about 6% of unique transactions) are missing at random; if they belong mainly to some customers, the value of those customers is understated.
  • RFM quintiles rely on arbitrary cut-offs, and because most buyers made one or two purchases, ntile() splits identical customers into different frequency scores.
  • The K-means segments depend on the three variables we chose and on k = 4, and the silhouette method slightly preferred fewer clusters.
  • Campaigns target particular segments, so the higher purchase rate of campaign-linked visits does not show that campaigns cause purchases.

docs.title: 5. Open Questions for Feedback
docs.text:
• Display and Affiliate campaigns received $1.2 million (38% of 2021–2023 spend), yet no visit is recorded under these channels, so how are these visits tracked?
  • Should the VIP segment be defined by K-means, or by a simple spending rule (such as the top 20% of buyers) that managers can update each month?
  • Should refunded purchases reduce a customer's value, rather than simply being excluded from it?

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text:
• We would repeat the segmentation for each year to see whether customers move between segments, especially from Regular Buyers to Lapsed Buyers.
  • We would link visits to segments to compare the traffic sources and devices each segment uses.
  • We would analyse the checkout experiment to test whether the new checkout designs raise purchase rates, particularly on mobile.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: We examined which Ferdeer Retail customers generate most of the company's revenue and how their website visits turn into purchases, using three years of customer, sales and website data. Two customer segments, VIP Spenders and Regular Buyers, make up one in three buyers but bring in two of every three dollars of revenue. These customers stand out by how they buy and by their loyalty status, not by their age, gender or country. Visits that arrive through marketing campaigns end in a purchase about twice as often as other visits, and desktop visits convert better than mobile ones.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Revenue is highly concentrated: the top fifth of buyers generates half of all revenue, while a quarter of registered customers have never bought.
  • VIP Spenders, 8% of buyers, place about five orders and spend $780 each, buy more premium and electronics products, and more than half hold Gold or Platinum status.
  • Email, Paid Search and Social visits end in a purchase 11–12% of the time, compared with 6% for Organic and Direct visits, and mobile visits, the majority of traffic, convert least often.

docs.title: Business Implications
docs.text:
• Losing a small number of high-value customers would remove a large share of revenue, so keeping VIP Spenders and Regular Buyers is the first priority.
  • Targeting by demographics is unlikely to find more high-value customers, because purchase history and loyalty status are far better guides.
  • Most visits happen on mobile, where visits are least likely to end in a purchase, so the mobile experience is where the largest number of sales opportunities is lost.

docs.title: Recommended Actions
docs.text:
• Launch a retention programme for VIP Spenders and Regular Buyers, selecting customers by purchase history and loyalty tier.
  • Run a first-purchase offer for the 2,373 registered customers who have never bought, and a win-back offer for Lapsed Buyers.
  • Review the mobile purchase journey, and confirm how Display and Affiliate visits are tracked before reallocating campaign budget.
