docs.title: Short Answer Question 01
docs.text:
You are an equity analyst at a large investment firm. As part of your role, you must forecast a company's quarterly earnings per share (EPS). Portfolio managers use your forecasts to value the stock and make investment decisions.

You have quarterly EPS data from 2015–2022. Use 2015–2021 as the training set and 2022 as the test set. Compare three models:

  • Model A (historical mean): predicts EPS using the average of all past values.
  • Model B (lag-1): predicts EPS in quarter t using EPS from quarter t–1.
  • Model C (multivariate OLS): predicts EPS using lagged financial statements data and current macroeconomic indicators.

Assume:

  • Outcome variable: eps
  • Quarterly timestamp: qtr_date (class Date)
  • Use a time-based split: train = qtr_date < 2022-01-01; test = qtr_date ≥ 2022-01-01.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Finish the R code to split the data into training and test sets. (5 marks)

train <- df |> filter(STARTER CODE HERE)
test  <- df |> filter(STARTER CODE HERE)

Answer:

train <- df |> filter(qtr_date < as.Date("2022-01-01"))
test  <- df |> filter(qtr_date >= as.Date("2022-01-01"))

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Finish the R code to calculate the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for Model B on the test set, where pred_B already contains the lag-1 predictions. (5 marks)

test_mape <- test |>
  YOUR_FUNCTION_NAME(
    perc_err = abs(YOUR_STARTER_CODE) * 100
  ) |>
  summarise(
    MAPE = YOUR_STARTER_CODE
  ) |>
  pull(MAPE)

Answer:

test_mape <- test |>
  mutate(
    perc_err = abs((eps - pred_B) / eps) * 100
  ) |>
  summarise(
    MAPE = mean(perc_err, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(MAPE)

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

Explain how MAPE can be used for model selection, and state one strength and one limitation of MAPE for EPS forecasting. (Answer in 3–4 sentences.) (5 marks)

Answer:

MAPE measures the average percentage error on the test set, making it scale-free and easy to compare across models. For model selection, choose the model with the lowest test-set MAPE, since it indicates the most accurate forecasts relative to the size of EPS. A strength is its intuitive interpretation in percentage terms. A limitation is that MAPE can explode when EPS is near zero, and it penalises over- and under-predictions equally, which may not reflect investor concerns.

docs.title: Short Answer Question 02
docs.text:
You are a hedge fund portfolio manager collecting sell-side analyst forecasts for listed firms. Data is provided in analysts.json, with each firm having multiple analyst recommendations nested under "recs".

For example:

{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "recs": [
    {"analyst": "BankA", "rating": "Buy", "target_price": 120},
    {"analyst": "BrokerB", "rating": "Hold", "target_price": 105}
  ]
}

You first run the following code in R:

analysts_nested <- read_json("analysts.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

You next run the following code:

analysts_tbl <- tibble(record = list(analysts_nested))

Explain what this code does. What column is in the tibble analysts_tbl and what does this column contain? (2 marks)

Answer:

This code wraps the parsed JSON into a tibble with one column record.

The tibble analysts_tbl has one row, one column containing the entire JSON as a list.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

You next run the following code:

analysts_wide <- analysts_tbl |>
  unnest_longer(record) |>
  unnest_wider(record)

Explain what these two unnesting steps do. What columns are in the tibble analysts_wide and what do they contain? (2 marks)

Answer:

First unnesting step unnest_longer(record) expands record so that there is one row per firm, where each cell is a list (of lists). Second unnesting step unnest_wider(record) expands these lists into separate columns. The new tibble has ticker (e.g., "ACME") and recs (a list column of recommendations).

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

You then run the following code:

analysts_long <- analysts_wide |>
  unnest_longer(recs) |>
  unnest_wider(recs)

Explain what these two unnesting steps do. What is each row in the tibble analysts_long? What columns are in this tibble? (2 marks)

Answer:

First unnesting step unnest_longer(recs) creates one row per analyst recommendation.

Second unnesting step unnest_wider(recs) expands each recommendation into columns analyst, rating, target_price.

The final tibble has one row per analyst with columns ticker, analyst, rating, target_price.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

Explain one advantage of storing this kind of nested data in JSON compared to storing it in a flat CSV. (Answer in 2–3 sentences.) (4 marks)

Answer:

JSON represents nested, hierarchical data directly. A CSV would repeat the ticker for each row, making it less efficient and harder to parse.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

Suppose you collect many such JSON files across multiple firms and years. Explain why using DuckDB may be more effective than keeping them as a list of JSON objects in R. (Answer in 2–3 sentences.) (5 marks)

Answer:

DuckDB queries across many JSON-derived tables efficiently without loading everything into memory. It supports joins, filtering, and aggregation, making it scalable compared to holding JSONs in R.

docs.title: Short Answer Question 03
docs.text:
A hotel chain wants to segment its customers based on length of stay and booking channel. A customer may book through an OTA (Online Travel Agency) such as Booking.com or Expedia, or Direct through the hotel's own website or phone line. Management proposes the following rule-based segments:

  • Segment A: Short stay (≤2 nights) + OTA booking
  • Segment B: Short stay (≤2 nights) + Direct booking
  • Segment C: Long stay (≥5 nights) + OTA booking
  • Segment D: Long stay (≥5 nights) + Direct booking

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Write R code using case_when() to assign customers to these four segments in a new column called segment. (4 marks)

Answer:

hotel_data <- hotel_data |>
  mutate(
    segment = case_when(
      length_of_stay <= 2 & booking_channel == "OTA"    ~ "Segment A",
      length_of_stay <= 2 & booking_channel == "Direct" ~ "Segment B",
      length_of_stay >= 5 & booking_channel == "OTA"    ~ "Segment C",
      length_of_stay >= 5 & booking_channel == "Direct" ~ "Segment D",
      TRUE ~ "Unassigned"
    )
  )

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

Suppose you run this code and find that 40% of customers are not assigned to any of the four segments. Explain why this might happen. (3 marks)

Answer:

Customers staying 3–4 nights don't fit either the short (≤2) or long (≥5) rules, so they remain unassigned. This shows that rule-based segmentation can leave gaps if the rules don't cover all cases.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

What are two shortcomings of relying on this kind of rule-based segmentation? (4 marks)

Answer:

  1. Arbitrary cut-offs may not reflect actual differences in behaviour.
  2. Ignores other variables (e.g., spend, room type, satisfaction).

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

How could a data-driven approach (e.g., clustering using multiple features) help overcome these shortcomings? (4 marks)

Answer:

A clustering approach could group customers based on multiple features without pre-defined cut-offs. This reduces gaps, captures richer behavioural patterns, and produces segments more reflective of the underlying data.

docs.title: Short Answer Question 04
docs.text:
You are an accounting analyst at a mid-sized firm. Management is considering a new automated invoice reminder system to reduce the number of overdue client payments.

To evaluate it, the firm runs an A/B test:

  • Group A (Control): Clients continue receiving manual reminders from the finance team.
  • Group B (Treatment): Clients receive automated reminders generated by the new system.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Why does random assignment of clients to Group A and Group B help identify the causal effect of the automated system? (3 marks)

Answer:

Randomisation balances observed and unobserved characteristics across groups, so differences in overdue payment rates can be attributed to the reminder system rather than other factors.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

Write R code to calculate the overdue payment rate (percentage of invoices paid late) for each group. (3 marks)

Answer:

invoices |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(overdue_rate = mean(overdue, na.rm = TRUE))

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

Suppose the overdue payment rate is 28% in Group A and 22% in Group B. Interpret this result in business terms in 2–3 sentences. (4 marks)

Answer:

Automated reminders reduce late payments by 6 percentage points (28% → 22%). This suggests the system is effective in improving cash flow and reducing working capital tied up in receivables.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

Using client payment history for experiments raises ethical and data governance issues. Identify one such concern and explain why it matters for accounting analytics. (5 marks)

Answer:

Using client payment data may raise privacy and governance concerns. Clients might not expect their information to be used in experiments, and mishandling sensitive financial data could breach regulations or erode trust. Accounting analytics must ensure compliance with legal standards (e.g., data protection laws) and maintain professional ethics.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Which of the following best captures this subject’s definition of business analytics?

Options:

  • A. The use of intuition and experience to make decisions in uncertain environments.
  • B. The application of data and analytical tools to support and improve decision-making.
  • C. The automation of all business decisions through artificial intelligence.
  • D. The gathering of empirical insights to guide the development of theoretical models of consumer and producer behaviour.
  • E. The process of replacing business managers with algorithms.

Answer: B

  • A. Incorrect - describes “gut instinct” (HIPPO era), not business analytics.
  • B. Correct - this is the working definition provided in lectures and notes.
  • C. Incorrect - analytics supports decisions, it does not automate all of them.
  • D. Incorrect - analytics is not primarily concerned with theory development.
  • E. Incorrect - analytics supports managers; it does not replace them.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

Consider the following business questions. Which require causal analytics? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Would offering a loyalty program increase repeat purchases among existing customers?
  2. How many units of our new product are likely to sell in its first quarter?
  3. What proportion of last year's revenue came from online sales?
  4. Would introducing a bonus scheme for sales reps increase the number of new client acquisitions?
  5. Which stores had the highest return rates last month?

Options:

  • A. 1 and 2
  • B. 2 and 3
  • C. 1 and 4
  • D. 2, 4, and 5
  • E. 1, 2, and 3

Answer: C

  • A. Incorrect - Q2 is predictive, not causal.
  • B. Incorrect - both Q2 (predictive) and Q3 (descriptive) are not causal.
  • C. Correct - both Q1 and Q4 ask "what if" about business actions.
  • D. Incorrect - Q2 is predictive, Q5 is descriptive.
  • E. Incorrect - mixes causal with non-causal questions.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

A consulting team is tasked with analysing why customer wait times at a bank have increased. Which core skills are most directly relevant at the start of the project? (Select all that apply.)

Options:

  • A. Institutional detail (understanding how banks operate)
  • B. Analytical modelling (choosing a data modelling tool)
  • C. Creativity & judgment (framing answerable questions)
  • D. Computational skills (coding the analysis immediately)
  • E. Business theory (thinking about incentives and trade-offs)

Answer: A, C, E

  • A. Correct - understanding the industry context is crucial.
  • B. Incorrect - modelling comes later, once the problem is framed.
  • C. Correct - asking the right questions is foundational.
  • D. Incorrect - jumping into coding skips problem framing.
  • E. Correct - theories of incentives and constraints help structure thinking.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

Which practices contribute to making an analysis reproducible? (Select all that apply.)

Options:

  • A. Clearly commenting code
  • B. Saving raw data separately from transformed data
  • C. Using short names for objects and outputs so results can be easily retrieved
  • D. Organising scripts or markdown files into logical sections
  • E. Documenting assumptions and choices

Answer: A, B, D, E

  • A. Correct - comments help others follow.
  • B. Correct - preserves the integrity of raw data.
  • C. Incorrect - short names do not make objects or output more retrievable.
  • D. Correct - logical organisation aids clarity.
  • E. Correct - assumptions and decisions must be transparent.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

Two analysts are examining customer satisfaction survey scores across departments of a large financial services firm. One analyst argues a table of summary stats is sufficient; the other insists on also plotting the raw data. Which of the below supports the second analyst's position?

Options:

  • A. Plots are only useful when sample sizes are very small.
  • B. Visualisation can reveal patterns and structures not visible in summary statistics.
  • C. Tables are always superior for communicating variation.
  • D. Plots make it easier to calculate means and standard deviations.
  • E. Visualisation is helpful for adding cosmetic polish to presentations.

Answer: B

  • A. Incorrect - visualisation is valuable at any sample size.
  • B. Correct - Anscombe's quartet and Datasaurus Dozen show that identical stats can mask very different patterns.
  • C. Incorrect - tables don't always reveal shape or anomalies.
  • D. Incorrect - plots are not necessary for calculating descriptive statistics.
  • E. Incorrect - visualisation is central to business analytics.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

An airline analyst plots flight delays (minutes) against distance flown (miles).

ggplot(flights, aes(x = distance, y = delay)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Flight Delays vs Distance",
    x = "Distance flown (miles)",
    y = "Delay (minutes)"
    )

Which of the following best explains both the visualisation choice and the managerial insight?

Options:

  • A. The analyst used alpha = 0.5 to reduce overplotting, which reveals that most flights have small delays and only a few long-distance flights drive extreme delays.
  • B. The analyst used alpha = 0.5 to make the points larger, which shows that delays increase linearly with distance.
  • C. The analyst used alpha = 0.5 to highlight average trends, which shows that distance has no effect on delays.
  • D. The analyst used alpha = 0.5 to hide data points, which shows that all long-distance flights are unreliable.
  • E. The analyst used alpha = 0.5 to colour points by airline, which shows similar reliability across all carriers.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - transparency (alpha) reduces overplotting, revealing dense clusters and the insight that most flights are fine, but a few long-distance outliers drive delays.
  • B. Incorrect - alpha changes transparency, not point size; delays are not linear.
  • C. Incorrect - visualisation shows some effect (outliers), not "no effect."
  • D. Incorrect - transparency reveals patterns, it doesn't hide points; not all long flights are unreliable.
  • E. Incorrect - colouring by airline was not used here.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

An analyst produces a bar chart of Revenue by Category.

In the code that produces this plot, what does fct_reorder(category, revenue, .fun = sum, .desc = TRUE) do - and why would the analyst want to do this?

Options:

  • A. It orders the categories by their total revenue from highest to lowest, so the bar chart makes it easy to compare total revenue across product categories.
  • B. It flips the chart horizontally so labels are easier to read, which automatically reveals rank.
  • C. It colours bars by revenue to highlight the largest bars.
  • D. It increases bar width so differences look bigger.
  • E. It filters the data to only keep the top category.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - fct_reorder(..., .desc = TRUE) arranges the category factor by total revenue, highest → lowest, which makes the ranking easy to see.
  • B. Incorrect - flipping orientation (coord_flip()) can help readability, but does not sort categories.
  • C. Incorrect - no colour mapping is used here; ordering (not colour) conveys rank.
  • D. Incorrect - bar width doesn't change ordering or clarify rank.
  • E. Incorrect - no filtering occurs; all categories are kept and ordered.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

Consider the following:

firms |>
  group_by(industry) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_profit = mean(profit),
    median_profit = median(profit)
  )

What does this code do, and why might an analyst want to do it?

Options:

  • A. It calculates the average and median profit for each industry, allowing the analyst to observe how skewed profits are in different industries.
  • B. It removes all missing values so profits can be compared fairly across industries.
  • C. It ranks industries from most to least profitable and filters out those with below-average profit.
  • D. It reshapes the dataset from long to wide so each industry becomes a separate column.
  • E. It computes cumulative profit over time to show industry growth trajectories.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - group_by(industry) then summarise() computes both mean and median profit per industry; comparing mean vs median helps assess skew (e.g., mean >> median suggests right-skew due to a few very high-profit firms).
  • B. Incorrect - no explicit missing-value handling is included.
  • C. Incorrect - no ranking or filtering occurs; it only summarises.
  • D. Incorrect - this is aggregation, not reshaping.
  • E. Incorrect - there is no time variable or cumulative operation here.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

Which of the following best describes why managers would care about tidy data principles?

Options:

  • A. Tidy data makes coding outputs look impressive.
  • B. Tidy data ensures consistent structure, making analysis easier to implement and results easier to interpret, share, and act on.
  • C. Tidy data automatically improves profits.
  • D. Tidy data prevents missing values from appearing.
  • E. Tidy data guarantees causal results.

Answer: B

  • A. Incorrect - appearance isn't the goal.
  • B. Correct - tidy data supports clarity and reproducibility.
  • C. Incorrect - profits are not automatic.
  • D. Incorrect - missing values can still occur.
  • E. Incorrect - causality is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

An analyst examines a transaction-level data frame and wants to know how many purchases each customer made. They use:

transactions |> count(customer_id)

Which of the following code chunks produces an equivalent result, and why might an analyst prefer using count()?

Options:

  • A. transactions |> group_by(customer_id) |> summarise(n = n()) - count() is more concise and easier to read.
  • B. transactions |> group_by(customer_id) |> mutate(n = n()) - count() is more concise and easier to read.
  • C. transactions |> filter(customer_id) - count() is less computationally demanding.
  • D. transactions |> arrange(customer_id) - count() is more computationally demanding.
  • E. transactions |> select(customer_id) - count() handles missing values in a more appropriate manner.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - equivalent to count().
  • B. Incorrect - mutate() adds a column without collapsing rows; it does not produce a count per customer.
  • C. Incorrect - filter() subsets rows, not counts them.
  • D. Incorrect - arrange() reorders rows, not counts them.
  • E. Incorrect - select() subsets columns, not counts them.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Which action best explains why managers would want to use arrange()?

Options:

  • A. To identify top or bottom performers by quickly ranking rows.
  • B. To remove unneeded variables.
  • C. To filter out missing observations.
  • D. To create new calculated fields.
  • E. To summarise into one row.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - arranging ranks firms or products for decisions.
  • B. Incorrect - variable removal is select().
  • C. Incorrect - row removal is filter().
  • D. Incorrect - new fields are created with mutate().
  • E. Incorrect - summarise() produces one row.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

An analyst wants to calculate return on assets (ROA = profit / assets) for each firm. Why is mutate() the appropriate function to use?

Options:

  • A. It creates new variables based on existing ones, adding them so analysts can study ratios like ROA alongside raw numbers.
  • B. It permanently deletes old variables and replaces them with new ones, saving storage space.
  • C. It aggregates results and reduces rows, making summaries easier to present.
  • D. It reorders rows, helping managers quickly scan for outliers.
  • E. It automatically fixes missing values, saving the analyst effort.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - mutate() adds new variables while preserving existing ones.
  • B. Incorrect - it doesn't delete variables.
  • C. Incorrect - summarisation reduces rows, not mutation.
  • D. Incorrect - ordering is done with arrange().
  • E. Incorrect - missing values remain unless handled.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

An analyst at an online auction platform has two datasets:

  • bids table (bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount)
  • bidders table (bidder_id, username, country, reputation_score)

They run the following code:

bids |>
  left_join(
    bidders |> select(bidder_id, country),
    by = "bidder_id"
  )

Which columns will be in the resulting data frame?

Options:

  • A. bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount, username, country, reputation_score
  • B. bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount, country
  • C. bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount
  • D. bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount, username, country
  • E. bidder_id, username, country

Answer: B

  • A. Incorrect - username and reputation_score were dropped by the select().
  • B. Correct - all columns from bids are retained plus the country column from bidders.
  • C. Incorrect - misses the joined country column.
  • D. Incorrect - username was not included in the select().
  • E. Incorrect - a left join always retains the original bids columns (bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, amount).

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

An HR analyst uses semi_join(employees, payroll, by = "employee_id"). What does this return?

Options:

  • A. Employees with payroll records, but without payroll variables attached.
  • B. All employees, with NAs for missing payroll.
  • C. Payroll records unmatched to employees.
  • D. A count of all matched employees.
  • E. Employees without payroll records.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - semi_join() filters employees to those with matches, without attaching payroll columns.
  • B. Incorrect - that's left_join().
  • C. Incorrect - that's anti_join() from payroll → employees.
  • D. Incorrect - no count is produced automatically.
  • E. Incorrect - opposite of semi-join.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

Why might a product manager use pivot_wider() on a dataset that logs daily sales by product and channel?

date product channel sales 2025-06-01 Widget Online 120 2025-06-01 Widget Store 80 2025-06-01 Gizmo Online 60 2025-06-02 Widget Online 150 2025-06-02 Widget Store 70 2025-06-02 Gizmo Online 55

Options:

  • A. To make comparisons across channels easier by putting each channel in its own column.
  • B. To ensure missing values are automatically removed.
  • C. To calculate total sales across all channels.
  • D. To reduce the number of variables in the dataset.
  • E. To group products by channel.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - channel sales become side-by-side columns.
  • B. Incorrect - pivot doesn't drop NAs by default.
  • C. Incorrect - summarisation required.
  • D. Incorrect - often increases columns.
  • E. Incorrect - grouping requires group_by().

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

A messy dataset records survey responses with both age and gender in one column:

respondent age_gender response 1 25_M Yes 2 30_F No

Which transformation makes this tidy?

Options:

  • A. Use separate() to split age_gender into two variables.
  • B. Use pivot_longer() to move age and gender into rows.
  • C. Use pivot_wider() to spread responses into columns.
  • D. Use filter() to keep only female respondents.
  • E. Use mutate() to calculate mean age.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - separate() splits combined values into tidy variables.
  • B. Incorrect - pivot_longer() is for wide → long reshaping.
  • C. Incorrect - pivot_wider() spreads row values into new columns.
  • D. Incorrect - filtering doesn't tidy.
  • E. Incorrect - calculating doesn't fix messy structure.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

A marketing analyst has customer transaction data stored in a CSV file. Why might moving this data into a relational database be better as the company grows?

Options:

  • A. Databases scale better for large datasets and allow multiple users to query simultaneously.
  • B. Databases automatically produce visualisations of results.
  • C. CSVs cannot store numeric data.
  • D. Databases ensure that missing values are never present.
  • E. Databases always run faster than any other storage option, regardless of size.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - databases handle scale and concurrency, unlike flat files.
  • B. Incorrect - visualisation requires separate tools.
  • C. Incorrect - CSVs can store numeric values.
  • D. Incorrect - missing data can exist in databases.
  • E. Incorrect - performance depends on context.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

A portfolio manager is working with analyst recommendations for a stock. The data should have a ticker symbol ("ACME") and a list of recommendations under "recs", where each recommendation has three fields: "analyst", "rating", and "target_price". Which JSON correctly represents this structure?

Options:

  • A.
{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "recs": [
    {"analyst": "BankA", "rating": "Buy", "target_price": 120},
    {"analyst": "BrokerB", "rating": "Hold", "target_price": 105},
    {"analyst": "AdvisoryC", "rating": "Sell", "target_price": 90}
  ]
}
  • B.
{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "recs": {
    "analyst": ["BankA", "BrokerB", "AdvisoryC"],
    "rating": ["Buy", "Hold", "Sell"],
    "target_price": [120, 105, 90]
  }
}
  • C.
{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "recs": "BankA: Buy 120, BrokerB: Hold 105, AdvisoryC: Sell 90"
}
  • D.
{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "analyst": "BankA",
  "rating": "Buy",
  "target_price": 120
}
  • E.
{
  "ticker": "ACME",
  "recs": [
    ["BankA", "Buy", 120],
    ["BrokerB", "Hold", 105],
    ["AdvisoryC", "Sell", 90]
  ]
}

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - each recommendation is its own JSON object inside the recs array, with named fields for analyst, rating, and target_price.
  • B. Incorrect - this nests vectors under keys; it works structurally, but not as an array of records (harder to unnest).
  • C. Incorrect - this collapses everything into a single string, losing structure.
  • D. Incorrect - this only includes a single recommendation, not a list.
  • E. Incorrect - uses arrays of values instead of objects with named fields, so the meaning of each position must be remembered.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

A sales analyst connects to a database with:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
tbl(con, "sales") |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(total = sum(amount)) |>
  collect()

What is the purpose of adding collect() at the end of this query?

Options:

  • A. To ensure missing values are filled with zero.
  • B. To speed up the SQL query.
  • C. To remove duplicates in the result.
  • D. To automatically export results to Excel.
  • E. To bring results into R for local analysis and visualisation.

Answer: E

  • A. Incorrect - The function that fills missing values is mutate(if_else(is.na(total), 0, total)), not collect().
  • B. Incorrect - collect() does not speed up the query; it executes it and retrieves results.
  • C. Incorrect - The function that removes duplicates is distinct(), not collect().
  • D. Incorrect - The function that exports to Excel is write_xlsx(), not collect().
  • E. Correct - collect() executes the query and retrieves the results into R for further manipulation or visualisation.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

An equities analyst wants to collect daily stock prices from a public API. The API returns data in JSON format. In R, she writes:

library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
res <- GET("https://api.example.com/stocks/ACME")
data <- fromJSON(content(res, "text"))

What does this code do?

Options:

  • A. It sends a request to the API, retrieves the JSON response, and converts it into an R object.
  • B. It scrapes stock prices directly from the HTML of the company's website.
  • C. It opens a CSV file containing historical stock data.
  • D. It connects to a SQL database storing ACME's financial records.
  • E. It simulates fake data for stock prices.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct - GET() queries the API, content(...,"text") pulls the JSON response, and fromJSON() converts it into a usable R object.
  • B. Incorrect - scraping HTML would use rvest, not httr + jsonlite.
  • C. Incorrect - no CSV is being read here.
  • D. Incorrect - no database connection (DBI::dbConnect) is used.
  • E. Incorrect - no simulation is done.

docs.title: Introduction. Working with Product Review data.
docs.text:
Imagine you are a business analyst working in Amazon's Pet Supplies team. You have been given a dataset of customer reviews for pet products sold on Amazon. Your task is to use these data to understand customer feedback, identify patterns in product reviews, and support business decisions based on the information available.

The dataset includes the following variables:

  • customer_id : unique ID for the customer who wrote the review
  • product_id : unique ID for the product being reviewed
  • product_title : name of the product
  • star_rating : star score given by the customer, from 1 to 5
  • helpful_votes : number of users who marked the review as helpful
  • review_date : date the review was submitted

docs.title: Part A. Understanding the business question and the data
docs.text: Before diving into analysis, it is important to understand what this dataset contains, what kinds of questions it can answer, and how to inspect it in R.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Question:

Which of the following business questions could be answered directly using this dataset alone?

Options:

  • A. Which pet products received the most reviews?
  • B. Whether customers who bought dog products later switched to cat products
  • C. Whether higher-rated pet products sold more units
  • D. Whether a 0.5-star increase in rating causes higher sales

Answer: A

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Question:

The data are stored in the data directory of a posit cloud workspace in a file called "pet_supplies.csv". Which line of code would correctly read the dataset into R and store it in an object called pet_supplies?

Options:

  • A. pet_supplies <- read_csv("pet_supplies.csv")
  • B. pet_supplies <- read_csv("data/pet_supplies.csv")
  • C. pet_supplies <- read_csv(data/"pet_supplies.csv")
  • D. pet_supplies <- read_csv("data_pet_supplies.csv")

Answer: B

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Question:

Which two functions would directly return the number of rows and the number of columns in pet_supplies?

Options:

  • A. nrow() and ncol()
  • B. rows() and cols()
  • C. count_rows() and count_columns()
  • D. glimpse() and names()

Answer: A

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Question:

A small preview of the dataset is shown below.

customer_id product_id product_title star_rating review_date 1001 B001E4KFG0 Dog Chew Toy 5 2015-01-03 1001 B009PLS8KQ Cat Litter Mat 4 2015-02-11 8845 B001E4KFG0 Dog Chew Toy 3 2015-03-20 7712 B004A7X27A Bird Seed Mix 5 2015-03-20 5520 B00HZX9OQY Pet Shampoo 2 2015-01-03

Based on this preview, what does each row in the dataset most likely represent?

Options:

  • A. A review of a pet product written by a customer
  • B. All reviews posted on a given date
  • C. A single pet product
  • D. A single customer

Answer: A

docs.title: Part B: Transforming the Data with dplyr
docs.text: In this section, you will work with the pet_supplies review dataset to answer business questions using data transformation tools from dplyr.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Question:

You want to keep only the variables needed to study which products received the highest ratings and when those reviews were posted. Which code does this correctly?

Options:

  • A. pet_supplies |> select(product_id, product_title, star_rating, review_date)
  • B. pet_supplies |> summarise(product_id, product_title, star_rating, review_date)
  • C. pet_supplies |> distinct(product_id, product_title, star_rating, review_date)
  • D. pet_supplies |> filter(product_id, product_title, star_rating, review_date)

Answer: A

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
Question:

You want a single-number summary showing how many different customers appear in pet_supplies. Which code best does this?

Options:

  • A. pet_supplies |> summarise(n_customers = n())
  • B. pet_supplies |> distinct(customer_id)
  • C. pet_supplies |> summarise(n_customers = n_distinct(customer_id))
  • D. pet_supplies |> select(customer_id)

Answer: C

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
Question:

Suppose an analyst writes the following code:

pet_supplies |>
  group_by(star_rating) |>
  summarise(n = n())

What does the resulting table contain?

Options:

  • A. One row for each star rating, with the number of reviews in each rating category
  • B. One row for each customer, with the number of ratings they gave
  • C. One row for each review date, with the average star rating on that date
  • D. One row for each product, with its average star rating

Answer: A

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
Question:

An analyst has already created the following summary table:

rating_summary <- pet_supplies |>
  group_by(star_rating) |>
  summarise(n = n())

They now want to add a new column showing the percentage of all reviews in each star-rating category. Which line of code would do this correctly?

Options:

  • A. rating_summary |> mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))
  • B. rating_summary |> summarise(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))
  • C. rating_summary |> mutate(pct = 100 * n / n)
  • D. rating_summary |> summarise(pct = 100 * n / n)

Answer: A

docs.title: Q9
docs.text:
Question:

You want to produce a table showing the products with the largest number of reviews at the top. Which code does this correctly?

Options:

  • A. pet_supplies |> group_by(product_id) |> summarise(n = n()) |> arrange(n)
  • B. pet_supplies |> arrange(desc(product_id)) |> summarise(n = n())
  • C. pet_supplies |> summarise(n = n(product_id)) |> arrange(desc(n))
  • D. pet_supplies |> group_by(product_id) |> summarise(n = n()) |> arrange(desc(n))

Answer: D

docs.title: Q10
docs.text:
Question:

You want to count the number of reviews for each combination of product and star rating. Which code does this correctly?

Options:

  • A. pet_supplies |> group_by(product_id) |> summarise(n = n(star_rating))
  • B. pet_supplies |> group_by(product_id, star_rating) |> summarise(n = n())
  • C. pet_supplies |> group_by(star_rating) |> summarise(n = n())
  • D. pet_supplies |> group_by(product_id, star_rating) |> summarise(n = count())

Answer: B

docs.title: Q11

docs.title: Tutorial Class 01 Set 01 - Core Skills of a Business Scientist in the GenAI Era
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this workshop, you should be able to:

  • Define key concepts in the Uber surge-pricing case in clear, non-technical language.
  • Formulate a decision-relevant research question that is specific, measurable, and appropriately scoped.
  • Identify the data Uber would need to investigate suspected coordination and distinguish plausible signals from confounds.
  • Propose a first-pass detection idea and explain ways in which the analysis could go wrong.
  • Evaluate how different workflows with GenAI shape the quality and defensibility of your analysis and your ownership of the work.

docs.title: The Business Challenge
docs.text:
Uber is facing a new challenge in cities like Sydney and Melbourne. Some drivers have found a way to game the surge pricing system by temporarily logging off in groups to reduce supply. This triggers a surge in prices—and when they log back in, they benefit from higher fares.

While this behavior doesn’t technically break any rules, it raises serious concerns. Should Uber treat it as clever strategy or as manipulation? Should it intervene—and if so, how? Cracking down too hard could upset drivers and hurt morale. Doing nothing might damage rider trust and public perception.

Uber’s analytics and operations teams need to investigate what’s really going on, what’s driving this behavior, and whether (and how) to respond in a way that balances fairness, incentives, and platform health.

docs.title: Prepare these Exercises before Class
docs.text: Prepare these exercises before coming to class. Plan to spend 30 minutes on these exercises.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Identifying the key concepts
docs.text:
Watch this short news story: “Uber drivers creating artificial surge prices” (ABC News, 29 July 2025).

In your own words, define the following key terms or ideas mentioned in the article:

  • Surge pricing
  • Algorithmic pricing
  • Platform manipulation
  • Driver incentives

Tip: You don’t need to provide formal or technical definitions. Focus on explaining each concept in your own words, based on how it was used in the video.

Solution

These are example solutions, there are many ways one could answer these questions:

  • Surge Pricing: A dynamic pricing system used by Uber to increase fares when demand from riders exceeds the number of available drivers in an area. It’s designed to encourage more drivers to come online during peak times by offering higher earnings.

  • Algorithmic Pricing: The automated process by which Uber’s system adjusts fares based on real-time data like supply, demand, traffic, and location. Prices are determined not by a person but by algorithms using live inputs.

  • Platform Manipulation: When users—drivers in this case—intentionally alter their behavior to exploit the rules or algorithms of a digital platform to their advantage. In the video, this involves drivers coordinating to log off in order to trigger artificial price surges.

  • Driver Incentives: The rewards or earning opportunities Uber offers to encourage certain behaviors—like staying online during busy times, completing a certain number of rides, or accepting trips in high-demand areas. These incentives shape driver decisions and are central to how the platform functions.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Defining the Problem
docs.text:
Imagine you’re part of Uber’s analytics + operations team investigating this in Sydney and Melbourne.

Part A (3–4 sentences): Define the problem for Uber. Your answer must include:

  • What’s happening: one sentence describing the suspected behavior in concrete terms.
  • Why it matters: one sentence naming who is affected and what Uber risks (e.g., revenue, trust, retention, regulation).
  • What Uber needs to decide: one sentence stating the decision Uber faces next week (e.g., monitor, redesign surge, enforce rules).
  • How we’d judge success: one sentence naming one measurable indicator that would improve if Uber responds well (e.g., fewer extreme surges, shorter wait times, fewer cancellations, improved rider ratings, stable driver online time).

Part B (one sentence): Write one research question to guide analysis. Your question should include:

  • an outcome (what you will measure),
  • a behavior/exposure (what you think is driving it), and
  • a scope (a location and/or time of day to focus on).

Solution

This is an example solution, there are many ways one could answer this question.

Part A

  • What’s happening: In Sydney and Melbourne, groups of drivers may be coordinating short periods of logging off at the same time in the same areas, making supply look artificially low and triggering surge pricing before they log back on to earn higher fares.

  • Why it matters: This can raise prices and wait times for riders in a way that feels unfair, damage trust in the platform, and create reputational or regulatory risk—while also affecting Uber’s relationship with drivers if the company responds too aggressively.

  • What Uber needs to decide: Uber needs to decide whether to treat this as normal strategic behaviour to monitor, or as harmful manipulation that requires an intervention (e.g., changes to surge design, warnings, or enforcement).

  • How we’d judge success: A good response would reduce “spiky” or unusual surge events that appear to be driven by sudden supply drops, while keeping rider wait times stable and maintaining normal driver participation (e.g., driver online time doesn’t fall).

Part B

In Sydney and Melbourne during peak periods (e.g., weekend nights), do sudden clustered driver log-offs within a local area increase the frequency or intensity of surge pricing?

docs.title: Exercise 3: Proposing a way forward
docs.text:
Your manager turns to you and says: "Where should we start?"

Part A: Write 5 bullet points describing your approach. You must include:

  • one bullet on what context/institutional detail you’d want to understand,
  • one bullet on what data you’d want to find or request,
  • one bullet on what analysis or method you’d try first,
  • one bullet on what could go wrong / what might mislead you,
  • one bullet on how you’d communicate results to a decision-maker.

Part B: Which TWO of the 8 Business Scientist skills will matter most here, and why?

Solution

Example solution – there’s many ways to approach this

Part A

  • Institutional detail: Clarify how surge pricing works in practice in Sydney/Melbourne (e.g., how “surge zones” are defined, how often prices update, and what driver actions affect the algorithm).

  • Data to request: Pull time-stamped logs on driver online/offline status by location, surge multipliers by zone, trip requests, wait times/ETAs, cancellations, and basic context (weather, major events).

  • First analysis: Look for “coordination events” — unusually sharp drops in active drivers within a small area over a short time window — and check whether these are followed by spikes in surge pricing compared with similar times/areas.

  • What could go wrong: Demand spikes (events, rain), app outages, traffic disruptions, or normal shift changes could create similar patterns, so we could falsely label normal market changes as manipulation.

  • How to communicate: Summarize findings in a short manager memo with one simple chart (surge vs driver supply over time), a clear estimate of how often these patterns occur, and a “confidence/limits” section explaining what we can and cannot conclude yet.

Part B

  • Data Discovery: Without the right logs (especially precise online/offline timing and location-level surge history), we can’t distinguish coordination from normal fluctuations.

  • Analytical Theory: This situation is full of ways to get fooled (confounds like weather/events, measurement limits, false positives), so we need to be explicit about what could go wrong and how we’d check robustness before recommending action.

docs.title: In-Class Exercises
docs.text:
You will discuss these exercises in class with your peers in small groups and with your tutor. These exercises build from the exercises you have prepared above, you will get the most value from the class if you have completed those above before coming to class.

In the workshop you will work in groups of 3–4 on the same business problem (Uber surge pricing in Sydney and Melbourne). Your group will work through the in-class exercises.

To help us reflect on how different tools shape analytical thinking, each group will be assigned a different workflow. The goal is to notice how your workflow affects the quality of your reasoning, your confidence, and which Business Scientist skills you use.

Workflow allocation

Your tutor will allocate one of the following workflows to your group:

  • Search-only: You can use web search and your pre-class notes, but you must not use GenAI tools.

  • AI-only : You must use a GenAI tool of your choice to answer the questions, but your group must not browse the web or consult external sources during the task. In addition, you should not add your own analysis or explanations. Your job is to act like an reporter of the AI’s output:

    • You may copy/paste and format the AI’s output, but you must not change the substance. (If something is wrong/unclear, fix it by asking the AI to revise, not by rewriting it yourself.)
    • You may ask the AI clarifying questions (e.g., “define this term,” “give an example,” “rewrite more clearly,” “list assumptions,” “suggest metrics,” “format as a memo”).
    • If you need a judgment call, ask the AI to make it and explain its reasons.
    • If you disagree with the AI, you must resolve it by asking the AI further questions, not by inserting your own reasoning.

  • Hybrid: You may use any combination of search, AI, and notes in any way you choose.

At the end of the tutorial, the class will reflect on how different workflows shaped your answers.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Choosing the right question to answer
docs.text:
Your group will choose one research question to guide the rest of your work in the session.

  • Step 1: Propose four candidate research questions.

  • Step 2: Score each question from 0–2 on each criterion below (0 = weak, 1 = okay, 2 = strong).

    • Useful: Would answering it help Uber decide what to do?
    • Answerable: Could you imagine what you would measure to answer it?
    • Specific: Is it narrow enough to be answered in a short investigation?

  • Step 3: Choose the highest-scoring question and rewrite it to be as clear as possible.

Solution

No solution provided. Depends on what the group comes up with.

docs.title: Exercise 5: What data do we need, and how could we be misled?
docs.text:
Using the research question your group selected in Exercise 4, your manager asks: "What data would we need to answer your question?""

As a group, complete the following.

Part A: Must-have data List 5–7 data fields you would request or create to answer your question. For each item, add one sentence explaining what it would help you observe or measure.

Part B: What patterns would you expect to see? List three patterns you’d expect in the data if your hypothesis is correct.

Part C: What else could explain the same patterns? List two alternative explanations that could produce similar patterns,

Solution

There are multiple ways one could tackle this question. Here we provide one example.

Suppose the research question is: In Sydney and Melbourne during peak periods (e.g., weekend nights), do clustered driver log-offs within a local area increase the frequency or intensity of surge pricing, relative to similar times/areas without clustered log-offs?

Note that this question features the following structure:

(Outcome = surge frequency/intensity; Exposure = clustered log-offs; Scope = Sydney/Melbourne + peak periods + local area.)

Part A: Must-have data (5–7 fields) — with why each matters

A strong list usually includes time + location + supply + demand + pricing + rider experience + context.

  • Driver online/offline status with timestamps (by driver) - Lets us detect sudden drops in supply and whether they are clustered in time.

  • Driver location / operating zone at time of log-off (geofence/zone ID) - Lets us see whether log-offs are concentrated in the same area rather than spread across the city.

  • Surge multiplier (or price adjustment) by zone over time - Measures the outcome directly: when and where surge appears, and how large it is.

  • Trip requests (demand) by zone over time - Helps separate a surge caused by real demand spikes from a surge driven by supply manipulation.

  • Rider wait times / ETA (or pickup times) by zone - Captures rider experience and whether any surge coincides with a real shortage in service.

  • Cancellations (rider and driver) by zone/time - A surge episode might lead to more cancellations; also helps indicate instability in matching.

  • Context controls: weather + major events + app outage logs - Key confounds: rain/events create real demand spikes; outages can mimic coordinated log-offs.

Part B: Signals (3 patterns we’d expect if coordination is happening)

  • Clustered supply drop: Many drivers go offline within a short window (e.g., 5–10 minutes) in the same zone.
  • Surge follows supply drop: A surge multiplier increase occurs shortly after the clustered log-off (in that zone), even when demand is not unusually high.
  • Re-entry timing: Drivers return online after surge rises (or trip acceptance spikes right after surge), consistent with attempting to benefit from the higher fare.

Part C: Confounds (2 alternative explanations that mimic the same pattern)

  • Real demand shock: A concert ends / rain begins → demand spikes; drivers appear “insufficient,” surge rises even without coordination.
  • Non-strategic supply shock: App outages, connectivity issues, traffic disruptions, or normal shift changes create a sudden supply drop and surge.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Next Steps
docs.text:
Using your work from Exercise 5, answer these two questions:

  • What is the first pattern you would look for in the data to investigate your question?
  • What are two outcome indicators you would track to answer your research question? For each, add a short reason.

Solution

Carrying the same example RQ over from Q5: In Sydney and Melbourne during peak periods (e.g., weekend nights), do clustered driver log-offs within a local area increase the frequency or intensity of surge pricing, relative to similar times/areas without clustered log-offs?

First pattern to look for in the data

  • A strong first pattern is a simple, concrete comparison that links the exposure to the outcome with timing and location.

  • Example answer: Look for short windows (e.g., 5–10 minutes) where many drivers go offline in the same zone, and check whether a surge spike occurs in that zone shortly afterward (e.g., within the next 10–15 minutes), compared to similar times/zones without a clustered log-off.

Two outcome indicators to track (with reasons)

  • Two good indicators often combine pricing + service quality.

  • Example answers: Surge intensity or frequency (e.g., average surge multiplier, % of minutes/trips with surge in a zone): Directly measures the outcome in the research question and captures how big/common surge events are. Rider wait time / ETA (e.g., average pickup ETA, % rides with ETA above a threshold): Tells whether surge corresponds to a real shortage affecting riders, and helps distinguish “price spike only” from meaningful service disruption.

Other acceptable alternatives (if justified):

  • Cancellation rate (rider/driver) — indicates instability and friction during suspected events
  • Completed trips per hour per zone — shows whether matching/throughput changes during suspected events
  • Driver online minutes — helps check whether interventions/conditions harm participation (more for later, but can be justified)

docs.title: Exercise 7: Workflow reflection
docs.text:
One of our aims today was to notice how different workflows shape the quality of your work and how much of it you genuinely feel you own.

Before discussing with other groups, reflect on the four lenses below:

  • Speed: How quickly did you get to your answer? What helped or slowed you down?
  • Confidence: How confident were you in what you wrote? What drove that confidence (or lack of it)?
  • Defensibility: If someone challenged your work, would you feel able to defend it verbally in a meeting?
  • Ownership: Did the final output feel like your group’s work?

Solution

Here’s some examples of what you might experience in the conversation. Ultimately there is no right answer:

Sample reflection: Search-only

  • Speed: We were slower to get started because we had to read and agree on what mattered, but once we had a direction our answers became clearer.
  • Confidence: Medium–high. We felt better when we could point to something we read, but we weren’t sure we’d found the “right” sources.
  • Defensibility: Fairly defensible—we can explain our logic and show where claims came from, though we might miss some angles.
  • Ownership: High. The output feels like ours because we had to decide what to focus on and how to phrase it ourselves.

Sample reflection: AI-only

  • Speed: Very fast—we got full answers quickly and the writing sounded professional.
  • Confidence: Initially high because the output was fluent, then lower once we noticed we couldn’t verify claims or justify details.
  • Defensibility: Weak. If challenged in a meeting, we’d mostly be repeating what the AI said rather than explaining why it’s true.
  • Ownership: Low. The output doesn’t feel like our work—it feels like we assembled text, and some parts don’t match what we actually understand.

Sample reflection: Hybrid

  • Speed: Moderate—we moved quickly when we used AI for structure, but slowed down when we tried to check and reconcile different inputs.
  • Confidence: Medium. Using multiple sources helped, but sometimes the AI and search results pushed us in different directions.
  • Defensibility: Better than AI-only. We can defend our main points because we checked a couple of key claims and made our assumptions explicit, but some details are still shaky.
  • Ownership: Mixed. The overall logic feels like ours, but some phrasing and a few claims feel “borrowed,” especially where we leaned on AI-generated text.

docs.title: Tutorial Class 02 Set 01 - From Data to a Managerial Briefing
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Explain what Quarto is and why analysts use it
  • Run R code inside a .qmd file and render a report
  • Load a small dataset and compute a few inventory KPIs
  • Produce a simple table and a basic plot
  • Write a manager-friendly recommendation that separates facts vs interpretation vs decision

docs.title: The Business Challenge
docs.text:
David Jones sells a wide range of seasonal products, including fashion items that see strong swings in demand around holidays like Christmas.

Inventory decisions are especially challenging for seasonal products because:

  • Demand can spike unpredictably
  • Promotions and discounts influence customer behaviour
  • Regional preferences can differ
  • Suppliers need advance notice to adjust deliveries

Right now, David Jones is using a fixed restocking rule: Every week, 100 units are delivered to each region, no matter what.

But with the holiday season approaching, this rigid approach might not be enough.

Management wants a one-page briefing outlining whether they should adapt their restocking rule.

Your task is to review last year’s data and advise David Jones on how to improve inventory decisions.

docs.title: Prepare these Exercises before Class
docs.text: Prepare these exercises before coming to class. Plan to spend 45 minutes on these exercises.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Approaches to Inventory Planning
docs.text:
Read the article, “A New Approach to Production and Inventory Planning,” and answer the following questions in 2–3 sentences:

  1. Define the term “inventory management”. What makes inventory management complicated for seasonal products?
  2. What is one key challenge businesses face in managing inventory today?
  3. How could this apply to a retailer like David Jones, especially during busy seasons like Christmas?

Solution

  1. Inventory Management is the process of planning, tracking, and controlling stock so that a business can meet customer demand without holding excess or running out.

    • For David Jones, the challenge stems from when demand for gift hampers can spike quickly — poor planning could mean lost sales, unhappy customers, or leftover stock that must be heavily discounted.

    • Extra info: There are three key techniques in inventory management:

      • Economic Order Quantity (EOQ): A formula used to determine the optimal quantity to order that minimises total inventory costs — including both ordering costs and holding costs. Think of EOQ as the sweet spot: not too frequent, not too much.

      • Safety Stock: Extra buffer stock kept on hand to prevent stockouts due to unexpected spikes in demand or delays in delivery. It’s like a “just-in-case” cushion for uncertainty.

      • Reorder Point: The inventory level at which a new order should be placed so stock arrives before you run out. It accounts for delivery lead time + expected demand.

  2. One key challenge is balancing efficiency with flexibility. Many traditional inventory systems aim to minimise costs by keeping stock levels low (like with just-in-time models), but these systems struggle when there is uncertainty or sudden changes in demand. This makes businesses vulnerable to stockouts or delays when things don’t go as planned.

  3. David Jones experiences unpredictable demand spikes during the holiday season. If they rely on a rigid or overly efficient inventory rule, they risk running out of popular items like gift hampers or over-ordering and being left with excess stock. To avoid this, they need a more flexible approach that can adjust to regional sales trends, promotion effects, and delivery timing issues.

docs.title: Exercise 4: R + Quarto Vocabulary Check (5 Quick Definitions)
docs.text:
Answer each in one short sentence.

  • What does <- do in R?

  • What is a data frame (and what does a row represent in our David Jones data)?

  • What is a function in R? Give one example.

  • What is a code chunk in a Quarto .qmd file?

  • What does Render do in Quarto?

Solution

  • What does <- do in R? It assigns the value on the right to the object name on the left (e.g., x <- 5 stores 5 in x).

  • What is a data frame (and what does a row represent in our David Jones data)? A data frame is a table with rows and columns; here, one row represents one region-week observation (e.g., Sydney in the week commencing 2 Dec).

  • What is a function in R? Give one example. A function is a command that takes inputs and returns an output (e.g., sum(x), mean(x), min(x)).

  • What is a code chunk in a Quarto .qmd file? A code chunk is a block where you write R code that Quarto runs when rendering, and it shows the results (numbers/tables/plots) in the output.

  • What does Render do in Quarto? Render runs all code chunks and converts the .qmd into an output document (e.g., HTML/PDF) with the results inserted.

docs.title: In-Class Exercises
docs.text: You will discuss these exercises in class with your peers in small groups and with your tutor. These exercises build from the exercises you have prepared above, you will get the most value from the class if you have completed those above before coming to class.

docs.title: Exercise 5: Quick Recap of Preparation Work
docs.text:
With your group answer the following questions:

  • In one sentence, what is the core trade-off in inventory management for a retailer like David Jones?

  • What are the two biggest issues with the dataset presented in Exercise 2? Justify your choices.

Solution

  • Inventory management is about avoiding stockouts (and consequently lost sales/customer frustration) while avoiding overstock (holding costs/markdowns).

  • Two biggest dataset issues (example strong pairs + justifications). There isn’t a single right pair — the key is that students pick issues that materially affect interpretation or computation and justify them clearly. Here are high-quality answers you can accept, but there are other suitable answers if well justified:

    • Pair 1 (code/type + meaning):

      • Ending Inventory = -20 (backorder) mixes numbers with text → breaks numeric analysis (min/comparisons) and hides how backorders are recorded.
      • Timing ambiguity (do deliveries arrive before or after sales each week?) → changes the inventory flow story, so “risky weeks” and recommended orders could be wrong.

    • Pair 2 (structure + decision risk):

      • Promotion mixes Y and Y (Christmas) → unclear whether this is the same treatment; complicates grouping and comparisons.
      • Units Sold may be constrained by stockouts → observed sales may understate true demand, so forecasting based on sales can mislead.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Loading and Inspecting Some Data
docs.text:
(a) Open the Posit Cloud Workspace for this workshop.

(b) Load the dataset by running this line of code:

library(readr)

inventory <- read_csv("data/inventory.csv")

(c) We want to explain the code in (b) is doing, line by line.

  • What does ```{r} mean in Quarto?
  • What does #| eval: false do?
  • Do you need to change the #| eval: false setting to run the code when you render the file?
  • What does library(readr) do?
  • Explain what the assignment operator <-?, does.
  • Is read_csv() a function or a variable?
  • What does "data/inventory.csv" refer to?

(d) Run each of the following commands, and explain the output to your group:

  • class(inventory)
  • names(inventory)
  • head(inventory)
  • nrow(inventory)
  • ncol(inventory)

Solution

(c) Explaining the code chunk line by line

  • What does ```{r} mean in Quarto? - It starts an R code chunk. Code inside the chunk can be run and its output can appear in the rendered document.
  • What does #| eval: false do? - It tells Quarto not to run this code chunk when rendering (it will be shown, but not executed).
  • Do you need to change the #| eval: false setting to run the code when you render the file? - Yes. To load the dataset during rendering, you must remove it or change it (e.g., to #| eval: true) so the chunk executes.
  • What does library(readr) do? - It loads the readr package so you can use functions from it (including read_csv()).
  • Explain what the assignment operator <- does. - It stores the value on the right-hand side into the object name on the left-hand side. Example: inventory <- ... creates an object called inventory.
  • Is read_csv() a function or a variable? - It is a function (a command that takes inputs and returns an output).
  • What does "data/inventory.csv" refer to? - It is the file path to the CSV inside the project. data/ is a folder; inventory.csv is the file name. It is relative to the project directory.

(d) Inspect commands (what they return / how to interpret them)**

  • class(inventory) - Tells you the type of object inventory is (typically something like a tibble/data frame).
  • names(inventory) - Lists the column names (variable names) in the dataset.
  • head(inventory) - Shows the first few rows so you can sanity-check that the data imported correctly.
  • nrow(inventory) - Returns the number of rows (how many observations).
  • ncol(inventory) - Returns the number of columns (how many variables).

docs.title: Exercise 8: Turning Numbers into a Story (Before We Recommend Anything)
docs.text:
You’ve just computed a few KPIs in R (revenue, units sold, minimum ending inventory, and whether backorders occurred).

Before we jump to “what should David Jones order?”, we need to answer a more basic question: What do the numbers actually tell us — and what do they not tell us?

(a) What are the two most important facts you learned from your KPIs?

Write them as two short bullet points (each should reference a KPI you computed).

(b) Based on those facts, what is your group’s best guess about what will happen next week if David Jones keeps doing the same thing?

(c) What is one caveat you would tell management about your answer to (b)?

Solution

There isn’t a single “correct” set of sentences. A good answer uses the group’s computed KPIs and stays disciplined about what the data can (and can’t) support.

(a) Two most important facts (examples of strong answers) - Accept any two that reference computed KPIs clearly, for example:

  • Fact (demand/value): Melbourne generated higher total units sold / revenue than Sydney over these weeks.
  • Fact (risk): Inventory risk is higher in Melbourne: it has the lowest ending inventory, and there is at least one backorder (ending inventory < 0).
  • Fact (timing spike): The Christmas promo week coincides with the largest jump in units sold and a sharp drop in ending inventory in both regions.

(b) Best guess for next week if nothing changes (examples) - A strong answer is predictive but conditional, e.g.:

  • If David Jones keeps delivering 100 units and demand stays similar, Melbourne is likely to stock out / backorder again, while Sydney is less likely to (but could still run low).
  • Expect higher risk in Melbourne because its sales appear higher and its ending inventory hit the lowest/negative values.

(c) One caveat to tell management (examples) - Good caveats point to a specific limitation:

  • We don’t know when deliveries arrive relative to sales within the week, which affects the interpretation of “ending inventory risk.”
  • The dataset is small (few weeks), so forecasts are uncertain and sensitive to assumptions.

docs.title: Exercise 9: Planning for This Year’s Holiday Season
docs.text:
David Jones’ supplier is asking you to confirm delivery quantities now, so they can prepare for the season ahead.

  1. How many units should you order for Sydney and Melbourne for the first week of the holiday season?
  2. Justify your decision based on last year’s patterns and your reasoning. Consider factors like demand trends, regional differences, price effects, and promotion timing.
  3. Suppose the supplier has limited capacity and can only supply 200 units total for the first week. How would you allocate this stock between Sydney and Melbourne? What are the risks of your choice?

Solution

Unconstrained scenario:

Based on last year’s sales in the first week of the season (25 Nov), Melbourne sold 150 units while Sydney sold 100. Given this pattern and assuming similar demand and pricing this year, we recommend ordering:

  • Melbourne: 150 units
  • Sydney: 100 units

This matches observed demand and adjusts the previous fixed rule to better reflect regional differences.

Constrained Scenario:

Based on last year’s Week 1 sales (25 Nov), Melbourne sold 150 units and Sydney sold 100 — a 60:40 demand split. Assuming similar demand patterns this year, we propose the following allocation:

  • Melbourne: 120 units
  • Sydney: 80 units

This proportional allocation preserves observed demand ratios while fitting within the 200-unit constraint.

Assumptions:

  • We assume last year’s demand is a reasonable guide for this year.
  • We assume supply constraints are fixed and inflexible (i.e. we can’t reorder mid-season).
  • We assume there are no major regional marketing changes this year (e.g. no extra advertising / price changes).

Risks:

  • If demand increases (e.g. due to earlier or stronger promotions), understocking is likely.
  • If regional patterns shift, the proportional rule may misallocate units — e.g. underestimating growth in Sydney.
  • Without real-time data, it’s hard to adjust — we’d ideally revisit this weekly.

Data reasoning: Our decision uses descriptive analysis (last year’s observed sales), predictive reasoning (similar patterns expected), and light causal inference (we infer regional differences reflect customer demand, not supply issues).

Tutorial Class 03 Set 01 - Data Visualization for Business Analytics
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Explain how different ggplot2 visualization techniques reveal patterns in the Melbourne housing market that would be difficult to see in tables or raw numbers.
  • Use ggplot2 to create histograms, and scatterplots that analyze relationships between property prices, location, and dwelling types.
  • Apply transformations such as log scales, proportions, and faceting to improve the interpretability of price distributions and spatial trends.
  • Customize ggplot2 plots using themes, color palettes, and annotations to enhance clarity and storytelling.
  • Evaluate and compare visualization approaches, identifying which effectively communicate insights about housing price trends and spatial patterns.
  • Build and refine a visual analysis workflow that could inform practical decision-making for home buyers, investors, or urban planners

docs.title: The Topic: Understanding Melbourne’s Housing Market
docs.text:
Melbourne’s real estate market is one of the most dynamic in Australia. Property prices are influenced by several factors, including location, dwelling type, and proximity to the Central Business District (CBD). Buyers, sellers, and policymakers constantly analyze housing trends to make informed decisions. Understanding these trends is crucial in a $2 trillion+ housing market, where even small fluctuations in pricing expectations can have significant financial impacts.

A key question we will explore is: How do property prices vary by region, dwelling type, and location? By analyzing real estate data, we can identify patterns that help explain the drivers of Melbourne’s housing prices and their implications for different stakeholders in the market.

docs.title: The Data: The Melbourne Housing Market Dataset
docs.text:
We will use a dataset containing real estate sales data from Melbourne. The dataset provides insights into housing trends and includes key variables that influence property prices.

The dataset captures the property location within broader metropolitan regions (regionname), allowing us to compare trends across different areas. It also includes the type of dwelling, classified as House (h), Townhouse (t), or Apartment (u), enabling us to assess price differences based on housing type. The sale price (price) provides a measure of market value, while the distance to the CBD (distance) helps analyze the impact of proximity to the city center on property prices.

Similar datasets are widely used by real estate analysts, banks, and property investors to assess housing trends, predict future movements, and guide investment decisions. Through this tutorial, we’ll work with real-world data to uncover patterns and develop a deeper understanding of Melbourne’s property market. Let’s dive in!

docs.title: Exercise 1: Understanding ggplot2 Syntax
docs.text:
Consider the code below:

ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Number of Listings by Region"
  )

(a) What does ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname)) do?

(b) What is the role of aes(x = regionname) in this code?

(c) What does geom_bar() add to the plot?

(d) What does labs() do?

(e) In this code, what does the + operator do?

(f) Run the code above to produce the bar plot.

Solution

(a) ggplot(housing, aes(x = regionname)) starts a plot using the housing dataset and maps the variable regionname to the x-axis.

(b) aes(x = regionname) defines the aesthetic mapping. It tells ggplot2 which variable from the dataset should be shown on the x-axis.

(c) geom_bar() adds bars to the plot. It creates a bar plot that counts how many observations fall into each category of regionname.

(d) labs() adds or changes labels on the plot, such as the x-axis label, y-axis label, and title.

(e) The + operator adds new layers or components to the plot. In ggplot2, we build plots step by step by adding pieces together.

(f) When you run the code, it produces a bar plot showing the number of listings in each region.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Visualizing the distribution of Prices by Dwelling Type
docs.text:
By the end of this exercise, your plot should look similar to this one:

(a) Why is a histogram useful for understanding price distributions? What insights can we gain from plotting price distributions separately for each dwelling type?

Tip - What is a Histogram?

  • A histogram is a visualization that represents the distribution of numerical data by dividing values into bins and counting the number of observations in each bin. Unlike a bar plot, which displays categorical data, a histogram is used for continuous variables like price, age, or distance.

  • Histograms help identify patterns in data, such as skewness, outliers, and central tendencies, making them a crucial tool for understanding how values are distributed in a dataset.

(b) Use the starter code below to create a basic histogram of house prices. Replace YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME with the correct variable.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50)

(c) Extend the plot above by adding labels to the x-axis, y-axis, and title using the labs() function.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    x = "YOUR_X_AXIS_LABEL", 
    y = "YOUR_Y_AXIS_LABEL", 
    title = "YOUR_TITLE"
  )

(d) Modify the plot so that you create separate histograms for each dwelling type by adding the facet_wrap(~type) layer to the plot

ggplot(housing, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    x = "YOUR_X_AXIS_LABEL", 
    y = "YOUR_Y_AXIS_LABEL", 
    title = "YOUR_TITLE"
  ) +
  YOUR_CODE_HERE

(e) What does the histogram tell you about price differences between dwelling types?

Solution

(a) Why is a histogram useful here?

A histogram is useful for understanding the distribution of prices across properties. It shows how prices are spread out, where most of the listings fall, and whether there are outliers or skewed distributions.

  • By plotting prices separately for each dwelling type, we can:
  • Compare typical price ranges across types (e.g., Units vs. Houses).
  • Spot differences in distribution shape (e.g., skewness, bimodality).
  • Better understand market segmentation: do certain types dominate in certain price brackets?
