    x = "Price", 
    y = "Number of Listings", 
    title = "Distribution of Dwelling Prices"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ type)

(e)

The histogram reveals clear differences in price distributions across dwelling types:

  • Apartments have the lowest prices, with most listings clustered below $1 million. The distribution is strongly right-skewed, indicating that while most apartments are affordable, a few are much more expensive.
  • Houses span a much wider price range and dominate the middle of the market. Most listings fall between $500,000 and $1.5 million, but the distribution again shows right skew, with a notable number of high-end listings exceeding $2 million.
  • Townhouses are tightly concentrated around $750,000 to $1.25 million, with fewer extreme values. Their distribution is narrower and more symmetric compared to the other two dwelling types.

Key takeaways:

  • Houses are the most numerous and show the greatest variation in price.
  • Apartments tend to be lower-priced, making them more accessible to entry-level buyers or investors.
  • Townhouses occupy a mid-range niche, potentially appealing to buyers seeking a balance between space and affordability.

docs.title: Exercise 3: The Price - Distance Relationship
docs.text:
By the end of this exercise, your plot should look similar to this one:

(a) Why might we expect a relationship between price and distance to the CBD?

(b) Use the starter code below to build a scatter plot of price vs. distance, replacing YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME with the correct column names.

TipWhat is a Scatter Plot?

A scatter plot is used to visualize the relationship between two continuous variables by plotting individual data points. Each dot represents one observation, helping identify patterns, clusters, and trends. In this case, it allows us to explore how house prices change with distance.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME, y = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_point()

(c) Since we have a large number of data points, many overlap, making it difficult to distinguish individual observations. Modify the geom_point() function to reduce over-plotting by adjusting the alpha value. Experiment with different values (e.g., 0.1, 0.05, 0.01) and describe how each affects the visualization.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME, y = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_point(alpha = YOUR_NUMBER)

(d) We can better understand the relationship by adding a statistical transformation to the plot. Add a fitted line using geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE).

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME, y = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_point(alpha = YOUR_NUMBER) +
  YOUR_CODE_HERE

(e) Finally, add labels to the x-axis, y-axis, and title using the labs() function. Adjust the x- and y-axis scales as you deem appropriate.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME, y = YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME)) +
  geom_point(alpha = YOUR_NUMBER) +
  YOUR_CODE_HERE +
  labs(
    x = "YOUR_LABEL", 
    y = "YOUR_LABEL", 
    title = "YOUR_TITLE"
  )

(f) What does the scatter plot reveal about the relationship between house prices and distance to the CBD? How does the line help interpret this relationship?

Solution

(a). Why might we expect a relationship between price and distance to the CBD?

In most cities, being closer to the Central Business District (CBD) is associated with higher property prices due to:

  • Better access to jobs, transport, and amenities
  • Scarcity of land and high demand in central locations
  • Prestige or desirability of inner-city living

As distance from the CBD increases, we often expect prices to fall — although this relationship may not be perfectly linear due to other factors like transport links, school zones, or regional variation.

(b)

ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point()

(c)

ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05)

Notes:

  • alpha = 0.1: Points are semi-transparent — overlap is reduced but still busy.
  • alpha = 0.05: Good balance — dense regions become visibly darker.
  • alpha = 0.01: Almost all points are extremely faint; hard to see sparsely populated areas.

Lower alpha values reduce overplotting and help reveal density of data in crowded areas.

(d)

ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

This adds a linear regression line, helping us see the overall trend in how price changes with distance.

(e)

ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Distance to CBD (km)", 
    y = "Price", 
    title = "House Price vs. Distance"
  )

(f) The scatter plot shows a negative relationship between distance from the CBD and house price:

  • As distance increases, price tends to decrease
  • This is visible in the downward slope of the linear trend line
  • There’s also substantial variation in prices at all distances — distance is a strong predictor, but not the only factor
  • The line helps summarize the average trend, even in the presence of noisy data
  • This supports the idea that proximity to the CBD carries a price premium, though other drivers of housing value are clearly at play

docs.title: Exercise 4: Improving the Price Distribution Plot
docs.text:

(b). Work with your tutor to create an agreed upon list of changes to make to the plot. What steps do you need to take to make these improvements?

Non exhaustive list of potential changes:

Analytical changes

presentation changes:

Some changes improve the substance of comparison, while others improve clarity and communication.

(c)

  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +

docs.title: Exercise 5: Improving the Price-Distance Relationship Plot
docs.text:
(a). Together with your peers, propose two changes you want to make to the plot in Exercise 3. Discuss the rationale behind each change and how it might improve the visualization.

(b). Work with your tutor to create an agreed upon list of changes to make to the plot. What steps do you need to take to make these improvements?

(c). Implement the changes suggested in the R.

Solution

(a) and (b)

Analytical structure mostly unchanged

  • same variables on the axes
  • same scatterplot
  • same transparency level

But we might want to move away from a linear trend line

Non exhaustive list of potential changes focussed around presentation improvements

  • clearer color contrast between points and line
  • easier-to-read price axis
  • more polished theme and title formatting

(c)

Below we give 3 possible lines for the plot. Based on your discussion with your TA and group, you may have chosen one of these. None of these is “more correct” than others, it depends what you want to show. We recommend against plotting more than one in the same figure, as its hard for managers to read.

# Improved scatterplot: price vs. distance
scttr <- ggplot(housing, aes(x = distance, y = price)) +
  # Scatter plot with reduced alpha to handle overplotting
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, color = "grey") +
  # Here's alternative lines we could use. Pick ONE.
  # 1. stay linear
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "coral",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  # 2. move to non-linear / quadratic - "one bend" 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 2),   # Allow one bend in the trend line
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#9db964",
    linewidth = 1 
  ) +
  # 3. move to something non-parametric
  # The default is a 'loess' polynomial - "many bends"
  # Intuitively, think of this as using points in the close neighborhood of each other 
  # to determine the 'local' slope of the line.
  # Note that local slope may violate notions of 'correct' theoretical direction of relationship
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#0b6be9ff",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  # Format y-axis as dollars
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  # Add labels and center the title
  labs(
    x = "Distance to CBD (km)",
    y = "Price",
    title = "Dwelling Price vs. Distance"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) 

scttr

docs.title: Exercise 8: Synthesizing the Findings
docs.text:
If you were presenting these results in a business meeting, how would you explain the key takeaways? Structure your summary to include:

  • What you analyzed (data, variables)
  • What you found (key insights from the visualizations)
  • What decisions could be made based on this information?

Solution

Here’s one possible (long) answer:

What We Looked At

We analyzed dwelling listings from Melbourne to explore three key questions:

  • Where are dwellings being listed, and how does the volume vary by region?
  • How do prices differ between dwelling types (Houses, Units, Townhouses)?
  • How does distance from the CBD relate to dwelling prices?

What We Found

Listing Activity by Region:

  • Some metro regions (e.g., Northern and Western Metro) had a larger share of listings than others.
  • Presenting these as proportions made the comparison clearer, especially for less active regions.

Price Differences by Dwelling Type:

  • Houses had the highest prices on average and the widest spread.
  • Units were more affordable and tightly clustered in price.
  • Townhouses sat inbetween.

Price and Distance from the CBD:

  • Prices generally decline as distance increases — in a relatively linear way
  • The quadratic line and non-parametric line do not suggest strong non-linearities

What This Helps Us Understand

These visuals don’t tell us everything, but they provide a starting point for smarter conversations:

  • If you’re pricing or positioning properties, it’s helpful to understand how type and location shape price expectations.
  • Regional variation in listing volume could flag where market activity is strongest — or where supply may be tight. That’s worth exploring further.
  • The price–distance relationship aligns with what we might expect: proximity adds value.

docs.title: Tutorial Class 04 Set 01
Tutorial Class 04 Set 01 - Data Wrangling for Business Analytics
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Recognize and choose appropriate dplyr verbs for filtering rows, creating variables, selecting columns, ranking observations, and summarising groups.
  • Create and verify key strategy variables by using filter() and mutate() to construct profit_margin and asset_turnover, then checking whether the results are sensible.
  • Compare firms on different dimensions of performance by identifying those with the highest profit margins and those with the highest asset turnover.
  • Analyse industry-level patterns by using group_by() and summarise() to calculate and interpret grouped summaries.
  • Evaluate the limits of summary measures by explaining why averages may hide important differences within industries.
  • Synthesize results for decision-makers by communicating the main findings in a short executive-style summary.

docs.title: The Topic: Understanding firm strategy in the Australian economy
docs.text:
Firms can generate strong results in different ways. One firm may earn a lot of profit from each dollar of sales. Another may earn less on each sale, but generate very high sales relative to the assets it uses. These are different ways of operating, and they often reflect differences in business model and industry structure.

In this tutorial, we focus on two measures:

\[ \mathrm{Profit\ Margin} = \frac{\mathrm{EBIT}}{\mathrm{Sales}} \] \[ \mathrm{Asset\ Turnover} = \frac{\mathrm{Sales}}{\mathrm{Assets}} \]

These measures help us think about two different dimensions of performance:

  • Profit margin tells us how much profit a firm earns from each dollar of sales
  • Asset turnover tells us how effectively a firm turns its asset base into sales

Using dplyr, we will create these variables, check that they were calculated correctly, and then use them to answer a series of business questions.

In particular, we will ask:

  • Which firms appear strongest on profit margin, and which appear strongest on asset turnover?
  • Do the same firms appear at the top of both rankings, or do different firms succeed in different ways?
  • When we move from individual firms to industries, do the same patterns still appear?
  • Do some industries seem to rely more on high margins, while others rely more on high turnover?
  • What do these patterns suggest about how executives should interpret firm performance?

By the end of the tutorial, you should be able to use dplyr to turn raw accounting data into a short executive-style summary of how firms and industries generate strong results.

docs.title: The Data: Financial Statement Observations from Yahoo Finance
docs.text:
To answer these questions, we draw on audited 2024 financial statements for the 200 largest ASX-listed firms (as measured by assets).

Financial statements provide a standardised snapshot of a company’s performance and financial health. In our data set, the key variables are:

  • Company name (conml) – the name of the firm as listed on the ASX
  • Industry (industry) – the industry classification, allowing comparison across sectors such as mining, banking, or healthcare
  • Profit (ebit) – earnings before interest and taxes, representing core business profit after expenses (from the income statement)
  • Assets (at) – the total resources the company owns that have economic value (from the balance sheet)
  • Invested Capital (invested_capital) – the total capital invested in the company by both shareholders and debt holders to fund operations and growth. It generally includes:

By working with these statements and variables, we can replicate the kind of assessments that professional analysts and fund managers use to guide billion-dollar investment decisions.

As you will see, just a few lines of R code can wrangle raw financial statements information into orderly data summaries that allow us to understand how businesses across different industry sectors perform across various metrics.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Meet the Main dplyr Verbs
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will use a small set of dplyr verbs to build variables, inspect data, rank firms, and compare industries.

Before we start coding, it helps to know what each verb is designed to do.

(a)

Match each dplyr verb below to its plain-English meaning.

  • Verb:

    • filter()
    • mutate()
    • select()
    • arrange()
    • slice_max()
    • group_by()
    • summarise()

  • Meaning:

    • A. Create a new variable
    • B. Sort the rows
    • C. Keep only the rows that match a condition
    • D. Keep only the columns you want
    • E. Keep the top rows based on a variable
    • F. Split the data into groups
    • G. Collapse many rows into summary measures

(b)

For each business task below, write the dplyr verb that best fits the task.

  1. Keep only firms with positive sales and positive assets
  2. Create a new variable called profit_margin
  3. Show only company name, sales, and profit margin
  4. Sort firms from highest to lowest profit margin
  5. Keep the five firms with the highest asset turnover
  6. Set up the data so that each industry is analysed separately
  7. Calculate the average ROIC for each industry

Solution

Here is one set of correct answers.

(a)

Match each dplyr verb below to its plain-English meaning.

  • filter(): C. Keep only the rows that match a condition
  • mutate(): A. Create a new variable
  • select(): D. Keep only the columns you want
  • arrange(): B. Sort the rows
  • slice_max(): E. Keep the top rows based on a variable
  • group_by(): F. Split the data into groups
  • summarise(): G. Collapse many rows into summary measures

(b)

For each business task below, write the dplyr verb that best fits the job.

  1. Keep only firms with positive sales and positive assets: filter()
  2. Create a new variable called profit_margin: mutate()
  3. Show only company name, sales, and profit margin: select()
  4. Sort firms from highest to lowest profit margin: arrange()
  5. Keep the five firms with the highest asset turnover: slice_max()
  6. Set up the data so that each industry is analysed separately: group_by()
  7. Calculate the average ROIC for each industry : summarise()

docs.title: Exercise 2: Understanding the Pipe Operator
docs.text:
In this exercise, we use two animals — a lion and a giraffe — to explore how the pipe operator, |>, works. This lets us focus on the order of the steps without needing to think about data yet.

Suppose we start with an object called lion. We want the lion to do the following actions in order:

  1. stand up
  2. lift its head by 30 degrees
  3. roar at volume 10

(a)

One way to write this is to create a new object after each step.

lion_step1 <- stand_up(lion)
lion_step2 <- lift_head(lion_step1, angle = 30)
lion_step3 <- roar(lion_step2, volume = 10)

What does lion_step2 represent?

(b)

We could also write the same sequence by placing one function inside another.

roar(lift_head(stand_up(lion), angle = 30), volume = 10)

This version is shorter, but it can be harder to read because we have to work from the inside out.

Which function runs first in this version?

(c)

The pipe operator lets us write the same sequence in the order the actions happen.

lion |>
  stand_up() |>
  lift_head(angle = 30) |>
  roar(volume = 10)

In the line lift_head(angle = 30), what is being piped in, and what is the extra argument?

(d)

Now try this yourself. Suppose we start with an object called giraffe. We want the giraffe to do the following actions in order:

  1. step forward by 2 steps
  2. lower its neck by 45 degrees
  3. drink water for 5 seconds

Write this sequence in the three ways shown above.

Step-by-step with intermediate objects

# Write your answer here

Function inside function

# Write your answer here

With the pipe

# Write your answer here

(e)

Complete the sentence: The pipe operator takes _ and passes it into _.

(f)

In one sentence, explain how the pipe helps us write code in an “and then” way.

Solution

(a)

lion_step2 represents the lion after it has stood up and then lifted its head by 30 degrees.

(b)

The first function to run is stand_up().

(c)

The object being piped in is the lion. The extra argument is angle = 30.

(d)

One correct way to write the giraffe sequence is shown below.

Step-by-step with intermediate objects

giraffe_step1 <- step_forward(giraffe, steps = 2)
giraffe_step2 <- lower_neck(giraffe_step1, angle = 45)
giraffe_step3 <- drink_water(giraffe_step2, seconds = 5)

Function inside function

drink_water(lower_neck(step_forward(giraffe, steps = 2), angle = 45), seconds = 5)

With the pipe

giraffe |>
  step_forward(steps = 2) |>
  lower_neck(angle = 45) |>
  drink_water(seconds = 5)

(e)

One correct completion is: The pipe operator takes an object and passes it into the next function.

(f)

One possible answer is: The pipe helps us write code as a sequence of actions: do this, and then this, and then this.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Create the Analysis Dataset
docs.text:
In the rest of this tutorial, we will work with a dataset called firm_strategy. To create firm_strategy, we need to construct some variables from the ASX dataset.

(a)

Load the ASX data located in data/asx_200_2024.csv into an object called asx_data.

asx_data <- YOUR_CODE_HERE

(b)

We now want to create a new dataset called firm_strategy from asx_data.

To do this, we need to:

  1. keep only firms for which the ratios can be calculated sensibly, and

  2. create two new variables:

    • profit_margin
    • asset_turnover

Before writing any code, look at the formulas for these variables and think about which original variables must be strictly positive.

(c)

Use your answer to complete the code below. Replace YOUR_CONDITIONS and fill in the two missing ratio definitions.

firm_strategy <- asx_data |>
  filter(YOUR_CONDITIONS) |>
  YOUR_CODE_HERE(
    profit_margin = YOUR_CODE_HERE,
    asset_turnover = YOUR_CODE_HERE
  )

(d)

In one sentence, explain why we use filter() before mutate() in our solution to (c).

Solution

(a)

Load the ASX data into an object called asx_data.

asx_data <- read_csv("data/asx_200_2024.csv")

(b). The variables that must be strictly positive are the ones in the denominators of the ratios:

  • sale for profit_margin
  • at for asset_turnover

(c). One correct completed version is:

firm_strategy <-
  asx_data |>
  filter(sale > 0, at > 0) |>
  mutate(
    profit_margin = ebit / sale,
    asset_turnover = sale / at
  )

(d).

One possible answer is: We use filter() before mutate() so that we only calculate the ratios for firms where the denominators are valid.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Create a Smaller Checking Dataset

docs.title: Exercise 5: Which Firms Rely Most on Margin? Which Rely Most on Volume?
docs.text:
Some firms generate strong profits from each dollar of sales. Others generate large sales from a given asset base. In this exercise, we compare firms at the top of each of these two dimensions.

(a)

Use slice_max() to identify the five firms with the highest profit_margin.

Your table should include:

  • conml
  • industry
  • ebit
  • at
  • sale
  • profit_margin
  • asset_turnover
firm_strategy |>
  slice_max(YOUR_CODE_HERE) |>
  select(YOUR_VARIABLES_HERE)

(b)

Now produce the equivalent table for the five firms with the highest asset_turnover.

firm_strategy |>
  slice_max(YOUR_CODE_HERE) |>
  select(YOUR_VARIABLES_HERE)

(c)

Compare the two tables.

  • Do the same firms appear in both tables?
  • What kinds of industries seem more common in each table?
  • What does this suggest about different ways firms generate profits?

Solution

(a)

Use slice_max() to identify the five firms with the highest profit_margin.

firm_strategy |>
  slice_max(profit_margin, n = 5) |>
  select(conml, industry, profit_margin, asset_turnover)

| Emerald Resources NL | Metals & Mining | 0.4280829           | 0.5208612            |

(b)

Produce the equivalent table for the five firms with the highest asset_turnover.

firm_strategy |>
  slice_max(asset_turnover, n = 5) |>
  select(conml, industry, profit_margin, asset_turnover)

| conml <chr>                  | industry <chr>                                        | profit_margin <dbl> | asset_turnover <dbl> |
|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Peoplein Limited             | Professional Services                                 | 0.010606953         | 3.018577             |
| Jb Hi-Fi Ltd                 | Specialty Retail                                      | 0.067282432         | 2.751219             |

(c)

One possible interpretation is:

  • The same firms do not appear in both tables, which suggests that high profit margin and high asset turnover capture different ways of operating.
  • Firms in the high-margin table earn more profit from each dollar of sales. These firms may benefit from pricing power, favourable cost conditions, scarce resources, or stable demand.
  • In this output, the high-margin table includes industries such as mining, gas utilities, and building products.
  • This makes economic sense because some firms in these sectors can earn strong margins without needing extremely high sales relative to their asset base.
  • Firms in the high-turnover table generate more sales from a given asset base. These firms may rely more on high volume, fast-moving sales, or relatively asset-light operations.
  • In this output, the high-turnover table includes industries such as professional services, specialty retail, commercial services, construction and engineering, and distribution/retail.
  • This also makes sense because firms in these sectors often operate by generating lots of sales or work relative to the assets recorded on their balance sheets.
  • The broader lesson is that firms can generate strong performance in different ways: some rely more on margin, while others rely more on turning assets into sales quickly.
  • A useful intuition is that a mining firm may sell fewer units but earn much more on each sale, while a retailer may earn much less on each sale but sell many more units.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Comparing Industries Using Average Values
docs.text:
In Exercise 5, you compared individual firms at the top of the profit margin and asset turnover distributions. We now take a step back and look at broader patterns across industries. To do this, we will group the data by industry and calculate average values for each group.

(a)

Complete the code below to create a summary table that shows, for each industry:

  • the number of firms
  • average profit_margin
  • average asset_turnover
industry_summary <-
  firm_strategy |>
  group_by(YOUR_VARIABLE) |>
  summarise(
    n_firms = n(),
    avg_profit_margin = mean(YOUR_VARIABLE, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_asset_turnover = YOUR_CODE
  )

(b)

Now focus only on industries with at least 3 firms, and sort industry_summary from highest to lowest average profit_margin.

industry_summary |>
    filter(YOUR_CONDITION) |>
    arrange(YOUR_CODE)

(c)

Which industries appear near the top of the table when sorted by average profit_margin? What does this suggest about how firms in these industries tend to make money?

(d)

Again focusing only on industries with at least 3 firms, sort industry_summary from highest to lowest average asset_turnover.

industry_summary |>
  YOUR_CODE |>
  YOUR_CODE

(e)

Compare the two rankings. How do these industry-level patterns comapre to what you saw earlier in Exercise 5, where different kinds of firms appeared in the high-margin and high-turnover tables?

(f)

In this exercise, we focused on industries with at least 3 firms. Why might that be useful? And even after doing this, why might an average still give a slightly misleading picture of an industry?

(g)

In this exercise, we focused on industry averages. Another summary measure analysts often use is the standard deviation, which tells us how spread out the firms in an industry are. What do you think it would mean if an industry had:

  • a high standard deviation in profit_margin?
  • a low standard deviation in profit_margin?

Solution

(a)

Create a summary table by industry.

industry_summary <-
  firm_strategy |>
  group_by(industry) |>
  summarise(
    n_firms = n(),
    avg_profit_margin = mean(profit_margin, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_asset_turnover = mean(asset_turnover, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  filter(n_firms >= 3) |>

  • These sectors often generate large sales relative to their asset base because they depend more on high volume, fast-moving goods or projects, service delivery models that generate substantial revenue without a very large stock of physical assets, or operational models built around turning assets into revenue quickly.
  • The two rankings are different, which suggests that industries vary in how firms generate performance.
  • The firm-level differences seen earlier reflect broader industry patterns in how sectors operate.
  • It is also useful to notice that some industries, such as Professional Services and Commercial Services & Supplies, perform reasonably well on both dimensions, which suggests that not every industry fits neatly into only one strategy type.

(f)

One possible interpretation is:

  • Focusing on industries with at least 3 firms helps reduce the risk of over-interpreting averages based on only one or two companies.

  • A high standard deviation in profit_margin would mean that firms in the industry differ a lot in how much profit they earn from each dollar of sales.
  • A low standard deviation in profit_margin would mean that firms in the industry are more similar to one another on this measure.
  • This means that two industries could have similar average profit margins but very different amounts of variation across firms.

docs.title: Exercise 7: Summarising the Findings for Executives
docs.text:
Imagine you work at a large consulting company that is preparing an annual report on the financial results of Australian firms.

Your team has been asked to analyse how large Australian listed firms generate strong results across different industries. As part of this project, you need to present an interim result to the executives overseeing the report.

Write 3–4 sentences that could appear in the interim report’s executive summary.

Your summary should answer the following:

  1. What did you analyse?
  2. What were the main patterns you found?
  3. What is the main business lessons one should take from these results?

Write for a non-technical audience and focus on the business meaning of the results.

Solution

Here is one strong example of the kind of answer we are aiming for.

  • We analysed how the 200 largest ASX-listed firms generate performance by examining profit margins and asset turnover across their 2024 financial statements.
  • Industries tend to generate strong performance in one of two ways. Some — such as mining and software — earn a large share of each sales dollar as profit, often because of pricing power or the economics of scaling intangible products. Others — such as retail and distribution — generate large sales relative to their asset base by operating at high volume or through asset-light business models.
  • The key lesson is that benchmarking firms using a single metric in isolation, without accounting for these industry structures, risks drawing misleading conclusions and steering corporate strategy in the wrong direction.

A strong answer will include all four of these elements. Use this checklist when reviewing student responses:

  • Identifies what was analysed and names specific industries as examples
  • Notes that industries differ on margin vs. turnover, and gives economic reasoning for why — e.g. pricing power / scarce resources / intangible scale for high-margin industries; volume / asset-light models for high-turnover industries
  • Notes that the tradeoff is a tendency, not a universal rule — e.g. professional services performs reasonably well on both
  • Closes with a specific, actionable executive takeaway — not just “don’t use one metric” but “metrics must be interpreted relative to how that industry creates value”

A weaker answer typically:

  • Describes the code or process rather than the findings
  • Names the pattern without explaining the economic reasoning behind it
  • Ends with a vague takeaway that does not guide executive action
  • Misses the nuance that the tradeoff is not universal across all industries

docs.title: Exercise 8 [Optional]: Visualising the Profit Margin – Asset Turnover Relationship
docs.text:
In Exercises 5 and 6, you identified that firms and industries tend to perform strongly on either profit margin or asset turnover, but rarely both. In this exercise, you will visualise that pattern using a scatter plot.

(a)

Using industry_summary, create a scatter plot with avg_profit_margin on the x-axis and avg_asset_turnover on the y-axis.

industry_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE, y = YOUR_VARIABLE)) +
  YOUR_CODE()

(b)

Does the plot look the way you expected? Is anything making it hard to read?

(c)

Filter industry_summary to keep only industries with at least 3 firms and an average profit margin above -5, then recreate the scatter plot from (a).

industry_summary |>
  filter(YOUR_CONDITIONS) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE, y = YOUR_VARIABLE)) +
  YOUR_CODE()

(d)

Add a geom_smooth() layer to the plot from (b).

industry_summary |>
  filter(YOUR_CONDITIONS) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = YOUR_VARIABLE, y = YOUR_VARIABLE)) +
  YOUR_CODE() +
  YOUR_CODE(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

(e).

What does the line suggest about the relationship between average profit margin and average asset turnover across industries?

Solution

(a)

industry_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_profit_margin, y = avg_asset_turnover)) +
  geom_point()

(b)

The unfiltered plot displays all industries but may have a distorted x-axis due to one or two industries with very negative average profit margins

(c)

industry_summary |>
  filter(
    n_firms >= 3, 
    avg_profit_margin > -0.5
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_profit_margin, y = avg_asset_turnover)) +
  geom_point()

(d)

industry_summary |>
  filter(n_firms >= 3, avg_profit_margin > -0.5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_profit_margin, y = avg_asset_turnover)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

(e)

We filter before plotting because extreme or unreliable values can distort the picture and lead to misleading conclusions.

docs.title: Tutorial Class 05 Set 01 - Shaping and Joining Data for Business Analytics
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between tidy and messy data, and use pivot_longer() to tidy up wide data.
  • Summarize and visualise financial data, and explain why tidy formats make analysis easier.
  • Plot and interpret relationships between share price and earnings per share (EPS).
  • Combine data from multiple tables using joins (left_join(), inner_join(), anti_join()), and understand what each join includes or excludes.

docs.title: The Topic: What shapes how the market values Australian firms?
docs.text:
Investors do not just care about whether a company is profitable. They also care about how much they are paying for those earnings.

In this tutorial, we will work with data on large Australian firms to explore a simple question: How strongly are share prices and valuation ratios related to company earnings, and how do those patterns vary across firms and industries?

To answer that question, we first need to prepare the data. Some of the financial variables are stored in a messy wide format, and other information is spread across separate files. So before we can analyse anything, we need to:

  • reshape the data into tidy form
  • join together firm, industry, and valuation data
  • check what information is missing after those joins

Two key variables in today’s tutorial are:

\[ \text{EPS} = \frac{\text{Profit}}{\text{Shares Outstanding}} \] \[ \text{P/E} = \frac{\text{Share Price}}{\text{EPS}} \]

  • EPS tells us how much profit a company earns for each share.

  • The P/E ratio tells us how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of earnings.

By the end of the tutorial, you will have built and explored a dataset that lets you compare firms and industries using share prices, earnings, and valuation ratios.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Identifying Issues with Untidy Data
docs.text:
We will start with a deliberately messy version of the ASX stock price data. Run the following code to load the dataset.

asx_prices_messy <- read_csv("data/asx_prices_messy.csv")

Then inspect a subset of the data:

asx_prices_messy |>
  select(gvkey, conm, price_2023, price_2024, eps_2023, eps_2024) |> 
  head(10)

| gvkey <chr> | conm <chr>                | price_2023 <dbl> | price_2024 <dbl> | eps_2023 <dbl> | eps_2024 <dbl> |
|-------------|---------------------------|------------------|------------------|----------------|----------------|
| 272690      | 1300 SMILES LTD           | NA               | NA               | NA             | NA             |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD          | 0.040            | 0.067            | -0.0091        | -0.0107        |
| 349318      | 29METALS LIMITED          | 0.375            | NA               | -0.7986        | NA             |
| 284698      | 3D ENERGI LIMITED         | 0.056            | 0.070            | 0.0129         | -0.0075        |
| 346142      | 3D METALFORGE LIMITED     | NA               | NA               | NA             | NA             |
| 317959      | 3P LEARNING LTD           | 1.270            | 1.020            | 0.0230         | -0.2077        |
| 253413      | 3Q HOLDINGS LTD           | NA               | NA               | NA             | NA             |
| 339106      | 4DMEDICAL LTD             | 0.450            | 0.675            | -0.1049        | -0.0971        |
| 314650      | 4DS MEMORY LTD            | 0.135            | 0.084            | -0.0038        | -0.0031        |
| 324960      | 5E ADVANCED MATERIALS INC | 2.260            | 0.540            | -0.7000        | -1.1800        |

(a)

In what ways is this data frame not tidy? What principles of tidy data are violated?

(b)

Use the starter code below to compute the average share price across all firms for 2023 and 2024.

asx_prices_messy |>
  summarise(
    # Add up all 2023 share prices
    sum_prices_2023 = sum(YOUR_CODE_HERE, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Add up all 2024 share prices
    sum_prices_2024 = sum(YOUR_CODE_HERE, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Count how many firms have a non-missing share price in 2023
    count_firms_2023 = sum(!is.na(price_2023)),
    # Count how many firms have a non-missing share price in 2024
    count_firms_2024 = sum(!is.na(price_2024))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Combine the 2023 and 2024 price totals
    total_sum = YOUR_CODE_HERE + YOUR_CODE_HERE,
    # Combine the number of non-missing firm prices across both years
    total_count = count_firms_2023 + count_firms_2024
  ) |>
  mutate(
  # Divide the total sum of prices by the total number of firms
    avg_price_23_24 = YOUR_CODE_HERE / YOUR_CODE_HERE
  ) |> 
  select(avg_price_23_24)

(c)

Why does the approach in part (b) not scale well as more years are added?

(d)

The code below plots share price against earnings per share in 2024.

asx_prices_messy |>
  filter(eps_2024 > -5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eps_2024, y = price_2024)) +
  YOUR_CODE_HERE +
  YOUR_CODE_HERE +
  labs(
    title = "YOUR_LABEL_HERE",
    x = "YOUR_LABEL_HERE",
    y = "YOUR_LABEL_HERE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

What relationship do you see? Why does this make sense economically?

(e)

Suppose you also wanted to include 2023 in this analysis. Briefly explain:

  • which extra columns you would need
  • what you would need to change in the plotting process
  • why this approach would become awkward if extended to 2019 to 2024

(f)

In two or three sentences, explain to a manager why this data structure makes analysis harder than it needs to be.

Solution

(a)

This data frame is not tidy because the year is stored in the column names rather than in its own variable. Columns such as price_2023 and price_2024 contain values of the variable year, which should instead appear in a separate column. The data also mix two variables, the measure (price or eps) and the year, inside a single column name. More broadly, one firm-year observation is spread across multiple columns rather than appearing as one row.

(b)

asx_prices_messy |>
  summarise(
    # Add up all 2023 share prices
    sum_prices_2023 = sum(price_2023, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Add up all 2024 share prices
    sum_prices_2024 = sum(price_2024, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Count how many firms have a non-missing share price in 2023
    count_firms_2023 = sum(!is.na(price_2023)),
    # Count how many firms have a non-missing share price in 2024
    count_firms_2024 = sum(!is.na(price_2024))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Combine the 2023 and 2024 price totals
    total_sum = sum_prices_2023 + sum_prices_2024,
    # Combine the number of non-missing firm prices across both years
    total_count = count_firms_2023 + count_firms_2024
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Divide the total sum of prices by the total number of firms
    avg_price_23_24 = total_sum / total_count
  ) |> 
  select(avg_price_23_24)

| avg_price_23_24 <dbl> |
|-----------------------|
| 2.765119              |

(c)

This approach does not scale well because every new year adds more columns that must be handled manually. We would need to keep adding extra sums, counts, and references to year-specific variables, making the code longer and easier to break.

(d)

asx_prices_messy |>
  filter(eps_2024 > -5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eps_2024, y = price_2024)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Share Price vs EPS (2024)",
    x = "Earnings per Share (EPS, 2024)",
    y = "Share Price (2024)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The plot suggests a positive relationship between earnings per share and share price in 2024. This makes sense economically because investors are buying a claim on the firm’s future earnings, so firms with stronger earnings tend to attract more demand and higher share prices.

(e)

A good answer would explain that we would need to bring in the 2023 columns, such as eps_2023 and price_2023, in addition to the 2024 ones. The plotting process would become more complicated because we would need to manually combine or stack information from multiple years before plotting. This would become increasingly awkward from 2019 to 2024 because each extra year would add more column references and more manual work, making the analysis repetitive and harder to maintain.

(f)

A manager-friendly explanation might be: The current structure makes even simple comparisons across years more cumbersome than they need to be. Reorganising the data would make it easier to summarise trends, build plots, and update the analysis when new years of data are added.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Combining Datasets
docs.text:
In this exercise, you will combine information from two datasets using a join.

To start, load the data:

firm_codes <-
  read_csv("data/asx_200_2024.csv") |>
  select(gvkey, conm, gsubind)

subindustry_names <-
  read_csv("data/GICS_subindustry.csv")

Take a quick look at the two datasets:

firm_codes |>
  head(10)

| gvkey <chr> | conm <chr>             | gsubind <dbl> |
|-------------|------------------------|---------------|
| 013312      | BHP GROUP LTD          | 15104020      |
| 210216      | TELSTRA GROUP LIMITED  | 50101020      |
| 223003      | CSL LTD                | 35201010      |
| 212650      | TRANSURBAN GROUP       | 20305020      |
| 100894      | WOOLWORTHS GROUP LTD   | 30101030      |
| 212427      | FORTESCUE LTD          | 15104050      |
| 101601      | WESFARMERS LTD         | 25503030      |
| 226744      | RAMSAY HEALTH CARE LTD | 35102020      |
| 220244      | QANTAS AIRWAYS LTD     | 20302010      |
| 017525      | ORIGIN ENERGY LTD      | 55101010      |

subindustry_names |>
  head(10)

| gsubind <dbl> | subind <chr>                               |
|---------------|--------------------------------------------|
| 10101010      | Oil & Gas Drilling                     |
| 10101020      | Oil & Gas Equipment & Services     |
| 10102010      | Integrated Oil & Gas                   |
| 10102020      | Oil & Gas Exploration & Production |
| 10102030      | Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing     |
| 10102040      | Oil & Gas Storage & Transportation |
| 10102050      | Coal & Consumable Fuels                |
| 15101010      | Commodity Chemicals                        |
| 15101020      | Diversified Chemicals                      |
| 15101030      | Fertilizers & Agricultural Chemicals   |

(a)

Look at the variables in firm_codes and subindustry_names. Which variable or variables look like they could be used to join these two datasets?

(b)

Which join variable would you choose? Explain why it is the best choice here.

(c)

Use a left join to add the subindustry name to each firm in firm_codes.

firm_info <-
  YOUR_DATASET_NAME |>
  left_join(YOUR_DATASET_NAME, by = join_by(YOUR_VARIABLE_NAME))

firm_info |>
  head(10)

(d)

What changed after the join? Briefly explain:

  • what information was added
  • whether the join mainly added rows or columns
  • why this makes the dataset more useful for analysis

(e)

Look at how gsubind behaves in the two datasets.

  • In which dataset would you expect each gsubind to appear only once?
  • In which dataset can the same gsubind appear many times?
  • Why does that make sense?

(f)

Fill in the variable name in each sentence below.

In subindustry_names, _____ behaves like a primary key because each code identifies one subindustry label.

In firm_codes, _____ behaves like a foreign key because many firms can share the same subindustry code.

(g)

Suppose we reversed the join and started with subindustry_names on the left-hand side. What would be different about the resulting dataset, and why?

Solution

(a) The most plausible join variable is gsubind. Depending on the columns shown in subindustry_names, students may also mention other code-like variables, but gsubind is the key variable we want here because it appears in both tables and represents the subindustry code.

(b) gsubind is the best choice because it is a structured code variable designed to represent the same subindustry in both tables. In general, numeric or code-based match keys are usually safer than text variables because they are more standardised and less likely to vary across datasets. A text variable like conm would be a worse choice because company names can be abbreviated, misspelled, formatted differently, or written inconsistently across files. So the key point is not just that gsubind fits the business meaning here, but that coded identifiers are often much more reliable join keys than text labels.

(c)

firm_info <-
  firm_codes |>
  left_join(subindustry_names, by = join_by(gsubind))

firm_info |>
  head(10)

| 210216      | TELSTRA GROUP LIMITED  | 50101020      | Integrated Telecommunication Services |
| 223003      | CSL LTD                | 35201010      | Biotechnology                         |
| 212650      | TRANSURBAN GROUP       | 20305020      | Highways & Railtracks             |

| 101601      | WESFARMERS LTD         | 25503030      | Broadline Retail (New)                |
| 226744      | RAMSAY HEALTH CARE LTD | 35102020      | Health Care Facilities                |
| 220244      | QANTAS AIRWAYS LTD     | 20302010      | Passenger Airlines (New name)         |
| 017525      | ORIGIN ENERGY LTD      | 55101010      | Electric Utilities                    |

(d)

The join adds subindustry names to the firm-level dataset. It mainly adds columns rather than rows, because we are attaching descriptive information to each existing firm. This makes the dataset more useful because we can now analyse firms using meaningful industry labels rather than just codes.

(e)

In subindustry_names, we would expect each gsubind to appear only once because each code should map to one subindustry label. In firm_codes, the same gsubind can appear many times because many firms can belong to the same subindustry. That makes sense because subindustry_names is a lookup table, while firm_codes is a firm-level table.

(f)

In both sentences, the missing variable name is gsubind.

In subindustry_names, gsubind behaves like a primary key because each code identifies one subindustry label.

In firm_codes, gsubind behaves like a foreign key because many firms can share the same subindustry code.

(g)

If we started with subindustry_names on the left-hand side, the resulting dataset would keep all subindustry rows rather than all firm rows. That means the structure of the output would be organised around subindustries, not firms. In a left_join(), the table on the left determines which rows are preserved.

subindustry_first <-
  subindustry_names |>
  left_join(firm_codes, by = join_by(gsubind))

subindustry_first |>
  head(10)

| gsubind <dbl> | subind <chr>                       | gvkey <chr> | conm <chr>               |
|---------------|------------------------------------|-------------|--------------------------|
| 10101010      | Oil & Gas Drilling                 | NA          | NA                       |
| 10101020      | Oil & Gas Equipment & Services     | NA          | NA                       |
| 10102010      | Integrated Oil & Gas               | NA          | NA                       |
| 10102020      | Oil & Gas Exploration & Production | 101392      | BEACH ENERGY LTD         |
| 10102020      | Oil & Gas Exploration & Production | 253322      | AMPLITUDE ENERGY LIMITED |
| 10102020      | Oil & Gas Exploration & Production | 271330      | STRIKE ENERGY LTD        |
| 10102030      | Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing     | NA          | NA                       |
| 10102040      | Oil & Gas Storage & Transportation | NA          | NA                       |
| 10102050      | Coal & Consumable Fuels            | 284808      | WHITEHAVEN COAL LIMITED  |
| 10102050      | Coal & Consumable Fuels            | 258444      | NEW HOPE CORP LTD        |

This version starts from the subindustry lookup table and then brings in the firms that match each subindustry code. The result is therefore anchored on subindustries rather than firms, which is different from the earlier join where every firm row was preserved first.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Tidying Data to Make Analysis Easier
docs.text:
(a)

Look at the column names in asx_prices_messy, and answer the following:

  • What two pieces of information are stored in these column names?
  • What character separates those two pieces of information?

(b)

We now want to reshape the stock price data so that each row corresponds to one firm in one year. Complete the starter code below to turn the data into a tidy format.

asx_prices_tidy <-
  asx_prices_messy |>
  pivot_YOUR_CODE(
    cols = YOUR_CODE_HERE,
    names_to = c(".value", "fyear"),
    names_sep = YOUR_CODE_HERE,
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(fyear = as.numeric(fyear))

asx_prices_tidy |>
  head(10)

(c)

In Exercise 1, calculating the average share price across 2023 and 2024 took several steps. Use the tidy dataset to calculate the average share price across those two years.

asx_prices_tidy |>
  YOUR_CODE(fyear %in% c(YOUR_YEARS)) |>
  YOUR_CODE(avg_price = mean(YOUR_VARIABLE, na.rm = TRUE))

(d)

Why is the calculation in part (c) easier to write using the tidy dataset than it was in Exercise 1?

What would we need to do if we added many more years of data?

(e)

We now want to recreate our plot of share price against EPS using the tidy dataset.

Complete the code below.

asx_prices_tidy |>
  filter(eps > -5) |>
  # create a scatterplot with EPS on the x-axis and price on the y-axis
  YOUR_CODE +
  # add points
  YOUR_CODE +
  # add a fitted straight line
  YOUR_CODE +
  # add a title and axis labels
  YOUR_CODE +
  # use a theme
  YOUR_CODE

(f)

Modify your code from part (e) so that the plot only shows observations from 2023 and 2024. Make this change by adding just one line to your existing pipeline.

(g)

Look at your plot from part (e) and answer the following:

  • What overall relationship do you observe between EPS and share price?
  • What might explain firms that lie well above or below the fitted line?
  • Do firms with very low or negative EPS seem to follow the same straight-line pattern as the rest of the data?

Solution

(a)

The column names contain two pieces of information:

  • the variable being measured, such as price or eps
  • the financial year, such as 2023 or 2024

These two pieces are separated by an underscore (_).

(b)

asx_prices_tidy <-
  asx_prices_messy |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("price") | starts_with("eps"),
    names_to = c(".value", "fyear"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(fyear = as.numeric(fyear))

asx_prices_tidy |>
  head(10)

| gvkey <chr> | conm <chr>       | fyear <dbl> | price <dbl> | eps <dbl> |
|-------------|------------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| 272690      | 1300 SMILES LTD  | 2019        | 6.280       | 0.3282    |
| 272690      | 1300 SMILES LTD  | 2020        | 6.110       | 0.3018    |
| 272690      | 1300 SMILES LTD  | 2021        | 8.100       | 0.4065    |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2019        | 0.200       | -0.0258   |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2020        | 0.135       | -0.0165   |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2021        | 0.100       | -0.0311   |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2022        | 0.076       | -0.0068   |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2023        | 0.040       | -0.0091   |
| 327267      | 1414 DEGREES LTD | 2024        | 0.067       | -0.0107   |
| 349318      | 29METALS LIMITED | 2021        | 2.740       | 0.4857    |

(c)

asx_prices_tidy |>
  filter(fyear %in% c(2023, 2024)) |>
  group_by(fyear) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE))

| fyear <dbl> | avg_price <dbl> |
|-------------|-----------------|
| 2023        | 2.746548        |
| 2024        | 2.788560        |

(d)

This version is easier because all share prices are stored in one price column and all years are stored in one fyear column. That means we can filter the years we want, then calculate the mean once, rather than referring to separate columns such as price_2023 and price_2024 individually.

If we added many more years of data, this tidy version would still work with the same basic code. We would just change the years inside filter(). In the wide version, we would need to keep adding more year-specific columns to the calculation, which becomes repetitive and harder to manage.

(e)

asx_prices_tidy |>
  filter(eps > -5) |>
  # create a scatterplot with EPS on the x-axis and price on the y-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = eps, y = price)) +
  # add points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  # add a fitted straight line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  # add a title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Share Price vs EPS (2019–2024)",
    x = "Earnings per Share",
    y = "Share Price"
  ) +
  # use a theme
  theme_minimal()

(f)

asx_prices_tidy |>
  filter(eps > -5) |>
  filter(fyear %in% c(2023, 2024)) |>
  # create a scatterplot with EPS on the x-axis and price on the y-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = eps, y = price)) +
  # add points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  # add a fitted straight line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "blue") +
  # add a title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Share Price vs EPS (2023–2024)",
    x = "Earnings per Share",
    y = "Share Price"
  ) +
  # use a theme
  theme_minimal()

(g)

The plot shows that:

  • There is a positive relationship between EPS and share price. In general, firms with higher earnings per share tend to have higher share prices.
  • Firms above the fitted line may have strong growth expectations, valuable intangible assets, or high investor confidence that is not fully captured by current EPS. Firms below the line may reflect lower growth prospects, greater risk, or weaker investor sentiment.
  • Firms with very low or negative EPS do not seem to follow the straight-line pattern as well as the rest of the data. This suggests that a simple straight line may be a rough summary for the middle of the data, but not a perfect description of the full relationship.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Adding P/E Ratios with a Join
docs.text:
(a)

We want to add P/E ratios to our tidy ASX firm-year dataset.

Run the code below to load and prepare the P/E ratio data.

pe_data <-
  read_csv("data/pe.csv") |>
  select(gvkey, fyear, pe) |>
  filter(!is.na(pe)) |>
  arrange(gvkey, fyear)

What variables in pe_data seem to identify each row?

(b)

In asx_tidy, what does one row represent?

Which variable or variables together identify a unique observation in this dataset?

(c)

Which two variables should we use to join asx_tidy and pe_data?

(d)

Why do we need both of these variables in the join?

(e)

Complete the code below to add the pe variable from pe_data to asx_tidy.

asx_with_pe <-
  asx_tidy |>
  left_join(
    pe_data,
    by = YOUR_CODE_HERE
  )

(f)

After the join, what changed in the dataset? In your answer, explain:

  • what new information was added
  • whether the join mainly added rows or columns

(g)

Now suppose we join the two datasets using only gvkey.

Run the code below.

asx_wrong_join <-
  asx_tidy |>
  left_join(
    pe_data,
    by = YOUR_CODE_HERE
  )

What goes wrong here, and why?

Solution

(a)

The variables that seem to identify each row are gvkey and fyear.

That is because each row appears to represent one firm in one year, with pe giving the P/E ratio for that firm-year observation.

(b)

One row in asx_tidy represents one firm in one year.

So the variables that together identify a unique observation are gvkey and fyear.

(c)

The two variables we should use are gvkey and fyear.

(d)

We need both variables because gvkey tells us which firm we are looking at, but it does not tell us which year. Since each firm appears in multiple years, joining only on gvkey would not uniquely identify the correct match. Adding fyear makes the match happen at the firm-year level, which is the correct observational unit in both datasets.

(e)

asx_with_pe <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  left_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey, fyear)
  )

(f)

The join added a new variable, pe, to the dataset.

It mainly added a column rather than rows, because we matched one firm-year observation in asx_tidy to one firm-year observation in pe_data.

(g)

asx_wrong_join <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  left_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey)
  )

This goes wrong because each firm in asx_tidy can now match multiple years in pe_data for the same firm. That creates duplicated rows and incorrect matches across years.

For example, a 2023 observation for one firm could be matched not only to its 2023 P/E ratio, but also to that firm’s 2022 or 2024 P/E ratios. So the join runs, but the resulting dataset is no longer correctly aligned at the firm-year level.

docs.title: Exercise 5: Comparing Industries with Grouped Summaries
docs.text:
(a)

We now want to compare valuation patterns across industries.

To do that, we first need to add industry codes to asx_with_pe.

Complete the code below to join firm_info, which you created in Exercise 2, onto asx_with_pe using gvkey.

asx_analysis <-
  asx_with_pe |>
  YOUR_CODE(
    YOUR_CODE,
    by = YOUR_CODE_HERE
  )

What new information does this join add?

(b)

Using asx_analysis, create a summary dataset called industry_year_summary that does all of the following:

  • groups the data by subindustry and year
  • calculates the average P/E ratio
  • calculates the average share price
  • calculates the average EPS
  • calculates the number of firms in each subindustry-year
industry_year_summary <-
  asx_analysis |>
  YOUR_CODE

(c)

Why do we need to group by both subindustry and year here, rather than just one of them?

(d)

Using industry_year_summary, create a scatterplot that does all of the following:

  • puts average P/E ratio on the x-axis
  • puts average share price on the y-axis
  • shows one point for each subindustry-year observation
  • includes a summary line describing the pattern in the data
  • includes a clear title and axis labels
  • uses a theme
  • only includes subindustries that have at least 3 firms
  • only includes subindustries with average P/E ratios less than 100
industry_year_summary |> 
  YOUR_CODE

(e)

What do you notice in the plot?

In a 2-3 sentences, comment on:

  • whether industry-year observations with higher average P/E ratios also tend to have higher average share prices
  • whether there are any clear clusters or outliers
  • what kinds of industry differences might help explain the pattern

Solution

(a)

asx_analysis <-
  asx_with_pe |>
  left_join(
    firm_info |> select(-conm),
    by = join_by(gvkey)
  )

This join adds firm code information based on gvkey, so the analysis dataset now carries the industry classification needed for grouped summaries.

(b)

industry_year_summary <-
  asx_analysis |>
  # remark adding subind just keeps us the human readable names
  group_by(gsubind, subind, fyear) |>
  summarise(
    avg_pe = mean(pe, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_eps = mean(eps, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_firms = n()
  )

(c)

We need to group by both industry and year because we want each row in the summary dataset to represent one industry in one year. Grouping only by industry would average across all years, and grouping only by year would average across all industries. Using both variables lets us compare industries while still keeping track of time.

(d)

industry_year_summary |>
  filter(n_firms >= 3, avg_pe < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_pe, y = avg_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Share Price vs Average P/E Ratio by Industry-Year",
    x = "Average P/E Ratio",
    y = "Average Share Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

(e)

The plot shows whether industry-year observations with higher average P/E ratios also tend to have higher average share prices, but the relationship is not necessarily very tight.

Some industries may cluster together, while others may stand out as outliers with unusually high average prices or valuation multiples.

Industry differences in growth expectations, profitability, risk, or business model may help explain why some industry-year observations sit in different parts of the plot.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Auditing Missing P/E Ratios Before an Analytics Meeting
docs.text:
Suppose your team is preparing for an analytics meeting. You have built a firm-year dataset with share prices, earnings, and P/E ratios, but many firm-year observations still have missing pe values.

Before moving ahead, you want to understand:

  • what the full dataset looks like
  • what the complete-match dataset looks like
  • which observations are missing P/E
  • what you should ask the data team before continuing

(a)

In Exercise 4, we used a left_join() to add P/E ratios from pe_data to asx_tidy.

What happened to the rows in asx_tidy that did not have a matching P/E ratio in pe_data? Briefly explain what the join did in those cases.

(b) Run the code below, which uses a different kind of join, called inner_join().

asx_with_pe_inner <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  inner_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey, fyear)
  )

How is asx_with_pe_inner different from asx_with_pe? What does inner_join() keep that left_join() does not?

(c)

Run the code below, which uses another kind of join, called anti_join().

missing_pe <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  anti_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey, fyear)
  )

What does missing_pe represent? How is this different from the dataset created with inner_join() in part (b)?

(d)

Compare the number of rows in the following datasets.

nrow(asx_prices_tidy)
nrow(asx_with_pe)
nrow(asx_with_pe_inner)
nrow(missing_pe)

[1] 9484
[1] 9484
[1] 2407
[1] 7077

What do you notice? What does this tell you about how much of the firm-year dataset has valid P/E coverage?

(e)

Look at the observations in missing_pe.

Use code to investigate whether missing P/E ratios seem to be concentrated in certain years or associated with certain EPS values. Write one or two short findings based on what you see.

(f)

The pe_data file was provided to us as a separate dataset.

Why might some firm-year observations in asx_tidy still fail to find a matching P/E ratio in that file, even when price and eps are present?

In your answer, think about possible differences in:

  • which firms were included
  • which years were covered
  • how P/E ratios were defined or filtered before the file was given to us

(g)

Suppose you are preparing for a meeting with the data team before using pe in your analysis.

What are two or three specific questions you would ask to check whether the missing P/E values reflect:

  • a normal feature of the data
  • a difference in firm or year coverage
  • a problem in how the file was sourced or matched

If the missing values seem to come from incomplete firm coverage, what might your team do next to source the missing data?

Solution

(a)

Rows in asx_tidy that did not have a matching P/E ratio in pe_data were still kept in the dataset.

The left_join() added pe where a match was found, and left pe as missing (NA) where no match was found.

(b)

asx_with_pe_inner <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  inner_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey, fyear)
  )

asx_with_pe_inner contains only the firm-year observations that have a match in both asx_tidy and pe_data.

Compared with asx_with_pe, it drops the rows where no matching P/E ratio was found.

So inner_join() keeps only complete matches, while left_join() keeps all rows from asx_tidy whether they match or not.

(c)

missing_pe <-
  asx_prices_tidy |>
  anti_join(
    pe_data,
    by = join_by(gvkey, fyear)
  )

missing_pe contains the firm-year observations in asx_tidy that did not find a match in pe_data.

This is different from the inner_join() result because inner_join() keeps the matched observations, while anti_join() keeps the unmatched ones.

(d)

asx_tidy and asx_with_pe should have the same number of rows, because the left_join() keeps every row from asx_tidy.

asx_with_pe_inner should have fewer rows if some firm-year observations do not have a matching P/E ratio.

missing_pe shows exactly the observations that were left out of the inner join.

Together, these row counts show how much of the firm-year dataset has valid P/E coverage and how much is missing.

(e)

Students’ exact answers will vary, but a good answer would identify one or two patterns in missing_pe.

For example:

  • missing P/E ratios may be concentrated in certain years
  • missing P/E ratios may occur more often when EPS is negative or very close to zero
  • missing P/E rations for certain firms

Illustrative code could include:

missing_pe |>
  count(fyear)

| fyear <dbl> | n <int> |
|-------------|---------|
| 2019        | 1178    |
| 2020        | 1189    |
| 2021        | 1186    |
| 2022        | 1286    |
| 2023        | 1245    |
| 2024        | 993     |

missing_pe |>
  summarise(
    min_eps = min(eps, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_eps = max(eps, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_eps = mean(eps, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

| min_eps <dbl> | max_eps <dbl> | avg_eps <dbl> |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| -2267         | 2.0479        | -0.4205366    |

missing_pe |>
  count(conm) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

| conm <chr>                   | n <int> |
|------------------------------|---------|
| 1414 DEGREES LTD             | 6       |
| 4DS MEMORY LTD               | 6       |
| 5G NETWORKS LIMITED          | 6       |
| 8COMMON LTD                  | 6       |
| ACCELERATE RESOURC           | 6       |
| ...                          | ...     |
| WOODSIDE ENERGY GROUP LTD    | 1       |
| WORLD.NET SERVICES LTD       | 1       |
| XCD ENERGY LTD               | 1       |
| YANCOAL AUSTRALIA LTD        | 1       |
| YOUFOODZ HOLDINGS LTD        | 1       |

(f)

Possible explanations include:

  • The supplied pe_data file may not cover every firm in our ASX dataset.
  • Some firms may appear in asx_tidy but be missing from pe_data for certain years.
  • The P/E file may cover a different time period from the main ASX dataset.
  • P/E ratios may be intentionally omitted when EPS is negative or very close to zero.
  • The data team may have filtered the file before giving it to us, so only a subset of firm-years was included.
  • The two datasets may have been sourced under different rules, even if they use the same identifiers.

(g)

Possible questions for the data team include:

  • Does pe_data cover all firms in our ASX dataset, or only a subset?
  • Are some years intentionally missing from the P/E file?
  • How is P/E defined in this dataset, and are firms with negative or near-zero EPS excluded?
  • Was the P/E file filtered before it was given to us?
  • Should missing P/E values be treated as expected missingness, or as a sign that the match or source file needs to be checked?

If the missing values seem to reflect incomplete firm coverage, the team might:

  • check whether the missing firms can be sourced from the original provider
  • request a broader extract from the data team
  • look for an additional source covering those firms and years
  • decide whether the analysis should be restricted to firms with reliable P/E coverage

docs.title: Tutorial Class 06 Set 01
docs.text:
In [3]: Copied! 
library(tidyverse)
library(ggokabeito)
library(tidyverse) library(ggokabeito) In [4]: Copied! 
# Load the raw files
gdp   <- read_csv("../../../../data/gdp.csv")
urban <- read_csv("../../../../data/urban.csv")
pop   <- read_csv("../../../../data/pop.csv")
codes <- read_csv("../../../../data/country_to_continent.csv")

# Tidy GDP:
# the year is currently stored inside the column names,
# so we reshape to make year a variable
gdp <- gdp |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("gdp_pcap_pp_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "gdp_pcap_pp_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "gdp_pcap_pp"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Tidy urbanisation:
# again, reshape so each row is one country-year
urban <- urban |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("urban"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "urban_pct_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "urban_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Tidy population:
# this can be useful later for bubble size or weighted summaries
pop <- pop |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pop"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "pop_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "pop"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Join the tidied files together.
# After this step, each row should represent one country-year.
analysis_df <- gdp |>
  left_join(
    urban |> select(-name),
    by = join_by(geo, year)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    pop |> select(-name),
    by = join_by(geo, year)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    codes |> select(-country_name),
    by = join_by(geo == iso3)
  )

# Check data coverage by year.
# This helps us see whether some years have much more missing data than others.
analysis_df |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    pct_complete = mean(
      !is.na(gdp_pcap_pp) &
      !is.na(urban_pct) &
      !is.na(pop) &
      !is.na(continent_name)
    ) * 100
  )

# Suppose we decide that coverage is much better from 1960 onward.
# We can then restrict the time window and remove incomplete rows.
analysis_df <- analysis_df |>
  filter(between(year, 1960, 2020)) |>
  drop_na()

# Inspect the final analysis dataset
glimpse(analysis_df)
# Load the raw files gdp <- read_csv("../../../../data/gdp.csv") urban <- read_csv("../../../../data/urban.csv") pop <- read_csv("../../../../data/pop.csv") codes <- read_csv("../../../../data/country_to_continent.csv") # Tidy GDP: # the year is currently stored inside the column names, # so we reshape to make year a variable gdp <- gdp |> pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("gdp_pcap_pp_"), names_to = "year", names_pattern = "gdp_pcap_pp_(\\d{4})$", values_to = "gdp_pcap_pp" ) |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) # Tidy urbanisation: # again, reshape so each row is one country-year urban <- urban |> pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("urban"), names_to = "year", names_pattern = "urban_pct_(\\d{4})$", values_to = "urban_pct" ) |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) # Tidy population: # this can be useful later for bubble size or weighted summaries pop <- pop |> pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("pop"), names_to = "year", names_pattern = "pop_(\\d{4})$", values_to = "pop" ) |> mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) # Join the tidied files together. # After this step, each row should represent one country-year. analysis_df <- gdp |> left_join( urban |> select(-name), by = join_by(geo, year) ) |> left_join( pop |> select(-name), by = join_by(geo, year) ) |> left_join( codes |> select(-country_name), by = join_by(geo == iso3) ) # Check data coverage by year. # This helps us see whether some years have much more missing data than others. analysis_df |> group_by(year) |> summarise( n_rows = n(), pct_complete = mean( !is.na(gdp_pcap_pp) & !is.na(urban_pct) & !is.na(pop) & !is.na(continent_name) ) * 100 ) # Suppose we decide that coverage is much better from 1960 onward. # We can then restrict the time window and remove incomplete rows. analysis_df <- analysis_df |> filter(between(year, 1960, 2020)) |> drop_na() # Inspect the final analysis dataset glimpse(analysis_df)

docs.title: Tutorial Class 06 Set 01 - Using Variation in Data to Tell a Story
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Identify whether a dataset contains cross-sectional, time series, or panel variation
  • Diagnose whether a dataset is tidy and explain how its structure affects analysis
  • Tidy and join multiple country-level datasets to build a usable country-year analysis dataset
  • Formulate and scope a question that can be answered with the available data
  • Create a clear graph or table that helps communicate a relationship in the data
  • Write a short, non-technical brief that explains what the data show and why it matters for policy

docs.title: The Policy Challenge
docs.text:
An international policy think tank is preparing a briefing on how countries change as they develop. Some policymakers are interested in whether rising incomes are closely tied to longer lives. Others want to know whether higher incomes are associated with greater urbanisation and the pressures that come with it, such as demand for housing, transport, and public services.

Your team has been given a set of messy country-level datasets, but the files are spread across multiple tables and are not yet ready for analysis. Your task is to work out what kind of variation the data contain, turn them into a usable dataset, and produce clear evidence that can support a short policy brief.
