library(ggokabeito)

docs.title: Prepare these Exercises before Class
docs.text: Prepare these exercises before coming to class. Plan to spend 40 minutes on these exercises.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Recognising Different Kinds of Data
docs.text:
Data can vary across people, firms, products, places, and time. Before we start working with this week’s datasets, it is useful to step back and think about the kinds of variation different datasets contain.

(a)

Look back at the datasets in the table below from earlier in the course. For each one:

  • classify the dataset as cross-sectional, time series, or panel
  • describe what one row represents
  • identify the cross-sectional unit where relevant
  • identify the time unit where relevant
Dataset Where it appeared in the course Data type What does one row represent? Cross-sectional unit Time unit Cookie Cats Week 2 Lecture Dominick Beer Sales Week 3 Lecture Melbourne Housing Week 4 Tutorial ASX 200 Firm Financials Week 4 Lecture

(b)

In your own words, explain the difference between the following three types of data:

  1. Cross-sectional data
  2. Time series data
  3. Panel data

Solution

(a)

Dataset Where it appeared in the course Data type What does one row represent? Cross-sectional unit Time unit Cookie Cats Week 2 Lecture Cross-sectional One player Player Not applicable Dominick Beer Sales Week 3 Lecture Panel One product in one store in one week Product and store Week Melbourne Housing Week 4 Tutorial Cross-sectional One house listing or sale Property Not applicable ASX 200 Firm Financials Week 4 Lecture Cross-sectional One firm in 2024 Firm Not applicable

The tricky case here is ASX 200 Firm Financials. Even though firms have financial data over time in the real world, the dataset we worked with only contained one year, so the dataset itself is cross-sectional.

(b)

Explanations of the three types of data:

  • Cross-sectional data record many units at one point in time, or with no meaningful time dimension in the dataset. Each row is usually a different person, firm, product, or place.
  • Time series data record one unit repeatedly over time. Each row is usually a different time period, such as a day, month, or year.
  • Panel data record many units repeatedly over time. Each row combines a cross-sectional unit with a time period, such as a firm-year or store-week observation.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Using Variation in Data to Tell a Story
docs.text:
Watch the Gapminder video available here and answer the following questions:

  • What relationship the visualisation is trying to show?
  • What makes the plot effective?
  • What is one thing that could be improved in the plot they use?

Solution

A strong response would identify the main pattern and then comment briefly on design.

For example:

  • The visualisation is trying to show the relationship between income and life expectancy across countries.
  • The plot is effective because it makes the broad pattern easy to see and uses colour to help distinguish different regions of the world.
  • One possible improvement is the use of population for dot size. Very large bubbles can dominate the plot, and differences in area are not always easy to interpret when size is mapped continuously.

Other reasonable answers are possible. The key is that students should identify the relationship, explain why the visual helps communicate it, and suggest an improvement that relates to interpretation rather than just appearance.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Inspecting the Structure of the Data
docs.text:
In class, you will work with several small datasets based on Gapminder-style country data. Before you start working with them, it is useful to inspect how each file is structured.

(a)

Open each of the following files from the data folder:

  • gdp.csv
  • urban.csv
  • pop.csv
  • country_to_continent.csv

For each dataset, complete the table below.

Dataset What does one row represent? Tidy or untidy? What is the main structural issue? gdp.csv urban.csv pop.csv country_to_continent.csv

Hint: When describing the main structural issue, be as specific as you can. For example, think about whether a variable is stored in the column names, or whether values that belong in one column have been spread across many columns.

(b)

Using what you observed in part (a), explain whether gdp.csv, urban.csv, and pop.csv contain cross-sectional variation, time variation, or both.

Then explain how the current layout of the files hides or reveals that structure.

Solution

(a)

Dataset What does one row represent? Tidy or untidy? What is the main structural issue? gdp.csv One country Untidy The year is stored in the column names, so GDP values for different years are spread across many columns. urban.csv One country Untidy The year is stored in the column names, so urbanisation values for different years are spread across many columns. pop.csv One country Untidy The year is stored in the column names, so population values for different years are spread across many columns. country_to_continent.csv One country Tidy No major structural issue. Each row is one country and the variables are already stored in their own columns.

(b)

A strong answer would explain that these files contain both cross-sectional variation and time variation. The data vary across countries, and they also vary across years, so the underlying structure is panel data.

The issue is that this panel structure is not displayed clearly in the current layout. At the moment, the files are untidy because the years are stored in the column names rather than in their own year column. Under tidy data principles, each row should represent one observation, so a tidied version of these files would have one row per country-year.

The first three files are all untidy in a similar way. They will need to be reshaped so that year becomes its own column before they can be joined cleanly.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Proposing a Question
docs.text:
You have now inspected the datasets and thought about the kind of variation they contain.

(a)

Write one question that you think could be answered using the datasets in this week’s data folder. Your question should be specific enough that it could be explored using a table or visualisation.

(b)

For the question you wrote in part (a), answer the following using dot points:

  • Is it descriptive, predictive, or causal?
  • Why does it belong to that category?
  • Which dataset(s) or variable(s) would you need?

(c)

Explain how you would scope the analysis:

  • Which countries or regions might you include?
  • Which years might you include?
  • What kind of variation would you be using: cross-sectional variation, time variation, or both?
  • Why do these choices make sense for your question?

Solution

There are many possible good answers to this question. What matters most is that the proposed question is clear, feasible, and well matched to the available data.

Here is one strong example.

(a)

Propose a question: How does the relationship between GDP per capita and urbanisation differ across continents?

(b)

Classify the question:

  • This is a descriptive question.
  • It is descriptive because it asks us to summarise a relationship in the observed data. It does not try to predict future outcomes or estimate the effect of one variable on another.
  • I would need gdp.csv and urban.csv.
  • I would also use country_to_continent.csv if I wanted to compare patterns across continents.

(c)

Scope the analysis:

  • I would include all countries with available data.
  • I would compare a smaller number of years, such as 1960, 1990, and 2020.
  • I would use both cross-sectional variation and time variation.
  • Cross-sectional variation would let me compare countries and continents, while time variation would let me see how the relationship changes over time.
  • These choices make sense because the question is about broad global patterns rather than a single country or a single year.

Other good examples are possible. For instance, a student might ask how urbanisation changes over time in selected countries, or whether richer countries tend to have higher life expectancy. Those could also work well, as long as the question is specific and the classification is justified clearly.

docs.title: In-Class Exercises
docs.text: You will discuss these exercises in class with your peers in small groups and with your tutor. These exercises build from the exercises you have prepared above, you will get the most value from the class if you have completed those above before coming to class.

docs.title: Exercise 5: Framing Your Group’s Analysis
docs.text:
Your tutor will assign your group one of the following questions:

  • How does life expectancy relate to GDP per capita?
  • How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

As a group, complete the tasks below before you begin wrangling and analysing the data.

(a)

Write down the question your group was allocated.

(b)

Using dot points, answer the following:

  • Is this best treated as a descriptive, predictive, or causal question with the data available in class?
  • Why?

(c)

Using dot points, answer the following:

  • Which countries or regions will you include?
  • Which years will you include?
  • Will you use cross-sectional variation, time variation, or both?
  • Why is this a sensible scope for today’s class?

Solution

There are different reasonable ways to answer this exercise. What matters most is that the group makes a clear and feasible plan before starting the data work.

Here is one strong example for the question How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

(a)

Record your allocated question: How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

(b)

Classify the question:

  • This is best treated as a descriptive question with the data available in class.
  • The goal is to summarise and visualise the relationship between two variables in the observed data.
  • We are not trying to predict future values or estimate the effect of GDP per capita on urbanisation.

(c)

Set the scope:

  • We would include all countries with available data.
  • We would focus on a smaller set of years, such as 1960 to 2025.
  • We would use both cross-sectional variation and time variation.
  • Cross-sectional variation lets us compare countries and regions, while time variation lets us see whether the relationship changes over time.
  • This is a sensible scope for today’s class because it keeps the analysis broad enough to draw conclusions but narrow enough to graph and interpret clearly.

A similarly strong answer for the life expectancy question would also classify it as descriptive and would make a sensible choice about countries, years, and variation.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Build Your Analysis Dataset
docs.text:
Work with your group to build the dataset you need to answer your allocated question. You should decide for yourselves how to prepare the data for analysis.

Hint: Depending on your question, you may need to think about some of the following:

  • which files you need to load
  • whether any datasets need tidying before they can be analysed
  • whether any datasets need to be joined together
  • whether you want to focus on particular countries, regions, or years
  • whether there are missing values that affect the years or observations you can analyse
  • what one row in your final analysis dataset should represent

Hint: Reshaping year columns - Some of the datasets store the year inside the column names rather than in a separate column. In cases like this, pivot_longer() can help you move from a wide format to a tidy format.

For example, if your GDP dataset has columns such as gdp_pcap_pp_1960, gdp_pcap_pp_1961, and so on, you could reshape it like this:

gdp <- gdp |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("gdp_pcap_pp_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "gdp_pcap_pp_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "gdp_pcap_pp"
  )

Here is what each part is doing:

  • cols = starts_with("gdp_pcap_pp_") selects the year columns you want to reshape
  • names_to = "year" creates a new column called year
  • names_pattern = "gdp_pcap_pp_(\\d{4})$" extracts the 4-digit year from the original column names
  • values_to = "gdp_pcap_pp" puts the GDP values into a single column

After this step, the dataset will be much closer to tidy form, where each row can represent one country-year observation.

Solution

There are different valid ways to build the analysis dataset. What matters most is that the final dataset is tidy, joined correctly, and suitable for the group’s question.

Here is one strong example for the question relating urbanisation to GDP per capita.

# Load the raw files
gdp   <- read_csv("out_data/gdp.csv")
urban <- read_csv("out_data/urban.csv")
pop   <- read_csv("out_data/pop.csv")
codes <- read_csv("out_data/country_to_continent.csv")

# Tidy GDP:
# the year is currently stored inside the column names,
# so we reshape to make year a variable
gdp <- gdp |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("gdp_pcap_pp_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "gdp_pcap_pp_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "gdp_pcap_pp"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Tidy urbanisation:
# again, reshape so each row is one country-year
urban <- urban |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("urban"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "urban_pct_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "urban_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Tidy population:
# this can be useful later for bubble size or weighted summaries
pop <- pop |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pop"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_pattern = "pop_(\\d{4})$",
    values_to = "pop"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# Join the tidied files together.
# After this step, each row should represent one country-year.
analysis_df <- gdp |>
  left_join(
    urban |> select(-name),
    by = join_by(geo, year)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    pop |> select(-name),
    by = join_by(geo, year)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    codes |> select(-country_name),
    by = join_by(geo == iso3)
  )

# Check data coverage by year.
# This helps us see whether some years have much more missing data than others.
analysis_df |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    pct_complete = mean(
      !is.na(gdp_pcap_pp) &
      !is.na(urban_pct) &
      !is.na(pop) &
      !is.na(continent_name)
    ) * 100
  )

This is a strong workflow because it does four things clearly:

  1. It reshapes the messy files into tidy form.
  2. It joins them into one country-year dataset.
  3. It checks missingness before moving to analysis.
  4. It makes an explicit filtering decision based on data coverage.

The key missingness lesson here is that dropping missing values should usually come after you inspect where the gaps are. A better workflow is:

  • build the joined dataset
  • check coverage
  • decide on a sensible analysis window
  • then remove incomplete observations if needed

docs.title: Exercise 7: Producing Evidence that Answers Your Question
docs.text:
Using the dataset your group prepared in Exercise 6, produce one or two graphs or tables that help answer your allocated question.

Your output should match the scope your group chose in Exercise 5.

Note: What should a good output make clear? Your graph or table should be clear enough that another group could understand:

  • what variables you are showing
  • what subset of the data you chose to use
  • what pattern or relationship the output is meant to highlight

Note: Presentation reminders: If you create a graph, make sure it has informative axis labels and a clear title. If you create a table, make sure it has clear column names and is easy to interpret.

Solution

There are many possible good answers to this exercise. What matters most is that the graph or table helps answer the group’s question clearly.

Below is one possible solution that continues the example from Exercise 6 for the question How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

One sensible approach is to create:

  1. a graph showing the relationship between GDP per capita and urbanisation for selected years
  2. a table summarising continent-level averages for a few benchmark years

In this case, we would usually prefer the graph because the main question is about the relationship between two variables, and a graph makes that pattern easier to see. That said, if a group is pressed for time, a clear summary table can still be a valid alternative.

# Graph: relationship between GDP per capita and urbanisation
analysis_df |>
  filter(year %in% c(1960, 1990, 2020)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = gdp_pcap_pp / 1e3,
      y = urban_pct,
      size = pop,
      colour = continent_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = gdp_pcap_pp / 1e3, y = urban_pct),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 2),
    linetype = "dashed",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  ggokabeito::scale_color_okabe_ito() +
  scale_size(guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(
    title = "Urbanisation and GDP per capita across countries",
    subtitle = "Selected years: 1960, 1990, and 2020",
    x = "GDP per capita ('000s of USD, 2021 PPP adjusted)",
    y = "Population living in urban areas (%)",
    colour = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Table: continent-level summary for the same benchmark years
table_continent_year <- analysis_df |>
  filter(year %in% c(1960, 1990, 2020)) |>
  group_by(continent_name, year) |>
  summarise(
    avg_gdp_pcap_pp = weighted.mean(gdp_pcap_pp, w = pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_urban_pct   = weighted.mean(urban_pct, w = pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_pop       = sum(pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_countries     = n_distinct(geo),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    avg_gdp_pcap_pp = round(avg_gdp_pcap_pp, 0),
    avg_urban_pct   = round(avg_urban_pct, 1),
    total_pop_m     = round(total_pop / 1e6, 1)
  ) |>
  select(
    continent = continent_name,
    year,
    n_countries,
    total_pop_m,
    avg_gdp_pcap_pp,
    avg_urban_pct
  ) |>
  arrange(continent, year)

table_continent_year |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Continent",
      "Year",
      "Countries",
      "Population (millions)",
      "Avg GDP per capita",
      "Avg urbanisation (%)"
    ),
    caption = "Urbanisation and GDP per capita by continent, 1960, 1990, and 2020"
  )

What makes this a strong answer is that:

  • the outputs match the question being asked
  • the scope is clear and consistent across the graph and table
  • the titles and labels help another group interpret the results
  • the graph is well suited to showing the relationship between two variables
  • the table is a useful fallback or complement when time is short or when a summary by continent is easier to interpret

docs.title: Exercise 8: Writing Up Your Findings
docs.text:
Use one graph or table from Exercise 7 and write a short executive brief for an international policy think tank.

Your brief should explain your group’s question, summarise the main pattern you found, and explain why it matters.

Instructions:

  • Length: about 400 words
  • Exhibit: 1 table or figure
  • Write for a non-technical audience
  • Use full sentences in dot points
  • Do not include code
  • Do not do any new analysis in this section. Use the evidence you already produced.
  • For writing style, refer to the “Write Like an Amazonian” document on Canvas.

Use the format below:

  1. Executive Summary: Write 3 to 4 sentences summarising the question, the main finding, and why it matters.

  2. Key Insights: Write up to 3 dot points explaining what the data show.

  3. Policy Implications: Write up to 3 dot points explaining why the findings matter for policymakers or policy organisations.

  4. Recommended Actions: Write up to 3 dot points suggesting clear next steps or actions.

Solution

There are many possible good responses to this exercise. What matters most is that the brief is clear, selective, and grounded in the evidence the group has already produced.

Below is one possible solution based on the question How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita? and a graph comparing countries in 1960, 1990, and 2020.

  1. Executive Summary: Across all years shown, countries with higher GDP per capita tend to have higher urbanisation rates. The relationship is clearly positive but nonlinear, and it appears to flatten somewhat in later decades as many countries reach already-high levels of urbanisation. Over time, the distribution shifts toward higher income and higher urbanisation, but substantial cross-country differences remain. For policymakers, this suggests that economic development and urban transition move together, though income alone is not enough to explain urbanisation patterns.

  2. Key Insights

    • In every benchmark year, countries with higher GDP per capita tend to be more urbanised.
    • The relationship appears curved rather than linear, and seems somewhat flatter in later decades.
    • Countries with similar income levels can still show quite different urbanisation rates, especially at low and middle income levels.

  3. Policy Implications

    • Policymakers should expect urban growth pressures to intensify as countries move through earlier and middle stages of economic development.
    • At higher income levels, further economic growth may be associated with smaller increases in urbanisation because many countries are already highly urbanised.
    • Because countries at similar income levels can still show different urbanisation patterns, policy design should be sensitive to local context rather than based on income alone.

  4. Recommended Actions

    • Use country-level urbanisation and income data together to identify where infrastructure demand is likely to rise most quickly.
    • Benchmark countries against peers at similar income levels to identify unusually fast or slow urban transition.
    • Use broad descriptive patterns like these as a starting point, then follow up with more detailed country-specific analysis before making major policy decisions.

This is only one possible solution. A strong response for the life expectancy question, or a response using a table rather than a graph, could also work well as long as it stays clear, concise, and faithful to the evidence.

docs.title: Tutorial Class 07 Set 01 - Descriptive Analytics in HRM
Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

  • Explain why employee attrition matters as a business analytics problem and why segmentation can help an analytics team explore different attrition profiles.
  • Construct a simple rule-of-thumb employee segmentation using fixed thresholds and interpret attrition patterns across the resulting groups.
  • Explain what K-means clustering is trying to achieve and compare its strengths and limitations with a hand-built rule-of-thumb segmentation.
  • Prepare numeric variables for K-means clustering by selecting, scaling, and checking a preprocessing workflow in R.
  • Implement and interpret K-means clustering models using both a simple two-variable setup and a richer five-variable employee profile.
  • Evaluate a defensible choice of the number of clusters using the elbow method and justify that choice in words.
  • Communicate segmentation results in a short analytics team memo, including the main patterns, implications, and limitations of the analysis.

docs.title: The Topic: Why are employees leaving, and can segmentation help us understand different attrition profiles?
docs.text:
Every time an employee leaves, companies incur real costs through recruitment, training, disruption to teams, and lost experience. For an HR analytics team, an important first step is to understand whether different types of employees show different patterns of attrition.

In this tutorial, we use segmentation to explore that question. We begin with a simple rule-of-thumb grouping based on a small number of variables, and then compare it to K-means clustering, a more data-driven way of grouping employees with similar characteristics. This helps us move beyond one-off cases and identify broader employee profiles, which is a common task in descriptive analytics.

Our goal is not to build a formal prediction model or identify the causes of attrition. Instead, the goal is to explore whether different segmentation approaches reveal useful patterns that an analytics team could investigate further.

docs.title: The Data: HR Analytics Data
docs.text:
We will work with an anonymised dataset from a company’s HR department. It contains information on 1,470 employees, including:

  • Personal characteristics: age, gender, marital_status, distance_from_home
  • Job-related features: job_satisfaction, monthly_income, years_at_company, department
  • Outcome: attrition – whether the employee has left the company

This gives us a useful set of variables for exploring whether different employee groups differ in meaningful ways.

docs.title: The Method: Rule-of-Thumb and K-Means Segmentation
docs.text:
Our goal is to segment employees into groups with similar profiles and examine whether attrition differs across those groups. To do this, we will:

  1. create a simple rule-of-thumb segmentation using two variables
  2. compare it to K-means clustering on those same variables
  3. build a richer K-means model using five scaled numeric variables
  4. use the elbow method to help choose a reasonable number of clusters
  5. interpret the resulting clusters using their average characteristics and attrition rates

This allows us to compare a simple hand-built segmentation to a richer data-driven one, and to ask whether the more flexible approach produces more useful insight.

docs.text:

library(janitor)    # cleaning column names
library(recipes)    # For data preprocessing
library(cluster)    # clustering
library(factoextra) # k-means visualization and cluster evaluation
library(broom)      # tidy output of clustering results

Let’s load the data that we will use today:

df <-
  read_csv("data/hr_attrition.csv") |> 
  # tidy up column names to snake_case 
  clean_names()

docs.title: Prepare these Exercises before Class
docs.text: Prepare these exercises before coming to class. Plan to spend 30 minutes on these exercises.

docs.title: Exercise 1: The What and Why of employee attrition
docs.text:
Employee attrition refers to people leaving the company — either voluntarily (resignation) or involuntarily (termination). While some turnover is normal, high attrition can signal deeper issues.

(a)

What kinds of consequences might high attrition have for a business?

(b)

What might cause employees to leave?

(c)

Why might an analytics team want to group employees into segments when studying attrition, rather than looking only at employees one by one?

Solution

(a)

What kinds of consequences might high attrition have for a business?

  • Increased costs: Hiring and training new employees takes time and money.
  • Loss of knowledge: Experienced employees may take valuable firm-specific knowledge with them.
  • Disruption to teams: Turnover can interrupt workflows and reduce team stability.
  • Reduced productivity: New hires may need time to become fully effective.
  • Morale and reputation effects: High attrition can lower morale and may signal a poor work environment.

(b)

What are some possible reasons employees might leave?

  • Job dissatisfaction: Employees may be unhappy with their role, workload, manager, or workplace culture.
  • Limited growth opportunities: Some employees may leave if they feel stuck or underutilized.
  • Compensation and benefits: Employees may move for better pay or conditions elsewhere.
  • Commute or location issues: Long travel times may make a job less sustainable.
  • Personal reasons: Family needs, health, or career changes may also matter.

(c)

Why might an analytics team want to group employees into segments when studying attrition, rather than looking only at employees one by one?

  • Pattern finding: Segments can reveal broader employee profiles with different attrition patterns.
  • Clearer interpretation: Grouping can make it easier to describe which types of employees are more likely to leave.
  • Better actionability: Firms may be able to design different retention responses for different employee groups.
  • Descriptive insight before prediction: Segmentation helps analysts understand the structure of the workforce before moving to more formal predictive tools.

docs.title: Exercise 2: A Simple Rule-of-Thumb Employee Segmentation
docs.text:
Suppose your analytics team wants to create a quick first-pass classification of employees using two variables:

  • job_satisfaction
  • distance_from_home

For this exercise, define:

  • lower satisfaction as a score below 2
  • longer commute as living 10 km or more from work

This gives four possible employee groups:

  • Higher satisfaction, shorter commute
  • Higher satisfaction, longer commute
  • Lower satisfaction, shorter commute
  • Lower satisfaction, longer commute

(a)

Why might an analytics team begin with a simple rule-of-thumb segmentation before trying a more data-driven method?

(b)

Complete the code below to classify each employee into one of the four segments.

df_rule <- 
  df |>
  mutate(
    rule_segment = case_when(
      YOUR_CONDITION ~ "Higher satisfaction, shorter commute",
      YOUR_CONDITION ~ "Higher satisfaction, longer commute",
      YOUR_CONDITION ~ "Lower satisfaction, shorter commute",
      .default = "Lower satisfaction, longer commute"
    )
  )

(c)

For each segment, calculate:

  • the number of employees
  • the attrition rate
# Write your answer here

(d)

Which segment or segments appear to have the highest attrition?

(e)

What are the advantages of this rule-of-thumb approach for an analytics team? What kinds of patterns might it fail to capture?

Solution

(a)

Why might an analytics team begin with a simple rule-of-thumb segmentation before trying a more data-driven method?

  • Easy to understand: Simple rules are transparent and easy to explain to others.
  • Fast to implement: Analysts can create an initial segmentation quickly.
  • Useful benchmark: A hand-built rule gives a baseline that can later be compared to more data-driven methods.
  • Business intuition: The chosen variables may reflect concerns that managers already care about.

(b)

Complete the code below to classify each employee into one of the four segments.

df_rule <- 
  df |>
  mutate(
    rule_segment = case_when(
      job_satisfaction >= 2 & distance_from_home < 10 ~ "Higher satisfaction, shorter commute",
      job_satisfaction >= 2 & distance_from_home >= 10 ~ "Higher satisfaction, longer commute",
      job_satisfaction < 2 & distance_from_home < 10 ~ "Lower satisfaction, shorter commute",
      .default = "Lower satisfaction, longer commute"
    )
  )

(c)

For each segment, calculate the number of employees and the attrition rate.

df_rule |>
  group_by(rule_segment) |>
  summarise(
    n_employees = n(),
    attrition_rate = mean(attrition == "Yes")
  )

| rule_segment <chr>                   | n_employees <int> | attrition_rate <dbl> |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Higher satisfaction, longer commute  | 426               | 0.1784038            |
| Higher satisfaction, shorter commute | 755               | 0.1258278            |
| Lower satisfaction, longer commute   | 104               | 0.2692308            |
| Lower satisfaction, shorter commute  | 185               | 0.2054054            |

(d)

Which segment or segments appear to have the highest attrition?

A strong answer should identify the segment or segments with the highest attrition rate based on the summary table, rather than relying on counts alone.

(e)

What are the advantages of this rule-of-thumb approach for an analytics team? What kinds of patterns might it fail to capture?

  • Advantages: The approach is simple, transparent, quick to implement, and easy to communicate.
  • What it might miss: It depends heavily on the chosen thresholds, may ignore more subtle combinations of variables, and may fail to capture patterns that are not well described by simple cutoffs.
  • Big picture: This is useful as a first-pass segmentation, but it may be cruder than a more data-driven clustering approach.

docs.title: Exercise 3: What Is K-Means Clustering?
docs.text:
In Exercise 2, you created a simple rule-of-thumb segmentation by assigning employees to groups using fixed cutoffs.

In later exercises, you will explore a different approach called K-means clustering.

(a)

Explain in your own words what K-means clustering is trying to achieve.

(b)

Explain how K-means clustering differs from the rule-of-thumb segmentation you created in Exercise 2.

(c)

What is one advantage of using a rule-of-thumb segmentation instead of K-means clustering?

(d)

What is one advantage of using K-means clustering instead of a rule-of-thumb segmentation?

(e)

In K-means clustering, which parts of the analysis are chosen by the analyst, and which parts are carried out automatically by the algorithm?

(f)

Suppose an analytics team wants to use K-means clustering with variables such as job_satisfaction, distance_from_home, and monthly_income. Explain why it is important that these variables are numeric.

(g)

Explain why it is usually important to scale variables before running K-means clustering.

Solution

(a)

Explain in your own words what K-means clustering is trying to achieve.

K-means clustering divides observations into a chosen number of groups so that observations within the same group are similar to one another, while observations in different groups are less similar.

For the analytically inclined: A more detailed explanation is that K-means begins with a chosen number of cluster centres, called centroids. Each observation is assigned to the nearest centroid. The centroid of each cluster is then recalculated, and the process repeats until the assignments become stable.

(b)

Explain how K-means clustering differs from the rule-of-thumb segmentation you created in Exercise 2.

Rule-of-thumb segmentation uses fixed cutoffs chosen by the analyst in advance. K-means clustering does not require the analyst to define the groups directly. Instead, it forms groups based on similarity in the data using the variables provided.

(c)

What is one advantage of using a rule-of-thumb segmentation instead of K-means clustering?

A rule-of-thumb segmentation is easy to understand, explain, and communicate. Because the grouping rule is explicit, it is often easier to justify to non-technical audiences.

(d)

What is one advantage of using K-means clustering instead of a rule-of-thumb segmentation?

K-means clustering can uncover patterns in the data that a simple hand-built rule may miss. It allows the grouping to be shaped by similarity across the variables rather than by fixed analyst-chosen cutoffs alone.

(e)

In K-means clustering, which parts of the analysis are chosen by the analyst, and which parts are carried out automatically by the algorithm?

The analyst chooses which variables to include, how the data are prepared, and the number of clusters k. The algorithm then uses those inputs to assign observations to clusters and update the cluster centres until the grouping becomes stable.

(f)

Suppose an analytics team wants to use K-means clustering with variables such as job_satisfaction, distance_from_home, and monthly_income. Explain why it is important that these variables are numeric.

K-means clustering works by comparing observations using numerical distance. To calculate how close or far apart two employees are, the method needs each observation to be represented as numbers. Numeric variables can be placed in a numerical feature space, which allows the algorithm to measure similarity across employees.

If a variable is stored as text or as a category label, K-means cannot directly interpret the difference between its values as numerical distance. That is why K-means is typically used with numeric variables, or with categorical variables that have first been converted into a suitable numeric form.

(g)

Explain why it is usually important to scale variables before running K-means clustering.

Scaling is important because K-means is distance-based. If one variable has a much larger numerical range than another, it can dominate the distance calculation even if it is not conceptually more important. For example, monthly_income may vary by thousands of dollars, while job_satisfaction may vary only between 1 and 4.

Scaling puts variables onto a more comparable footing, so the clustering is driven more by relative patterns across variables rather than by whichever variable happens to be measured on the biggest scale.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Preparing the Data for K-Means Clustering
docs.text:
In the remaining exercises, we will use the following five numeric variables to build and compare K-means clustering models:

  • job_satisfaction
  • monthly_income
  • years_at_company
  • distance_from_home
  • age

In this exercise, we prepare these five variables for the clustering analysis that follows.

(a)

Create a dataset that contains the five variables listed above.

df_kmeans <- 
  df |>
  select(
    job_satisfaction,
    monthly_income,
    years_at_company,
    YOUR_CODE,
    YOUR_CODE
  )

(b)

Complete the code below to create a recipe for df_kmeans and add a step that normalises all numeric predictors.

rec <- 
  YOUR_CODE(~ ., data = df_kmeans) |>
  YOUR_CODE(all_numeric_predictors())

(c)

Explain what the code in part (b) is doing.

(d)

Complete the code below to implement the preprocessing steps from the recipe in part (b) and apply them to the data.

df_scaled <- 
  rec |>
  YOUR_CODE() |>
  YOUR_CODE(new_data = NULL)

(e)

Explain what the two functions you used in part (d) are doing.

(f)

Run the code below to verify that the preprocessing achieves the desired result. What do you notice about the means and standard deviations?

df_scaled |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd)
    )
  )

Solution

(a)

The code below creates a smaller dataset containing only the five variables we will use. Complete the select() step.

df_kmeans <- 
  df |>
  select(
    job_satisfaction,
    monthly_income,
    years_at_company,
    distance_from_home,
    age
  )

(b)

Complete the code below to create a recipe for df_kmeans and add a step that normalises all numeric predictors.

rec <- 
  recipe(~ ., data = df_kmeans) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

(c)

Explain in plain language what the code in part (b) is doing.

This code creates a preprocessing plan for the variables in df_kmeans and adds a step that will normalise all numeric predictors so they are on a comparable scale.

(d)

Complete the code below to implement the preprocessing steps from the recipe in part (b) and apply them to the data.

df_scaled <- 
  rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

(e)

Explain in plain language what the two functions you used in part (d) are doing.

prep() works out what is needed to carry out the preprocessing steps in the recipe. In this case, it calculates the information needed to normalise each variable. bake(new_data = NULL) then applies those prepared steps to the data and returns the processed dataset.

(f)

Run the code below to verify that the preprocessing achieves the desired result. What do you notice about the means and standard deviations?

The means are now close to 0 and the standard deviations are close to 1 for each variable. This indicates that the variables have been normalised successfully.

docs.title: Exercise 5: Comparing Rule-of-Thumb Segmentation to K-Means
docs.text:
In Exercise 2, you created four employee groups using simple rules based on job_satisfaction and distance_from_home.

Now we will use K-means clustering on those same two variables and compare the result.

(a)

Create a new dataset called df_scaled_small that keeps only the scaled versions of:

  • job_satisfaction
  • distance_from_home

from df_scaled.

df_scaled_small <-
  df_scaled |>
  select(YOUR_CODE, YOUR_CODE)

(b)

Run K-means clustering on df_scaled_small using 4 clusters.

set.seed(123)

kmeans_small <-
  kmeans(
    YOUR_CODE,
    centers = YOUR_CODE,
    nstart = 10
  )

(c)

Use the code below to visualise the clustering result.

fviz_cluster(
  kmeans_small,
  data = df_scaled_small,
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
  main = "2-variable K-means clustering"
)

(d)

What do you notice about the shape of the clusters? Do they look very different from the rule-of-thumb groups in Exercise 2?

(e)

The code below combines the original employee data with the K-means cluster assignments.

Using df_compare, calculate the number of employees and the attrition rate in each cluster.

df_compare <-
  df |>
  select(attrition, job_satisfaction, distance_from_home) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(kmeans_small$cluster))

df_compare |>
  YOUR_CODE_HERE

(f) Compared with the rule-of-thumb segmentation, did K-means appear to add much in this two-variable setting? Explain briefly.

Solution

(a)

Create a new dataset called df_scaled_small that keeps only the scaled versions of job_satisfaction and distance_from_home from df_scaled.

df_scaled_small <-
  df_scaled |>
  select(job_satisfaction, distance_from_home)

(b)

Run K-means clustering on df_scaled_small using 4 clusters.

set.seed(123)

kmeans_small <-
  kmeans(
    df_scaled_small,
    centers = 4,
    nstart = 10
  )

(c)

Use the code below to visualise the clustering result.

fviz_cluster(
  kmeans_small,
  data = df_scaled_small,
  geom = "point",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
  main = "2-variable K-means clustering"
)

(d)

What do you notice about the shape of the clusters? Do they look very different from the rule-of-thumb groups in Exercise 2?

A strong answer should note that the clusters may look fairly similar to the earlier four-group rule-based segmentation. In a simple two-variable setting, K-means may not add dramatically different structure.

(e)

Using df_compare, calculate the number of employees and the attrition rate in each cluster.

df_compare <-
  df |>
  select(attrition, job_satisfaction, distance_from_home) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(kmeans_small$cluster))

df_compare |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n_employees    = n(),
    attrition_rate = mean(attrition == "Yes"),
    job_sat        = mean(job_satisfaction),
    distance       = mean(distance_from_home)
  )

| cluster <fct> | n_employees <int> | attrition_rate <dbl> | job_sat <dbl> | distance <dbl> |
|---------------|-------------------|----------------------|---------------|----------------|
| 1             | 415               | 0.1710843            | 1.496386      | 4.884337       |
| 2             | 154               | 0.2662338            | 1.480519      | 20.636364      |
| 3             | 234               | 0.1709402            | 3.495726      | 21.431624      |
| 4             | 667               | 0.1274363            | 3.514243      | 4.937031       |

(f)

Compared with the rule-of-thumb segmentation, did K-means appear to add much in this two-variable setting? Explain briefly.

The four clusters line up closely with the four combinations of lower versus higher job satisfaction and shorter versus longer commute distance. For example, clusters 1 and 2 both have lower average job satisfaction, while clusters 3 and 4 both have higher average job satisfaction. Clusters 2 and 3 both have longer average commute distances, while clusters 1 and 4 have shorter average commute distances.

The attrition rates also follow a familiar pattern. The highest attrition appears in the cluster with lower satisfaction and longer commute (cluster 2), while the lowest attrition appears in the cluster with higher satisfaction and shorter commute (cluster 4). The other two clusters sit in between. This suggests that in a two-variable setting, K-means may not add dramatically different insight beyond what a transparent rule-of-thumb segmentation already captured.

That does not mean K-means is useless. Rather, it shows that when the structure is simple and the variables are few, a hand-built segmentation can already do a reasonable job of describing the main pattern in the data.

docs.title: Exercise 6: Building a Richer K-Means Model
docs.text:
Your analytics team now wants to build a richer clustering model using all five scaled variables in df_scaled:

  • job_satisfaction
  • monthly_income
  • years_at_company
  • distance_from_home
  • age

One challenge remains: we still need to choose a value for k, the number of clusters.

A colleague suggests using the elbow method as a starting point.

(a)

Explain what the elbow method is trying to do.

(b)

Run the code below to create an elbow plot for K-means clustering on df_scaled.

fviz_nbclust(
  df_scaled,
  kmeans,
  method = "wss",
  k.max = 10,
  nstart = 10
)

(c)

Based on the elbow plot, what value of k would you choose? Briefly explain your answer.

(d)

Run K-means clustering on df_scaled using your chosen value of k.

set.seed(123)

kmeans_full <-
  kmeans(
    YOUR_CODE,
    centers = YOUR_CODE,
    nstart = 10
  )

(e)

Use the code below to visualise the clustering result.

fviz_cluster(
  kmeans_full,
  geom = "point",
  data = df_scaled,
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
  main = "5-variable K-means clustering"
)

(f)

What can the plot in (e) tell you about the clustering result? What can it not tell you on its own?

(g)

The code below combines the original employee data with the cluster assignments from your 5-variable K-means model.

Using df_compare_full, calculate:

  • the number of employees in each cluster
  • the attrition rate in each cluster
  • the average value of each clustering variable in each cluster
df_compare_full <-
  df |>
  select(
    attrition,
    job_satisfaction,
    monthly_income,
    years_at_company,
    distance_from_home,
    age
  ) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(kmeans_full$cluster))

df_compare_full |>
  YOUR_CODE_HERE

Solution

(a)

A colleague suggests using the elbow method. Explain what the elbow method is trying to do.

The elbow method helps analysts choose a reasonable number of clusters by plotting how within-cluster variation changes as k increases. As more clusters are added, this variation will always fall, but after a certain point the improvement becomes much smaller. The analyst then looks for the “elbow” in the plot, where adding another cluster no longer gives a large reduction in within-cluster variation.

(b)

Run the code below to create an elbow plot for K-means clustering on df_scaled.

fviz_nbclust(
  df_scaled,
  kmeans,
  method = "wss",
  k.max = 10,
  nstart = 10
)

(c)

Based on the elbow plot, what value of k would you choose? Briefly explain your answer.

A strong answer should choose a defensible value of k and justify it using the shape of the elbow plot. The key idea is that improvements become smaller after a certain point, even if the elbow is not perfectly sharp. We went with k = 4

(d)

Run K-means clustering on df_scaled using your chosen value of k.

set.seed(123)

kmeans_full <-
  kmeans(
    df_scaled,
    centers = 4,
    nstart = 10
  )

(e)

Use the code below to visualise the clustering result.

Students should produce the cluster plot and use it as one input into interpretation, alongside the cluster summaries.

fviz_cluster(
  kmeans_full,
  data = df_scaled,
  geom = "point",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
  main = "5-variable K-means clustering"
)

(f)

What can this plot tell you about the clustering result? What can it not tell you on its own?

The plot can give a broad sense of whether clusters appear reasonably separated, but it cannot fully describe the cluster profiles in a five-variable setting. For that, we still need summary statistics for each cluster.

(g)

Using df_compare_full, calculate the number of employees in each cluster, the attrition rate in each cluster, and the average value of each clustering variable in each cluster.

Follow the same logic as in Exercise 5, using group_by(cluster) and summarise() to calculate cluster sizes, attrition rates, and means for the five variables.

df_compare_full <-
  df |>
  select(
    attrition,
    job_satisfaction,
    monthly_income,
    years_at_company,
    distance_from_home,
    age
  ) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(kmeans_full$cluster))

df_compare_full |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n_employees    = n(),
    attrition_rate = mean(attrition == "Yes"),
    job_sat        = mean(job_satisfaction),
    income         = mean(monthly_income),
    years          = mean(years_at_company),
    distance       = mean(distance_from_home),
    age            = mean(age)
  )

docs.title: Exercise 7: Communicating Your Results in an Analytics Team Memo
docs.text:
You have now explored three ways to segment employees:

  • a simple rule-of-thumb segmentation
  • a 2-variable K-means model
  • a richer 5-variable K-means model

Your task is to write a short memo for an analytics team meeting. The goal is to help the team decide which approach produced the most useful insight into employee attrition patterns.

Writing Hints

  • Use the “Write Like an Amazonian” tips to guide your writing.
  • A strong memo should compare the approaches, not just describe the final one.
  • Focus on the analytical takeaway: what did each method reveal, and what did the richer model add?
  • Keep the writing clear and direct. Do not simply restate the code you ran.

Suggested Memo Structure - Use the outline below and provide 2–3 bullet points under each subheading.

  • Problem Statement (1 short paragraph summarising why the team is segmenting employees and what business problem this analysis is trying to address)

  • Approaches Compared

    • Briefly describe the three segmentation approaches you explored
    • Note one strength or weakness of each approach

  • Recommended Approach

    • Which approach would you recommend the team use as a starting point?
    • Why?

  • Key Employee Segments or Patterns

    • What were the most important patterns in attrition risk?
    • Did different approaches highlight different kinds of employee groups?

  • Proposed Implications

    • What might these results imply for how the firm thinks about retention risk?
    • Do different employee segments suggest different kinds of follow-up or intervention?

  • Limitations & Next Steps

    • What are the main limitations of the analysis?
    • What would you want the team to do next?

Solution - Illustrative answer only. This is not the only defensible memo.

  • Problem Statement The analytics team wants to understand whether different types of employees show different attrition patterns. Segmenting employees can help the firm move beyond one-off cases and identify broader risk profiles that may be useful for workforce planning and retention strategy.

  • Approaches Compared

    • The rule-of-thumb segmentation was simple and easy to explain, but it depended heavily on analyst-chosen cutoffs.
    • The 2-variable K-means model produced a result that looked quite similar to the rule-based grouping, suggesting that in a simple two-variable setting K-means may not add much new insight.
    • The 5-variable K-means model used a richer employee profile and appeared to uncover more informative differences across employee groups.

  • Recommended Approach

    • The 5-variable K-means model is the most useful starting point for the analytics team.
    • It captures a broader employee profile than the simpler methods and appears to reveal more than one higher-attrition segment.
    • The simpler approaches remain useful as transparent benchmarks, but they are less informative than the richer clustering model.

  • Key Employee Segments or Patterns

    • One higher-risk cluster appears to be characterised by low job satisfaction and relatively low income.
    • Another higher-risk cluster appears to be characterised by a much longer commute, even though job satisfaction is not especially low.
    • A more stable cluster appears older, higher-income, and longer-tenured, with substantially lower attrition.

  • Proposed Implications

    • The results suggest that the firm should not think about attrition risk as coming from a single type of employee.
    • Different employee segments may require different kinds of follow-up. For example, one group may point toward dissatisfaction and compensation concerns, while another may point toward commute burden and work-location issues.
    • The richer segmentation may therefore be more useful for targeting further analysis and designing more tailored retention responses.

  • Limitations & Next Steps

    • This analysis is descriptive, so the clusters do not show that these characteristics cause attrition.
    • Test whether these segments remain stable over time and examine whether targeted retention strategies differ across the higher-risk groups.
